Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen, usually arising in ventricular myocardium. The collagen-rich appearance of the supplied histology makes this a leading consideration.

Cardiac hemangioma.description: A benign tumor of blood vessels that can develop in any cardiac chamber or within myocardium. Some lesions contain substantial fibrous tissue.

Left ventricular myxoma.description: A benign cardiac tumor composed of myxoma cells in a gelatinous extracellular matrix. Most arise in the left atrium, but ventricular tumors occasionally occur.

Hamartoma of mature cardiac myocytes.description: A rare benign, tumor-like proliferation of mature cardiac muscle cells, often accompanied by fibrosis and abnormal vascular structures.

Organized left ventricular thrombus.description: A blood clot within the left ventricle that can become fibrotic and resemble a tumor. It usually develops with impaired ventricular contraction, myocardial infarction, or an apical aneurysm.

Infected intralobar pulmonary sequestrat.description: A congenital region of abnormal lung within the normal pleural covering that receives blood from a systemic artery, usually the aorta. The left basal lesion and apparent aortic feeding vessel make pulmonary sequestration a leading possibility, although the subtype cannot be established confidently from these images alone.

Inflamed or infected extralobar pulmonar.normalized_text: Inflamed or infected extralobar pulmonary sequestration
Inflamed or infected extralobar pulmonar.description: A congenital mass of nonfunctioning lung with its own pleural covering and systemic arterial supply. It often lies near the left diaphragm and can cause abdominal or pleuritic pain when inflamed, infected, or complicated by torsion.

Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragm.normalized_text: Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragmatic pleurisy
Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragm.description: An infection of the lower left lung that can irritate the diaphragm and present predominantly as upper abdominal pain in children.

Infected congenital pulmonary airway mal.description: A congenital abnormality of lung development containing malformed airways or cysts that may first become symptomatic during childhood infection. A hybrid lesion can also have the systemic arterial supply of a sequestration.

Left lower lobe lung abscess.description: A localized collection of pus caused by necrotizing lung infection, potentially developing within abnormal congenital lung tissue.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: A hepatic infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, sometimes presenting months or years after exposure in an endemic region. The CT shows hypodense hepatic lesions compatible with abscesses, although imaging alone cannot establish their cause.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing one or more pus-filled cavities in the liver, usually arising from biliary infection, intra-abdominal infection, or bloodstream spread.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscesses.description: An infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from contaminated soil or water in endemic areas, including northern Australia and Southeast Asia. It can produce multiple visceral abscesses.

Secondarily infected hepatic hydatid cys.description: A liver cyst caused by Echinococcus infection that develops secondary bacterial infection. Exposure may occur in sheep-raising regions, including parts of Australia, but cysts generally develop over a prolonged period.

Hepatic tuberculosis with tuberculous ab.description: An uncommon extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis that can cause focal hepatic lesions or abscesses. Confirmation generally requires tissue sampling and mycobacterial testing.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease causing steadily progressive neurological disability, often dominated by spinal cord dysfunction. This is a leading consideration, but the available findings alone do not establish diagnostic criteria.

OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: An inherited mitochondrial disorder causing optic atrophy, sometimes accompanied by neurological manifestations such as spastic paraplegia, peripheral neuropathy or ataxia.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with an MS-like syndrome (Harding disease)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.description: A mitochondrial optic neuropathy that can coexist with an inflammatory demyelinating syndrome resembling multiple sclerosis, particularly in women.

Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegi.normalized_text: Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy
Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegi.description: A group of inherited disorders causing progressive corticospinal tract dysfunction, with some subtypes also producing optic atrophy, sensory abnormalities and other neurological features.

Aquaporin-4-seronegative neuromyelitis o.description: An inflammatory disorder primarily affecting the optic nerves and spinal cord. Seronegative disease is possible, but stricter clinical and imaging criteria are required.

Wilson disease.description: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport causing hepatic, neurological, and ocular copper accumulation. The homozygous pathogenic ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) variant establishes this as the leading diagnosis; the ocular and brain findings provide additional support.

Herbal medicine-induced liver injury.description: Liver injury caused by toxic or idiosyncratic reactions to herbal products, sometimes producing cholestasis and impaired hepatic synthetic function. It could coexist with Wilson disease but does not explain the genetic findings.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that can occur in adolescent girls and cause chronic hepatitis, fibrosis, jaundice, and coagulopathy. It is a substantially less likely alternative given the diagnostic ATP7B finding.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the bile ducts that can occur in children and cause cholestatic liver disease. Confirmation requires biliary evaluation, and it does not account for the Wilson-specific findings.

Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.description: A group of inherited bile-transport disorders causing persistent cholestasis, often with severe itching and progressive liver fibrosis. Some forms present in adolescence, although the supplied ATP7B result instead supports Wilson disease.

Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome.description: A drug-triggered acute neutrophilic dermatosis causing fever and tender red plaques or nodules. The timing after azathioprine initiation and neutrophilic leukocytosis make this a leading possibility; skin biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An idiosyncratic systemic reaction to azathioprine, often developing within the first few weeks and producing fever, malaise, rash, and joint pain. It can overlap with drug-induced Sweet syndrome.

Serum sickness-like reaction to azathiop.description: A medication-associated inflammatory reaction characterized by fever, rash, and polyarthralgia, usually appearing one to two weeks after exposure. Unlike classic serum sickness, renal involvement is generally absent.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat causing tender red nodules, usually on the shins, sometimes triggered by medications, infections, or systemic inflammatory disease.

Drug-induced cutaneous small-vessel vasc.description: Inflammation of small skin vessels, potentially triggered by azathioprine, causing painful purpuric lesions and sometimes fever or joint pain. Skin biopsy can distinguish it from neutrophilic dermatoses.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the space behind the pharynx following neck trauma. This is the leading consideration given the marked prevertebral soft-tissue expansion on the supplied CT image and posterior pharyngeal swelling. Progressive expansion can cause life-threatening airway obstruction.

Blunt laryngeal injury with possible lar.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal injury with possible laryngeal cartilage fracture
Blunt laryngeal injury with possible lar.description: Trauma to the larynx can cause cartilage fractures, mucosal injury, and hematoma or edema, producing voice changes and potentially obstructing the airway. A fracture is not established by the supplied image.

Cervical ligamentous injury with associa.normalized_text: Cervical ligamentous injury with associated prevertebral hematoma
Cervical ligamentous injury with associa.description: A fall can injure cervical ligaments, particularly through hyperextension, causing bleeding anterior to the spine even without an obvious fracture. CT soft-tissue swelling may suggest this possibility, but MRI is generally needed to assess ligament integrity.

Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.normalized_text: Traumatic cervical vascular injury with expanding neck hematoma
Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.description: Injury to a cervical artery or vein can produce an expanding hematoma extending into deep neck spaces. CT angiography would be needed to identify an injured vessel or active bleeding; neither is established by this single image.

Traumatic hypopharyngeal perforation.description: A tear in the hypopharyngeal wall following blunt trauma can cause deep neck swelling, pain, dysphagia, and airway compromise. Extraluminal gas or a contrast leak would support this diagnosis, but these are not established by the supplied image.

Pancreatic insulinoma.description: An insulin-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. This is the most likely diagnosis given fasting hypoglycemia, elevated insulin and C-peptide, and a hypervascular pancreatic lesion.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: A rare disorder of excessive insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, sometimes associated with diffuse beta-cell abnormalities termed nesidioblastosis. It usually causes postprandial rather than fasting hypoglycemia.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome.description: Insulin-binding autoantibodies can cause inappropriate release of bound insulin and recurrent hypoglycemia without administered insulin. Episodes are often postprandial, although fasting episodes can occur.

Sulfonylurea- or meglitinide-induced hyp.description: Exposure to insulin-secretagogue medications can cause hypoglycemia with elevated insulin and C-peptide, mimicking insulinoma. A blood or urine drug screen during an episode helps distinguish this cause.

Adrenal insufficiency.description: Deficient cortisol production can impair maintenance of blood glucose during fasting and cause weakness, fatigue, and hypoglycemia. It is substantially less likely here because adrenal testing was normal and the biochemical findings indicate inappropriate insulin secretion.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility of the lower costal cartilages, usually ribs 8–10, can irritate adjacent intercostal nerves. This is the leading possibility; the ultrasound views suggest differing relative positions of the lower ribs, but confirmation requires dynamic imaging correlated with pain.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or injury of muscles between the ribs can cause localized chest wall pain during movements that load the thorax.

Rectus abdominis insertional strain.description: Overuse injury at the upper attachment of the rectus abdominis to the lower costal cartilages can produce pain near the anterior costal margin.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation or mechanical irritation of the rib cartilage attachments causes anterior chest wall pain, usually at the upper parasternal joints.

Rib stress fracture.description: Repetitive loading can cause a small rib fracture without a single traumatic event. The supplied ultrasound images alone do not establish a fracture.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia.description: A clonal myeloid malignancy characterized by persistent eosinophilia, abnormal marrow morphology, and possible eosinophil-mediated organ injury. The illustrated dysplastic cells and apparent chromosome 1/7 abnormality raise suspicion, but marrow evaluation and molecular testing are needed for classification.

Myelodysplastic neoplasm with associated.description: A clonal bone marrow disorder causing ineffective blood-cell production and cellular dysplasia. Anemia, illustrated megaloblastoid and abnormal granulocytic morphology, and an apparent chromosome 1/7 abnormality make this an important possibility.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A syndrome of persistent substantial eosinophilia with attributable organ injury. Pulmonary involvement can mimic asthma; an idiopathic diagnosis requires exclusion of reactive causes and clonal hematologic disease.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic inflammatory lung disease producing respiratory symptoms over weeks to months, peripheral eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities. Confirmation generally requires evaluation of lung eosinophilia and exclusion of secondary causes.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic small-vessel vasculitis associated with eosinophilia, asthma, and eosinophilic tissue inflammation. Pulmonary disease may precede recognizable extrapulmonary vasculitis.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphatic malignancy characterized by Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells within an inflammatory background. The extensive lymphadenopathy and large atypical cells in the supplied images make this a leading possibility, pending confirmation of the immunostains.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive T-cell lymphoma that can occur in children and cause systemic inflammation, lymphadenopathy, and extranodal disease. Its large atypical cells can resemble those of Hodgkin lymphoma; immunophenotyping is needed to distinguish them.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive B-cell malignancy that may involve abdominal lymph nodes, bowel, and liver, causing rapidly progressive systemic and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, intestinal bleeding, anemia, and impaired growth in children. The bulky lymphadenopathy and atypical biopsy cells make it less likely than lymphoma here.

Abdominal tuberculosis with disseminated.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving abdominal lymph nodes or bowel can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, and anemia. Thoracic and hepatic involvement may occur, but microbiologic or characteristic histologic evidence is required.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Mosquito-transmitted parasitic infection causing red blood cell destruction and potentially life-threatening organ dysfunction. This is the leading diagnosis: the supplied rapid test appears positive for falciparum malaria, and the blood smear shows numerous delicate ring forms, including double chromatin dots, compatible with P. falciparum. Acute kidney injury makes urgent treatment necessary.

Severe leptospirosis (Weil disease).description: A bacterial infection acquired through water or soil contaminated with infected animal urine. Severe disease can cause jaundice, kidney failure, and thrombocytopenia, but it does not explain the malaria-compatible blood smear and rapid test.

Dengue fever with severe organ involveme.normalized_text: Dengue fever with severe organ involvement
Dengue fever with severe organ involveme.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection that can cause thrombocytopenia, liver injury, and, in severe cases, kidney dysfunction. It is a travel-related alternative but is substantially less consistent with the parasitologic findings.

Yellow fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection found in parts of Africa that can progress to jaundice, liver injury, bleeding, and kidney failure. Exposure location and vaccination history affect its likelihood; it does not explain the malaria test findings.

Babesiosis.description: A usually tick-transmitted infection of red blood cells that can cause hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury. Its ring forms can resemble malaria on microscopy, but travel to Tanzania, mosquito exposure, and the apparent falciparum-positive test strongly favor malaria.

Delayed cervical esophageal perforation.normalized_text: Delayed cervical esophageal perforation caused by spinal fixation hardware erosion
Delayed cervical esophageal perforation.description: Cervical fixation plates or screws can erode into the pharynx or esophagus years after surgery, causing leakage and deep infection. The apparent exposed hardware and communication with a pus-containing cavity in the images strongly suggest this possibility.

Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess with thoracic extension
Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.description: A deep neck-space infection can cause a collection behind the pharynx or adjacent to the cervical spine and spread downward into the thorax.

Descending mediastinitis secondary to ph.normalized_text: Descending mediastinitis secondary to pharyngoesophageal leakage
Descending mediastinitis secondary to ph.description: A severe mediastinal infection can develop when contamination from a cervical pharyngeal or esophageal defect spreads into the chest. The images labeled with mediastinal pus support this complication.

Delayed cervical spinal implant infectio.normalized_text: Delayed cervical spinal implant infection with paraspinal abscess
Delayed cervical spinal implant infectio.description: An infection involving spinal fixation hardware can present years after implantation and cause extensive adjacent soft-tissue abscesses, sometimes following contamination from esophageal erosion.

Cervicothoracic vertebral osteomyelitis.normalized_text: Cervicothoracic vertebral osteomyelitis with paraspinal abscess
Cervicothoracic vertebral osteomyelitis.description: Infection of vertebral bone, sometimes involving adjacent discs, can arise near implanted hardware or spread from neighboring infected tissues and produce a paraspinal abscess. Confirmation requires evidence of vertebral or disc involvement.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness esophageal tear caused by forceful vomiting, allowing air and gastrointestinal contents to enter the mediastinum and pleural space. This is the leading concern and a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate specialist assessment.

Vomiting-induced spontaneous pneumomedia.description: Air leaks from ruptured alveoli into the mediastinum after a sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure, such as during vomiting. Esophageal rupture must be excluded in this presentation.

Spontaneous left pneumothorax.description: Air accumulates in the left pleural space, partially collapsing the lung. It may occur independently or as a complication of another thoracic process.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the aortic inner lining allows blood to separate layers of the aortic wall, producing potentially fatal vascular complications.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Reduced coronary blood flow causes myocardial ischemia or infarction. It is an important chest-pain differential, although the reported testing and imaging favor a noncardiac cause.

Functional seizures (psychogenic nonepil.description: Involuntary seizure-like episodes caused by altered nervous-system functioning rather than epileptic discharges. This is a leading possibility; the EEG image appears substantially affected by movement artifact, with some preserved posterior background activity, but confirmation requires synchronized video-EEG capture of a typical event.

Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.normalized_text: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.description: Epileptic activity beginning in one cerebral region and spreading to produce bilateral stiffening and shaking. A single artifact-heavy EEG image cannot establish or exclude this diagnosis.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral blood flow, sometimes accompanied by stiffening or brief jerking. Vasovagal mechanisms or a cardiac arrhythmia are possible causes.

Panic attacks with dissociative symptoms.description: Episodes of intense autonomic arousal that can cause palpitations, nausea, tremulousness, and impaired concentration; dissociation may accompany severe attacks.

Catatonia associated with a psychiatric.normalized_text: Catatonia associated with a psychiatric or medical disorder
Catatonia associated with a psychiatric.description: A psychomotor syndrome that can include mutism, abnormal posturing, rigidity, and either reduced activity or agitation. It could explain the examination findings but is less satisfactory as an explanation for the entire recurrent-event history.

Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.normalized_text: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.description: Small bowel herniates through the obturator canal and becomes trapped, causing obstruction and potentially strangulation. The CT images strongly suggest a bowel-containing right obturator hernia. This is an urgent surgical condition.

Incarcerated right femoral hernia causin.normalized_text: Incarcerated right femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right femoral hernia causin.description: Bowel becomes trapped in the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. Femoral hernias occur particularly in older women and can cause acute bowel obstruction.

Incarcerated sciatic hernia.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel passes through a sciatic foramen, potentially causing obstruction and pain from adjacent nerve compression.

Small-bowel volvulus.description: Twisting of small bowel around its mesentery produces mechanical obstruction and can compromise intestinal blood supply.

Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic ma.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic malignancy
Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic ma.description: A pelvic tumor can compress or invade bowel and cause obstruction; involvement of pelvic nerves can also produce referred lower-limb pain.

Susac syndrome.description: An immune-mediated small-vessel endotheliopathy affecting the retina, inner ear, and brain. This is the leading consideration given apparent branch retinal artery occlusions, low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and corpus callosum lesions.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause recurrent visual and sensory disturbances and corpus callosum lesions, but does not usually cause retinal arterial occlusions.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: A rare inflammatory vasculitis confined predominantly to the brain and spinal cord, producing headache, focal neurological deficits, and multifocal ischemic lesions.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune thrombotic disorder that can cause retinal arterial occlusion and cerebral ischemia; diagnosis requires appropriate clinical findings and persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare inflammatory disorder characterized by ocular inflammation, usually interstitial keratitis, and audiovestibular dysfunction; atypical forms can involve retinal vasculitis and systemic vessels.

Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.normalized_text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF spectrum mitochondrial disease)
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder with variable expression that can cause myopathy, cerebellar ataxia, hearing loss, seizures, and cardiac abnormalities. Myoclonus and epilepsy may be absent in atypical presentations. The maternal-pattern pedigree and apparent ragged-red fibers in the supplied biopsy strongly support a mitochondrial disorder; genetic testing is needed to establish the subtype.

Mitochondrial DNA deletion-associated my.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by single or multiple mitochondrial DNA deletions, producing progressive muscle weakness and sometimes cerebellar, auditory, cognitive, or cardiac involvement. Muscle pathology and molecular testing help distinguish it from other mitochondrial syndromes.

Late-onset hereditary axial myopathy.description: An inherited muscle disease predominantly affecting spinal muscles, causing paraspinal wasting and progressive bent-spine posture. Some forms also involve neck and proximal limb muscles, although an isolated axial myopathy would not explain the entire multisystem presentation.

Spinocerebellar ataxia.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders causing progressive cerebellar dysfunction. Certain subtypes can include cognitive changes or peripheral neuromuscular involvement, but marked axial myopathy is unusual.

Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associ.normalized_text: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis
Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associ.description: Also called Hashimoto encephalopathy, this uncommon diagnosis can produce cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and occasionally cerebellar ataxia in patients with thyroid autoantibodies. Antibody positivity alone is not diagnostic, and alternative explanations must be excluded.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma that can involve lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissues, and occasionally blood or bone marrow. Tissue morphology and additional molecular studies are needed for confirmation.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A rapidly growing mature B-cell lymphoma occurring in children, usually associated with a MYC rearrangement and an exceptionally high proliferation rate.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with blastoid or intermediate-sized cell morphology that does not meet criteria for another defined lymphoma. Classification requires tissue, proliferation, and genetic studies.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aber.description: A rare mature B-cell lymphoma that can resemble Burkitt lymphoma but lacks its defining MYC rearrangement and instead has a characteristic chromosome 11q gain-and-loss pattern. The unlabeled cytogenetic images alone cannot establish this diagnosis.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors common in young children. It can cause anemia, musculoskeletal pain, lymphadenopathy, and tissue masses, but the reported mature B-cell phenotype makes it substantially less likely here.

Pyogenic liver abscess associated with S.normalized_text: Pyogenic liver abscess associated with Schistosoma mansoni infection
Pyogenic liver abscess associated with S.description: A bacterial infection producing a pus-filled liver lesion. Schistosomal hepatic inflammation can predispose to bacterial abscess formation; the complex right-lobe lesion shown is concerning for this complication.

Hepatointestinal schistosomiasis.description: Schistosoma mansoni infection causes intestinal inflammation and hepatic egg-related granulomas, sometimes progressing to periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension. Stool eggs establish infection, but do not establish the cause of the focal liver lesion.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: Entamoeba histolytica infection can spread from the intestine to the liver, commonly causing an abscess in the right hepatic lobe.

Infected post-traumatic hepatic hematoma.description: Traumatic bleeding within the liver can form a complex collection that subsequently becomes infected, causing persistent fever and localized pain.

Hepatic echinococcosis with secondary in.description: Echinococcus infection produces hepatic hydatid cysts. Secondary bacterial infection can cause fever, pain, and a complex cystic appearance, although characteristic cyst features are not clearly established in these images.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute coronary artery occlusion causing anterior myocardial injury, often involving the left anterior descending artery. The severe symptoms and anterior ST-segment elevation with prominent hyperacute T waves on the supplied ECG are highly concerning and require emergency cardiac evaluation.

Polycythemia vera with coronary thrombos.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm causing increased red cell production, often accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis. Aquagenic pruritus and arterial thrombosis are characteristic; confirmation requires further testing, including JAK2 mutation analysis and serum erythropoietin.

Essential thrombocythemia with coronary.description: A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent thrombocytosis and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, including myocardial infarction. Elevated hemoglobin and aquagenic pruritus warrant careful exclusion of polycythemia vera.

Vasospastic angina.description: Transient coronary artery spasm causing myocardial ischemia, typically at rest or during the night. Sustained spasm can cause myocardial infarction, but the supplied ECG must be treated as possible acute coronary occlusion rather than presumed benign spasm.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus causing burning retrosternal discomfort, sometimes worse when lying down. It could explain the preceding month of symptoms but does not adequately explain the acute ischemic presentation or ECG findings.

Bronchopulmonary sequestration.description: Congenital abnormal lung tissue supplied by a systemic artery, usually arising from the aorta, rather than the pulmonary circulation. The apparent aortic feeding vessel to the left basal lesion makes this the leading structural diagnosis.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation, possibly a hybrid lesion with sequestration
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental malformation of the distal airways producing cystic or solid abnormal lung tissue. A hybrid lesion combines these changes with the systemic arterial supply of sequestration.

Neonatal pneumothorax, including possibl.normalized_text: Neonatal pneumothorax, including possible left tension pneumothorax
Neonatal pneumothorax, including possibl.description: Air in the pleural space can compress the lung and, under tension, shift the mediastinum and impair circulation. Resuscitation and positive-pressure ventilation increase the risk.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Aspiration of meconium around delivery causes airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, respiratory failure, and sometimes air-leak complications.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Brain injury caused by inadequate oxygen delivery and blood flow around birth. The profound neonatal depression and prolonged resuscitation raise strong concern, although neurological assessment is required for confirmation.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: Dysregulated alternative complement activation causes small-vessel endothelial injury, hemolysis, and renal failure. The biopsy images appear to show vascular narrowing and concentric intimal thickening compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy, although these findings do not establish its cause.

Hypertensive emergency with renal thromb.normalized_text: Hypertensive emergency with renal thrombotic microangiopathy
Hypertensive emergency with renal thromb.description: Severe hypertension can damage renal arterioles, causing hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, microangiopathic hemolysis, and progressive kidney failure.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can cause vasoconstriction, hypertension, and endothelial injury, producing renal small-vessel damage and sometimes thrombotic microangiopathy.

C3 glomerulopathy.description: Alternative complement pathway dysregulation causes C3-dominant glomerular deposits and progressive renal disease. Diagnosis requires immunofluorescence and usually electron microscopy.

Hepatitis C-associated cryoglobulinemic.description: Chronic hepatitis C can promote cryoglobulin-containing immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli, causing proteinuria, complement consumption, and renal dysfunction.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) presenting with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An inflammatory astrocytopathy associated with AQP4 antibodies. Involvement of the dorsal medulla and area postrema causes persistent nausea and vomiting. The apparent medullary MRI abnormality and positive cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG make this the leading consideration, although isolated CSF positivity warrants confirmation with a validated assay.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can involve the brainstem and produce bulbar, ocular motor, and motor deficits. Serum MOG-IgG testing would help evaluate this alternative.

Multiple sclerosis with brainstem involv.description: A central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause brainstem lesions, ocular motor abnormalities, weakness, and pyramidal signs. Additional characteristic MRI lesions and cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands would be needed to support this diagnosis.

Rhombencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the brainstem and cerebellum caused by infection, such as Listeria, or immune-mediated disease. It can produce asymmetric neurological deficits, bulbar dysfunction, and respiratory compromise.

Adult brainstem glioma involving the med.normalized_text: Adult brainstem glioma involving the medulla
Adult brainstem glioma involving the med.description: An infiltrative brainstem tumor that may progressively disrupt vomiting-control pathways, cranial nerve function, motor tracts, and respiratory centers. Contrast-enhanced MRI and follow-up imaging would be needed to assess this possibility.

Lactobacillus-associated aortic valve in.description: An uncommon bacterial infection of a heart valve. Some Lactobacillus species have intrinsic vancomycin resistance and variable cephalosporin susceptibility, making this a leading possibility given the reported susceptibility profile. Species identification and blood cultures are needed for confirmation.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare zoonotic bacterial infection that can cause destructive endocarditis, frequently involving the aortic valve. Intrinsic vancomycin resistance and relatively low penicillin MICs support consideration, although the extreme cephalosporin resistance is less characteristic.

Leuconostoc-associated infective endocar.description: A rare opportunistic infection of a heart valve caused by intrinsically vancomycin-resistant bacteria. It can resemble other forms of subacute bacterial endocarditis; microbiological identification is necessary to distinguish it from Lactobacillus and related organisms.

Enterococcal aortic valve infective endo.description: An infection of the aortic valve caused by Enterococcus species, often producing a subacute febrile illness. Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, and some strains are vancomycin resistant.

Viridans group streptococcal aortic valv.normalized_text: Viridans group streptococcal aortic valve infective endocarditis
Viridans group streptococcal aortic valv.description: A common cause of subacute endocarditis, especially on previously abnormal valves. The clinical presentation fits, but the supplied vancomycin and cephalosporin resistance profile argues strongly against typical viridans streptococci.

Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.normalized_text: Paradoxical air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.description: Venous air introduced during venesection can cross a patent foramen ovale into the arterial circulation, causing cerebral and coronary ischemia. This is the leading unifying possibility. The arrowed low-density focus on the CT may represent intravascular gas, although confirmation requires review of the full study.

Venous air embolism affecting the pulmon.normalized_text: Venous air embolism affecting the pulmonary circulation
Venous air embolism affecting the pulmon.description: Air entering the venous circulation can obstruct pulmonary blood flow and produce acute hypoxaemia, dyspnoea, and chest pain. An isolated venous air embolism would not fully explain focal cerebral ischemia without arterial passage through the demonstrated shunt.

Acute pulmonary thromboembolism with par.normalized_text: Acute pulmonary thromboembolism with paradoxical systemic thromboembolism
Acute pulmonary thromboembolism with par.description: A venous blood clot can embolize to the lungs, while clot crossing a patent foramen ovale can cause cerebral or coronary ischemia. This could explain the combined respiratory, cardiac, and neurological findings, but the procedural gurgling strongly favors air rather than thrombus.

Acute coronary syndrome, including non-S.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome, including non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Acute coronary syndrome, including non-S.description: Acute myocardial ischemia can cause characteristic chest pain, ECG changes, and elevated troponin. A primary coronary event alone does not adequately explain the simultaneous transient neurological deficit and the apparent venous air-entry event.

Acute aortic dissection with coronary an.normalized_text: Acute aortic dissection with coronary and cerebral malperfusion
Acute aortic dissection with coronary an.description: An aortic dissection can compromise coronary and cerebral arterial blood flow, producing abrupt chest pain, myocardial injury, and stroke-like deficits. It is a dangerous alternative, although no dissection is demonstrated in the provided information.

Residual or recurrent pleomorphic xantho.normalized_text: Residual or recurrent pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), CNS WHO grade 2
Residual or recurrent pleomorphic xantho.description: A circumscribed astrocytic tumor commonly affecting superficial temporal regions in young adults and frequently harboring BRAF V600E. This is the leading consideration given the established pathology; recurrence requires comparison with prior imaging.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, CNS WHO g.description: A higher-grade PXA that may arise through progression of a grade 2 tumor. Imaging alone cannot establish transformation; repeat tissue evaluation is needed.

Ganglioglioma.description: A usually slow-growing mixed neuronal and glial tumor associated with temporal-lobe epilepsy. BRAF V600E can occur, but the documented PXA pathology makes this a less likely alternative.

Epithelioid glioblastoma.description: An aggressive glioblastoma pattern that can harbor BRAF V600E and overlap with PXA morphologically. Consideration would require evidence of high-grade progression and additional pathological characterization.

Postoperative gliosis with reactive enha.description: Scarring and reactive changes after brain tumor surgery can produce FLAIR hyperintensity and enhancement near a resection cavity. Distinguishing these changes from residual or recurrent tumor requires serial imaging and treatment history.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin lesions. This is the strongest fit for the reported presentation; severe weakness and generalized edema can occur.

Overlap myositis associated with systemi.normalized_text: Overlap myositis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease
Overlap myositis associated with systemi.description: An inflammatory muscle disease occurring alongside another systemic autoimmune connective tissue disorder, sometimes with dermatomyositis-like skin findings, edema, and pulmonary or pleural involvement.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune syndrome associated with antibodies to aminoacyl-transfer RNA synthetases, often causing inflammatory myopathy, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, and characteristic hand changes.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: An autoimmune muscle disorder causing muscle fiber necrosis and often severe, subacute proximal weakness, sometimes associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies.

Hypothyroid myopathy.description: Muscle dysfunction caused by thyroid hormone deficiency, producing muscle pain and predominantly proximal weakness; family history of thyroid disease provides a limited supporting clue.

Phenytoin-associated osteomalacia.description: Defective bone mineralization associated with long-term phenytoin use, which can accelerate vitamin D breakdown. This is a leading consideration given the medication history and bilateral Looser’s zones.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia.description: An acquired phosphate-wasting disorder caused by excess FGF23 production, usually from a small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor. The focal abnormality near the left proximal femur on the supplied functional and MRI images raises this possibility but does not establish it.

Nutritional vitamin D deficiency osteoma.description: Insufficient vitamin D from low intake, limited sunlight exposure, or malabsorption impairs calcium and phosphate availability for bone mineralization.

Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemic o.description: Proximal renal tubular dysfunction causes urinary losses of phosphate and other solutes, potentially producing osteomalacia. Overall renal filtration can remain normal.

Primary hyperparathyroidism with metabol.normalized_text: Primary hyperparathyroidism with metabolic bone disease
Primary hyperparathyroidism with metabol.description: Excess parathyroid hormone increases bone turnover and renal phosphate loss, potentially causing bone pain, weakness, and skeletal fragility.

Group A streptococcal infective endocard.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis of the mitral valve
Group A streptococcal infective endocard.description: The leading unifying diagnosis: bacterial infection of the mitral valve with probable vegetation, complicated by mitral regurgitation and systemic septic embolization.

Acute cerebral embolic infarction second.normalized_text: Acute cerebral embolic infarction secondary to infective endocarditis
Acute cerebral embolic infarction second.description: A likely complication in which infected valvular material embolizes to a cerebral artery, causing ischemic brain injury. Additional MRI sequences are needed to characterize the displayed brain lesion definitively.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to severe mitral regurgitation
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Mitral valve incompetence, potentially caused by infective destruction, produces pulmonary congestion and cardiac volume overload. This is a likely cardiac complication rather than a separate explanation for the entire presentation.

Splenic abscesses from septic embolizati.description: Infected emboli from endocarditis can seed the spleen and produce abscesses. The hypoechoic lesions in the supplied abdominal ultrasound raise this possibility, although splenic infarcts are an alternative and further imaging is needed.

Group A streptococcal sepsis.description: Invasive streptococcal infection with systemic illness and possible organ dysfunction, likely arising from the suspected endocarditis. Sepsis may coexist with the embolic and cardiac complications.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare inherited ciliopathy affecting skeletal development, hair, teeth, nails, and kidneys. Progressive tubulointerstitial kidney disease can cause renal failure in early childhood. This is the strongest overall fit, although molecular testing is needed for confirmation.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: An inherited skeletal ciliopathy characterized by cone-shaped phalangeal epiphyses, chronic kidney disease, and retinal degeneration, with variable skeletal abnormalities.

Short-rib thoracic dysplasia (Jeune synd.description: A genetically heterogeneous ciliopathy causing a narrow thorax and short limbs, sometimes accompanied by progressive kidney disease, retinal disease, or liver involvement.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: An inherited SMARCAL1-related disorder combining skeletal dysplasia, progressive proteinuric kidney disease, and variable T-cell immunodeficiency.

Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrom.description: An X-linked OCRL-related disorder in males causing congenital ocular disease, neurologic abnormalities, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction that may progress to chronic kidney disease.

Malignancy-associated dermatomyositis, p.normalized_text: Malignancy-associated dermatomyositis, potentially associated with oesophageal carcinoma
Malignancy-associated dermatomyositis, p.description: An inflammatory muscle and skin disease that can occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome. The hand lesions resemble Gottron papules, and focal thoracic PET uptake together with abnormal endoscopy raises concern for an oesophageal malignancy; biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Dermatomyositis without an associated ma.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and characteristic skin eruptions. Swallowing muscles may also be affected.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing predominantly symmetrical proximal weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and sometimes swallowing impairment, but without the characteristic rash of dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: An autoimmune muscle disease causing substantial muscle fiber injury, often with severe weakness and very high creatine kinase levels. It may be associated with specific autoantibodies, statin exposure, or malignancy.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune syndrome involving inflammatory myopathy, often accompanied by interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and rough fissured skin on the hands called mechanic's hands.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Childhood osteonecrosis of the femoral head caused by disruption of its blood supply. This is the leading consideration given the age, examination, and apparent femoral head flattening and fragmentation on the radiographs.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A temporary, usually self-limited inflammation of the hip joint, often following a viral illness, that commonly causes limping in children.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.description: Displacement of the proximal femoral growth plate, usually occurring during adolescence, that produces hip or referred knee pain and restricted internal rotation.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis.description: Chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning in childhood that can cause joint pain, stiffness, restricted motion, and limping. Isolated hip involvement is less common.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint requiring urgent assessment and treatment. It usually causes acute severe pain, fever, and difficulty bearing weight, although atypical presentations occur.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing a pus-filled cavity within the liver. The large gas-containing fluid collection along the right hepatic margin strongly suggests an abscess, although its precise intrahepatic versus subcapsular location requires formal imaging review.

Right subphrenic abscess.description: An infected collection beneath the right diaphragm, often arising from an abdominal infection or perforation. Gas within the collection can mimic free intraperitoneal air on an erect chest radiograph.

Infected hepatic cyst.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a pre-existing liver cyst, causing fever, focal pain, and occasionally gas formation within the cyst.

Secondarily infected hepatic hydatid cys.description: A liver cyst caused by Echinococcus infection that has developed secondary bacterial infection. Geographic background can support consideration, but characteristic cyst structures or confirmatory testing are needed.

Contained perforated duodenal ulcer with.normalized_text: Contained perforated duodenal ulcer with a perihepatic abscess
Contained perforated duodenal ulcer with.description: A duodenal ulcer that perforates but is locally contained, allowing an infected gas-fluid collection to develop near the liver rather than producing widespread free air.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. The reported 5p15.2 deletion establishes this as the primary diagnosis. Associated brain abnormalities can include pontine hypoplasia, which appears present on the supplied MRI.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.description: A chromosome 4p deletion disorder associated with microcephaly, developmental impairment, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and congenital malformations. It is a phenotypic alternative, not an explanation for the documented chromosome 5 deletion.

1p36 deletion syndrome.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome causing developmental delay, hypotonia, variable microcephaly, eye abnormalities, and congenital heart disease. Confirmation requires a chromosome 1p36 deletion.

Pontocerebellar hypoplasia.description: A genetically heterogeneous group of disorders involving underdevelopment of the pons and cerebellum, often with microcephaly and severe developmental impairment. Apparent pontine hypoplasia warrants consideration, although the supplied images do not establish accompanying cerebellar hypoplasia.

Mowat-Wilson syndrome.description: A disorder usually caused by pathogenic variants or deletions involving ZEB2, characterized by developmental impairment, microcephaly, distinctive facial features, and variable congenital heart and brain abnormalities.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.normalized_text: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.description: A rare malignant germ cell tumor arising outside the gonads that typically produces alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). This is the leading diagnosis given the elevated AFP and characteristic combination of histologic patterns; confirmation requires appropriate immunohistochemistry and exclusion of another primary site.

Mixed extragonadal malignant germ cell t.normalized_text: Mixed extragonadal malignant germ cell tumor with a yolk sac component
Mixed extragonadal malignant germ cell t.description: A malignant tumor containing more than one germ cell tumor component. A yolk sac component can account for AFP elevation, while additional components must be established by tissue sampling and immunohistochemistry.

AFP-producing jejunal adenocarcinoma wit.normalized_text: AFP-producing jejunal adenocarcinoma with hepatoid or enteroblastic differentiation
AFP-producing jejunal adenocarcinoma wit.description: A rare intestinal epithelial malignancy with fetal intestinal or liver-like differentiation that may produce AFP and resemble a yolk sac tumor.

Extragonadal embryonal carcinoma.description: An aggressive malignant germ cell tumor that can show solid, glandular, and papillary architecture. AFP elevation can occur, particularly when a yolk sac component is also present.

Intestinal Burkitt lymphoma.description: A rapidly proliferating B-cell lymphoma that commonly involves abdominal structures in children and can cause intestinal masses, lymphadenopathy, and ascites.

Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.description: A congenital ileal outpouching that may contain acid-secreting gastric tissue, causing adjacent ulceration and substantial intestinal bleeding. The focal abdominal uptake on the provided scan suggests ectopic gastric mucosa and favors this diagnosis, although an enteric duplication can produce similar findings.

Ileocolic intussusception.description: Telescoping of one bowel segment into another, causing intermittent obstruction, impaired blood supply, and bloody stools. A Meckel diverticulum or duplication cyst can occasionally serve as a lead point.

Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst containing ectopic gastric mucosa
Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.description: A congenital duplication of the intestinal tract that may contain gastric tissue, causing ulceration, bleeding, pain, or obstruction. It can also produce focal uptake on gastric-mucosa scintigraphy.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.description: A non-IgE-mediated reaction to dietary proteins, commonly cow's milk, causing distal intestinal inflammation and blood-streaked stools in infants.

Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvu.description: Abnormal intestinal rotation permitting twisting around the mesenteric blood supply, leading to obstruction and potentially bowel ischemia. This is a surgical emergency.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, usually in older nonsmoking women, associated with constrictive bronchiolitis, air trapping, and pulmonary nodules or carcinoid tumors. This is the leading consideration, but confirmation requires further evaluation.

Pulmonary carcinoid tumors.description: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine lung tumors that may appear as rounded or lobulated nodules and cause bronchial obstruction. Multiple carcinoids can occur in association with DIPNECH.

Constrictive bronchiolitis.description: Fibrotic narrowing of small airways causing persistent airflow obstruction and expiratory air trapping. It may be idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease, exposures, infections, or DIPNECH.

Late-onset asthma.description: Inflammatory airway disease that can begin in older adults and cause marked airflow limitation and air trapping. Bronchodilator testing would help assess whether the obstruction is reversible.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.description: An immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens that can involve the small airways and produce breathlessness, mosaic attenuation, air trapping, and centrilobular nodules.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, possibly nod.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, possibly nodular sclerosis subtype, with pulmonary involvement
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, possibly nod.description: A lymphoid malignancy that commonly affects young adults and can involve supraclavicular nodes and lungs. The supplied histology appears to show broad fibrous bands and scattered large atypical cells, raising this possibility; immunohistochemistry is needed for confirmation. Associated granulomatous reactions can obscure diagnosis in small biopsies.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with tuberculous.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause upper-lobe cavitation, hemoptysis, and cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Negative routine cultures do not exclude tuberculosis; specific mycobacterial testing is required.

Sarcoidosis with atypical cavitary pulmo.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis with atypical cavitary pulmonary involvement
Sarcoidosis with atypical cavitary pulmo.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by noninfectious granulomas, often involving lungs and lymph nodes. Cavitation can occur but is rare, and infection and malignancy must be excluded.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that can cause cavitary lung lesions and pulmonary hemorrhage, often accompanied by upper-airway or kidney disease.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary d.description: Environmental mycobacteria can cause chronic granulomatous lung infection with upper-lobe cavities. Diagnosis requires organism-specific cultures and correlation with clinical and imaging findings.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: JC polyomavirus infection causing progressive brain demyelination in immunosuppressed patients. Prior natalizumab exposure and a high anti-JCPyV antibody index raise concern for carryover PML. Negative CSF JCPyV-DNA does not exclude early disease. The supplied image is a viral regulatory-region schematic, not diagnostic brain imaging.

PML-associated immune reconstitution inf.description: Inflammatory worsening of underlying PML as immune surveillance recovers after natalizumab withdrawal. It requires evidence supporting PML and an inflammatory response, neither of which is established by the supplied schematic.

Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound af.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound after natalizumab withdrawal
Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound af.description: Recurrent inflammatory demyelination after stopping natalizumab, potentially occurring during a transition to another disease-modifying treatment. Brain MRI is needed to distinguish this from PML and other causes.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A syndrome of predominantly posterior cerebral vasogenic edema that can occur with medication exposure or endothelial dysfunction. Fingolimod-associated PRES is rare; diagnosis requires compatible brain imaging.

Herpesvirus encephalitis.description: Brain infection caused by herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster virus, considered in an immunosuppressed patient with new seizures and focal deficits. CSF viral testing and brain MRI are needed to evaluate this possibility.

Fabry disease with cardiac and early ren.normalized_text: Fabry disease with cardiac and early renal involvement
Fabry disease with cardiac and early ren.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A, leading to glycosphingolipid accumulation. The markedly reduced enzyme activity and hemizygous GLA mutation strongly establish this diagnosis. The images appear consistent with ventricular hypertrophy and intracellular lamellar storage inclusions.

Sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder causing ventricular hypertrophy and sometimes myocardial ischemia or arrhythmias. It is a cardiac differential for the apparent hypertrophy and ECG abnormalities, but does not explain the multisystem findings or Fabry-specific laboratory results.

Systemic amyloidosis with cardiac and re.normalized_text: Systemic amyloidosis with cardiac and renal involvement
Systemic amyloidosis with cardiac and re.description: A disorder involving extracellular deposition of abnormal proteins that can produce ventricular wall thickening, neuropathy, and proteinuria. It is substantially less likely than Fabry disease because the specific enzyme, genetic, ocular, and skin findings are not explained.

Drug-induced phospholipidosis.description: Lysosomal phospholipid accumulation caused by medications such as chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, or amiodarone. It can mimic Fabry disease through corneal deposits and lamellar tissue inclusions, but no relevant drug exposure is reported and it does not explain the GLA findings.

Fucosidosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency. Angiokeratomas and childhood onset make it a remote phenotypic differential, but its usual progressive neurologic and developmental manifestations differ from this case, and it does not explain the Fabry-specific testing.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis.description: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, often caused by bile stasis and impaired blood supply in critically ill or severely injured patients. This is a leading consideration, although the single ultrasound image is not definitive.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a traumatic blood collection within the liver, potentially developing into an abscess.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection forming a pus-filled cavity in the liver, sometimes arising from an infected hematoma or biliary infection.

Infected post-traumatic biloma.description: An infected collection of leaked bile caused by traumatic injury to intrahepatic bile ducts.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Gallbladder inflammation caused by a gallstone obstructing the cystic duct. Ultrasound confirmation of an obstructing stone would help distinguish it from acalculous cholecystitis.

Iododerma induced by iodinated contrast.description: A rare inflammatory reaction to iodine exposure that can produce pustular, bullous, or vegetating skin lesions, often with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate. This is the leading consideration given the contrast exposure and biopsy findings.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: An acute, usually drug-induced eruption of numerous sterile, nonfollicular pustules. Iodinated contrast can trigger it, and eosinophilia may accompany the eruption.

Bullous Sweet syndrome.description: A variant of acute neutrophilic dermatosis in which inflammatory plaques develop vesicles or bullae. Biopsy typically shows a dense sterile neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis.

Generalized pustular psoriasis.description: A severe inflammatory form of psoriasis characterized by widespread sterile pustules that may coalesce into larger collections of pus.

Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.description: A severe, usually drug-induced reaction causing epidermal death, blistering, and detachment, commonly with mucosal involvement. The full-thickness epidermal necrosis warrants consideration, although the pustular morphology argues against it.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.description: A potentially fatal infection transmitted through dog saliva, especially after bites. Heavy alcohol use increases susceptibility. Sepsis can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation, widespread purpura, and tissue necrosis. This is the leading possibility; the pictured slender, fusiform bacteria are compatible but require laboratory confirmation.

Pasteurella multocida wound infection wi.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida wound infection with sepsis
Pasteurella multocida wound infection wi.description: A dog- or cat-associated bacterial infection that commonly causes rapidly developing wound cellulitis and can occasionally progress to bacteremia, severe sepsis, and coagulation abnormalities.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection arisin.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection arising from dog-bite wounds
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection arisin.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection of deeper soft tissues that may follow contaminated wounds and cause tissue destruction and systemic toxicity. It requires urgent surgical assessment; absence of visible gas on a radiograph does not exclude it.

Meningococcemia with purpura fulminans.description: An invasive Neisseria meningitidis bloodstream infection that can produce rapidly progressive sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpura, and peripheral tissue ischemia, sometimes without meningitis.

Alcohol-associated acute pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation commonly triggered by heavy alcohol intake. It can cause epigastric pain, vomiting, and a severe systemic inflammatory response, but would not adequately explain the bite-associated necrosis and apparent bacteremia.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MT-TL1-related mitochondrial disease wit.normalized_text: MT-TL1-related mitochondrial disease with a MELAS-like phenotype
MT-TL1-related mitochondrial disease wit.description: A mitochondrial energy-production disorder causing myopathy and neurological dysfunction. The m.3303C>T variant supports MT-TL1-related disease, although the apparent large-vessel occlusion raises concern for an embolic stroke rather than a purely metabolic MELAS stroke-like episode.

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac muscle dysfunction caused by defective mitochondrial energy metabolism. MT-TL1-associated cardiomyopathy may cause arrhythmias, syncope, and ventricular dysfunction that predisposes to intracardiac thrombosis.

Cardioembolic ischemic stroke.description: Brain infarction caused by an embolus originating in the heart. The focal brain lesion, apparent right-sided major arterial flow interruption, and possible intracardiac thrombi make this an important explanation for the current neurological deficits.

Left ventricular intracavitary thrombus.description: A clot within the left ventricle, often associated with impaired ventricular contraction, that can embolize to cerebral arteries. The echogenic masses indicated on the echocardiograms are suspicious for thrombi, although additional cardiac imaging is needed to distinguish them from other masses.

Moyamoya syndrome.description: A cerebral arteriopathy involving stenosis or occlusion of the terminal internal carotid arteries and development of collateral vessels. It is a less likely alternative explanation for young-onset recurrent strokes; the supplied angiographic image does not clearly demonstrate the characteristic collateral network.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of pancreatic duct cells. A pancreatic-head tumor can obstruct both the bile and pancreatic ducts. The apparent pancreatic-head lesion, ductal dilation, and irregular glands in fibrous stroma on the supplied images make this a leading possibility, although formal pathology interpretation is required.

Ampullary adenocarcinoma.description: A gland-forming cancer at the junction where the bile and pancreatic ducts empty into the duodenum. It can cause early obstructive jaundice and dilation of both ducts.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: A cancer of the lower common bile duct that causes progressive biliary obstruction. Its gland-forming histology can resemble pancreatic adenocarcinoma; determining the tumor's anatomical origin is essential.

Autoimmune pancreatitis.description: An immune-mediated pancreatic inflammatory disease that can produce a mass-like pancreatic enlargement and bile duct narrowing, mimicking cancer. It requires characteristic pathology and supporting clinical testing.

Choledocholithiasis.description: A stone lodged in the common bile duct that blocks bile drainage, causing jaundice, itching, and liver test abnormalities. It is a common alternative explanation for biliary obstruction but would not explain malignant glandular pathology.

Rectal gallstone impaction.description: A gallstone that has entered the intestinal tract and lodged in the rectum, causing mechanical difficulty with defecation. This is the best-supported explanation because the stone was identified and removed endoscopically.

Cholecystocolonic fistula.description: An abnormal connection between the gallbladder and colon that can allow a gallstone to pass directly into the large bowel. The arrowed gallbladder–bowel interface on the supplied images raises suspicion for this route, although confirmation requires review of the complete imaging study.

Cholecystoduodenal fistula.description: An abnormal connection between the gallbladder and duodenum, commonly related to chronic gallstone inflammation. It offers an alternative route for a gallstone to enter the bowel and eventually reach the rectum.

Crohn's-related anorectal stricture.description: Inflammation and scarring from Crohn's disease can narrow the anorectal lumen, impair stool passage, and potentially predispose to impaction of a migrated stone. No stricture is explicitly documented in this case.

Crohn's proctitis.description: Crohn's inflammation involving the rectum can cause bleeding and tenesmus, perceived as incomplete evacuation or a rectal foreign-body sensation. It is a possible coexisting condition but is less explanatory than the documented stone.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation with.normalized_text: Acute lateral patellar dislocation with osteochondral fracture and intra-articular loose body
Acute lateral patellar dislocation with.description: The leading diagnosis is lateral displacement of the patella with associated injury to the patellar or femoral articular surface, releasing a cartilage-and-bone fragment into the joint. The radiographs suggest an intra-articular fragment, but MRI is needed to establish its origin and extent.

Medial patellofemoral ligament tear asso.normalized_text: Medial patellofemoral ligament tear associated with patellar dislocation
Medial patellofemoral ligament tear asso.description: Damage to the principal soft-tissue restraint against lateral patellar displacement commonly accompanies an acute lateral patellar dislocation. An isolated tear would not explain a true osteochondral loose body.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee wi.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee with a detached fragment
Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee wi.description: A focal disorder of subchondral bone and overlying cartilage, typically affecting adolescents, that can produce an unstable or detached osteochondral fragment and mechanical knee symptoms.

Displaced meniscal tear.description: A torn meniscal fragment, particularly a bucket-handle tear, can displace into the joint and cause painful mechanical locking after an injury.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: An uncommon synovial disorder producing cartilage nodules that may detach as intra-articular loose bodies, causing swelling and locking. It is unusual at this age and generally has a more gradual presentation.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by scarring scalp alopecia, typically nonscarring axillary and pubic hair loss, and spiny follicular papules on the trunk and limbs. This is the strongest fit, although confirmation requires clinicopathologic correlation.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory disorder in which a lymphocytic immune response damages hair follicles, causing perifollicular scaling and permanent scarring alopecia.

Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides.description: A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma involving hair follicles that can produce persistent itchy follicular papules, plaques, and alopecia. Diagnosis requires assessment for atypical folliculotropic lymphocytes.

Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalva.description: A rare, usually inherited follicular keratinization disorder causing widespread spiny follicular papules and progressive scarring alopecia, most often beginning in childhood.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A benign follicular keratinization disorder producing grouped rough papules with central keratin spines, usually on the trunk and extremities.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by uncontrolled complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy, that produces hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and predominantly renal injury. This is the leading consideration, although confirmatory evaluation is required.

Hypertension-associated thrombotic micro.description: Severe hypertension can injure small vessels, producing renal failure, red-cell fragmentation, and platelet consumption. Hypertension may also be secondary to another thrombotic microangiopathy.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy typically caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, resulting in platelet-rich microvascular thrombosis, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia.

Antiphospholipid syndrome with renal thr.normalized_text: Antiphospholipid syndrome with renal thrombotic microangiopathy
Antiphospholipid syndrome with renal thr.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that can cause placental vascular disease, renal microvascular thrombosis, hypertension, and cutaneous thrombotic lesions.

HELLP syndrome.description: A pregnancy-associated syndrome of hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, usually occurring with preeclampsia late in pregnancy or shortly after delivery.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

KIT-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumo.normalized_text: KIT-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum
KIT-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumo.description: A mesenchymal gastrointestinal tumor associated with interstitial cells of Cajal, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations. The reported KIT exon 11 deletion strongly favors this diagnosis over the alternatives; the histology appears compatible with mixed spindle and epithelioid morphology.

Ileal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the intestinal wall and cause bleeding through mucosal ulceration. This is a substantially less likely alternative given the KIT mutation.

Well-differentiated ileal neuroendocrine.description: A tumor of intestinal neuroendocrine cells, often arising in the distal ileum and appearing as an enhancing mass. It may cause bleeding, but the molecular findings strongly favor GIST.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small-intestinal lining that can cause occult or overt bleeding and anemia. Its usual morphology and molecular profile differ from the findings reported here.

Ileal schwannoma.description: An uncommon, usually benign nerve-sheath tumor of the intestinal wall that can resemble GIST radiologically and occasionally cause bleeding. The KIT mutation makes this diagnosis unlikely.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.normalized_text: Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), possibly epithelioid type
Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract that can grow outward from the stomach into a large, lobulated mass. This is a leading possibility given the imaging and tumor morphology; confirmation requires identification of the immunostains and pathology review.

Gastric schwannoma.description: A usually benign tumor arising from nerve-associated cells in the stomach wall. It can produce an outward-growing gastric mass, although the apparent heterogeneity and hemorrhage here are less characteristic.

Nonfunctioning pancreatic neuroendocrine.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm without a clinically apparent hormone syndrome. Large tumors may cause pressure symptoms and show nested cellular architecture, but pancreatic origin and neuroendocrine markers would need confirmation.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant tumor of pancreatic enzyme-producing cells, often occurring in older adults and sometimes presenting as a bulky mass with necrosis. Pancreatic origin and acinar differentiation require confirmation.

Gastric leiomyosarcoma.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can grow outward from the stomach and become large, with hemorrhage and necrosis. It must be distinguished from GIST using smooth-muscle and GIST-associated immunostains.

Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign c.description: An inherited disorder of epidermal cell adhesion causing recurrent blistering and eroded plaques in skin folds. This is the leading possibility; the biopsy appears to show extensive acantholysis resembling a dilapidated brick wall.

Darier disease.description: An inherited keratinization disorder producing greasy, crusted keratotic papules, sometimes with prominent flexural involvement. Histology typically shows acantholysis and conspicuous dyskeratosis.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare autoimmune variant of pemphigus characterized by blisters that evolve into thick, vegetating plaques, often in intertriginous areas. Confirmation generally requires direct immunofluorescence.

Granular parakeratosis.description: A keratinization disorder causing reddish-brown or hyperpigmented keratotic papules and plaques in occluded skin folds. Diagnostic histology shows retained keratohyalin granules within a parakeratotic stratum corneum.

Candidal intertrigo.description: A yeast infection of moist skin folds causing inflamed, macerated plaques, often with peripheral satellite papules or pustules. It could complicate an underlying blistering disorder rather than explain the entire presentation.

Giant cell tumor of bone.description: A usually benign but locally aggressive bone tumor affecting skeletally mature young adults. Pelvic tumors can cause expansile bone destruction and a palpable mass; confirmation requires tissue diagnosis.
