Aneurysmal bone cyst.description: A benign, expansile bone lesion containing blood-filled spaces, occurring primarily in children and young adults. It may arise independently or develop within another bone tumor.

Osteoblastoma.description: A benign bone-forming tumor most common in adolescents and young adults. Larger lesions can be locally aggressive and may contain secondary aneurysmal bone cyst changes.

Telangiectatic osteosarcoma.description: A malignant bone-forming tumor with blood-filled cystic spaces that can resemble an aneurysmal bone cyst. Thick enhancing solid tissue and aggressive bone destruction raise concern; biopsy is needed to distinguish it.

Chondromyxoid fibroma.description: A rare benign cartilage-related bone tumor occurring mainly in young people. It typically produces an eccentric, lobulated, expansile lytic lesion and can occasionally involve the pelvis.

Stiff-person syndrome.description: An autoimmune disorder of impaired inhibitory neurotransmission causing axial and limb rigidity with painful spasms. The electrophysiologic recordings appear to show exaggerated muscle responses and reduced reflex inhibition, supporting a stiff-person spectrum disorder without establishing a specific antibody subtype.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, that produces rigidity, spasms, exaggerated startle, and brainstem or spinal dysfunction. Antibody testing and additional neurologic assessment are needed to distinguish it from classic stiff-person syndrome.

Acquired hyperekplexia.description: A disorder of exaggerated startle responses caused by impaired inhibitory signaling in brainstem and spinal circuits. Acquired forms can be autoimmune and overlap with stiff-person spectrum disorders.

Inflammatory myelopathy.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord can disrupt descending motor pathways and produce spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and progressive loss of mobility. Spinal MRI and cerebrospinal fluid testing would be needed to evaluate this possibility.

Acquired neuromyotonia (Isaacs syndrome).description: A peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder causing persistent muscle activity, stiffness, cramps, and delayed relaxation. Diagnostic needle EMG typically demonstrates neuromyotonic or myokymic discharges, which are not established by the supplied recordings.

Severe atherosclerotic supra-aortic arte.normalized_text: Severe atherosclerotic supra-aortic arterial disease with ischemic scalp necrosis
Severe atherosclerotic supra-aortic arte.description: Advanced narrowing or occlusion of arteries supplying the brain and scalp can cause cerebral hypoperfusion and, rarely, scalp tissue death. The angiographic image appears to show marked proximal arterial narrowing, but definitive interpretation requires the full study.

Takayasu arteritis.description: An inflammatory disease of the aorta and its major branches that can produce severe stenoses, cerebral hypoperfusion, and tissue ischemia.

Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis
Giant cell arteritis with scalp necrosis.description: Vasculitis involving cranial and sometimes large arteries; severe scalp ischemia can rarely cause ulceration and necrosis.

Subclavian steal syndrome.description: Proximal subclavian artery obstruction can reverse blood flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery, potentially causing vertebrobasilar hypoperfusion. Confirmation requires demonstration of the obstruction and reversed vertebral flow.

Pressure-induced scalp necrosis.description: Prolonged compression of the scalp, especially during unconsciousness or immobility, can impair local blood supply and cause ulceration, eschar, and hair loss.

Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary mi.normalized_text: Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary mixed cryoglobulinemia
Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary mi.description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites transmitted by sandflies. Mediterranean exposure and anti-TNF immunosuppression increase risk. The smear appears to show numerous organisms compatible with Leishmania amastigotes; confirmation requires expert microscopy or molecular testing.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, associated with infections, autoimmune disease, or lymphoproliferative disorders. It may be secondary to the underlying systemic infection rather than a separate primary disease.

Rheumatoid vasculitis.description: A systemic vascular complication of rheumatoid arthritis, usually occurring in longstanding, strongly seropositive disease and frequently affecting skin and peripheral nerves.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia and often splenomegaly, with increased susceptibility to infection. Splenomegaly is common but is not required for diagnosis.

Adalimumab-induced lupus-like syndrome.description: An uncommon autoimmune adverse effect of TNF inhibitors that can produce ANA positivity, inflammatory joint symptoms, fever, skin manifestations, and occasionally cytopenias or hypocomplementemia.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder associated with diabetes that typically produces yellow-brown pretibial plaques with an erythematous border and central atrophy. The clinical appearance and apparent layered collagen degeneration on biopsy make this the leading diagnosis.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign granulomatous skin condition producing annular papules or plaques, with collagen degeneration on biopsy. It can resemble necrobiosis lipoidica but usually lacks marked central atrophy.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A diabetes-associated condition causing small, brown, mildly atrophic shin spots, usually multiple and asymptomatic.

Morphea.description: Localized scleroderma causing slowly evolving plaques of dermal sclerosis that may develop pigment changes and central atrophy, sometimes with a reddish or violaceous inflammatory border.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disorder that can produce chronic reddish-brown plaques. Skin-limited disease may occur without systemic symptoms, but biopsy typically shows discrete noncaseating granulomas.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (GNAS m.description: The leading diagnosis: abnormal GNAS imprinting causes resistance to parathyroid hormone, producing hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated PTH. The supplied methylation plot shows increased NESP methylation and markedly reduced AS, XL, and A/B methylation, strongly supporting this diagnosis. Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires urgent treatment.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A.description: A disorder usually caused by a maternally inherited GNAS coding variant, resulting in resistance to PTH and other hormones. It commonly includes Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as brachydactyly, short stature, and subcutaneous ossification.

Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Chronic kidney disease with secondary hy.description: Reduced renal phosphate excretion and impaired activation of vitamin D can cause hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and compensatory elevation of PTH. Renal function testing would be necessary to assess this alternative.

Severe vitamin D deficiency with seconda.normalized_text: Severe vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Severe vitamin D deficiency with seconda.description: Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption and can cause hypocalcemia with compensatory PTH elevation. It is less consistent with this case because secondary hyperparathyroidism generally lowers serum phosphate when renal function is intact.

Eosinophilic esophagitis.description: An allergic inflammatory disease of the esophagus that can cause solid-food dysphagia, food impaction, vomiting, and food avoidance, especially in children with atopic disease. It could explain the swallowing presentation but not the endocrine abnormalities.

Cytomegalovirus infection with hepatitis.description: A systemic viral infection that can cause fever and hepatic inflammation. The apparent inclusion-like cell and positive immunostaining in the liver images raise this possibility, but the stain identity and virologic testing are needed for confirmation.

Acute Q fever with granulomatous hepatit.normalized_text: Acute Q fever with granulomatous hepatitis
Acute Q fever with granulomatous hepatit.description: Coxiella burnetii infection can cause high fever, hepatitis, and sometimes pneumonia. Ring-like hepatic granulomas in the supplied biopsy images make this a consideration; exposure history, serology, or PCR would be needed.

Dabrafenib–trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition that can cause recurrent fever, nausea, dehydration, and hypotension. The treatment timing and initial response to interruption strongly support this possibility.

Acute cholecystitis with systemic inflam.normalized_text: Acute cholecystitis with systemic inflammatory response
Acute cholecystitis with systemic inflam.description: Gallbladder inflammation, sometimes associated with gallstones, can cause fever and right upper quadrant pain and may progress to sepsis. The gallbladder ultrasound warrants formal assessment for stones, wall thickening, and a sonographic Murphy sign.

Bacterial sepsis from an occult infectio.normalized_text: Bacterial sepsis from an occult infection
Bacterial sepsis from an occult infectio.description: A systemic response to bacterial infection that can cause circulatory failure. The fever, hypotension, and ill appearance require urgent exclusion of bloodstream, biliary, pulmonary, or other bacterial infection.

Pancreatic metastasis from prostate aden.description: Rare spread of prostate cancer to the pancreas, potentially obstructing pancreatic or bile ducts. The cancer history and gland-forming malignant tissue shown make this an important possibility; confirmation requires pathology comparison and prostate-specific immunostains.

Primary pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A primary pancreatic glandular cancer that can cause pancreatic duct obstruction, pancreatitis, and biliary obstruction, particularly when located in the pancreatic head.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by cystic duct obstruction from a gallstone, although non-stone causes also occur.

Gallstone pancreatitis with transient co.normalized_text: Gallstone pancreatitis with transient common bile duct obstruction
Gallstone pancreatitis with transient co.description: Pancreatic inflammation caused by a gallstone transiently blocking the shared pancreaticobiliary outlet. A passed stone can leave normal bilirubin and subsequently normal lipase.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the distal bile duct that can mimic a pancreatic head tumor and cause progressive biliary obstruction; definitive distinction requires anatomical localization and pathology.

Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), w.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), with neurologic involvement
Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), w.description: An autosomal recessive disorder, usually caused by AAAS variants, characterized by alacrima, esophageal achalasia, and ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency. Progressive autonomic, peripheral nerve, and pyramidal dysfunction can occur. This is the strongest overall match; achalasia requires confirmation.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: An ABCD1-related disorder affecting adrenal function and nervous-system myelin. Childhood disease can cause adrenal insufficiency followed by progressive cognitive and neurologic deterioration, but normal very long chain fatty acids strongly argue against it in this boy.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: A genetically heterogeneous form of ACTH resistance causing cortisol deficiency with relatively preserved mineralocorticoid production. It explains the endocrine findings well but generally does not explain the complete progressive neurologic and gastrointestinal syndrome.

Familial dysautonomia (Riley-Day syndrom.description: An autosomal recessive sensory and autonomic neuropathy caused by ELP1 variants. It can produce reduced tears, feeding difficulties, vomiting crises, temperature dysregulation, and progressive gait dysfunction, but does not typically cause ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency.

Cervicothoracic syringomyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord that can cause segmental muscle wasting and weakness with long-tract signs below the lesion. The supplied MRI appears to show a central intramedullary fluid-signal cavity, although full imaging review is needed to distinguish syringomyelia from a prominent central canal. This could be a coexisting contributor rather than a unifying diagnosis.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.normalized_text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), with possible hemorrhagic complications
Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: An acute encephalopathy caused by disturbed cerebral vascular regulation and endothelial dysfunction. MRI commonly shows posterior-predominant edema; restricted diffusion and small hemorrhages can occur. Normal blood pressure does not exclude it.

Multifocal acute ischemic cerebral infar.description: Multiple cerebral infarcts can arise from emboli or cancer-associated hypercoagulability. Bilateral involvement may cause severe encephalopathy, and hemorrhagic transformation can produce susceptibility abnormalities.

Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrha.normalized_text: Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrhagic venous infarction
Cerebral venous thrombosis with hemorrha.description: Thrombosis of cerebral veins or dural sinuses can cause bilateral edema, restricted diffusion, and hemorrhagic infarcts. Malignancy is an important risk factor; venographic imaging is needed for confirmation.

Brain metastases from breast carcinoma.description: Breast cancer can spread to the brain, producing lesions with surrounding edema and occasionally hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced MRI is necessary to evaluate this possibility adequately.

Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, includin.normalized_text: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, including hepatic or hyperammonemic encephalopathy
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, includin.description: Systemic metabolic disturbances or impaired hepatic function can cause diffuse brain dysfunction, sometimes with bilateral MRI abnormalities. Liver metastases warrant evaluation, but hepatic failure or hyperammonemia cannot be inferred without laboratory testing.

Isolated spinal cord neurosarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation confined to the nervous system, potentially producing an enhancing cervical spinal cord lesion. This is the leading consideration given the mildly elevated ACE and the apparent granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells in the supplied histology; confirmation requires exclusion of infectious causes.

Intramedullary spinal tuberculoma.description: A localized granulomatous spinal cord lesion caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It can mimic an intramedullary tumor or neurosarcoidosis; tissue microbiology and assessment for caseating necrosis help distinguish it.

Fungal granulomatous myelitis.description: A rare spinal cord infection, such as cryptococcosis or histoplasmosis, that can cause granulomatous inflammation and a mass-like enhancing lesion. Fungal stains, cultures, and organism-specific testing are needed for confirmation.

Idiopathic transverse myelitis.description: Inflammatory spinal cord injury causing motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction, sometimes without abnormal autoimmune serology or brain MRI findings. The apparent granulomatous histology makes an idiopathic cause less likely.

Cervical intramedullary ependymoma.description: A spinal cord tumor that commonly occurs in adults and may produce progressive myelopathy with an enhancing intramedullary mass. It is an imaging differential, but the supplied tissue appears inflammatory rather than neoplastic.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis.description: A fungal lung infection that can occur in otherwise healthy adults and produce nodules, consolidation, or cavities. The tissue images suggest inflammatory changes with possible rounded organisms, but fungal stains and microbiologic testing are needed for confirmation.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia.description: A bacterial infection causing destruction of lung tissue and multiple cavities within consolidation, sometimes following a viral respiratory infection.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: An infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce persistent cough, cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation. Sputum molecular testing and cultures are needed to establish the diagnosis.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic bacterial infection, usually arising after aspiration of organisms from the mouth, that may cause peripheral consolidation, abscesses, and cavitation. Confirmation requires compatible tissue findings or appropriately collected cultures.

Localized cystic bronchiectasis with sup.normalized_text: Localized cystic bronchiectasis with superimposed infection
Localized cystic bronchiectasis with sup.description: Permanent dilation of bronchi can appear as clustered ring-shaped or cystic spaces on CT. A respiratory infection may trigger increased cough, sputum, and surrounding consolidation; full CT review is needed to distinguish dilated airways from true cavities.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis caused by Di.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis caused by Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis caused by Di.description: A mosquito-transmitted filarial infection associated with dogs that causes localized subcutaneous nodules in humans. It occurs in Croatia. The supplied microscopy appears to show a nematode with a thick, externally ridged cuticle, strongly favoring D. repens; definitive identification requires pathology review or molecular testing.

Dirofilariasis caused by Dirofilaria imm.description: A mosquito-transmitted canine filarial infection that usually produces pulmonary nodules in humans but can rarely involve subcutaneous tissue.

Cutaneous gnathostomiasis.description: A tissue-invasive nematode infection, usually acquired through raw or undercooked infected freshwater animals, that causes migrating subcutaneous swellings.

Subcutaneous sparganosis.description: Infection by a Spirometra tapeworm larva, acquired through contaminated water or infected animal tissues, that can produce slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules.

Onchocerciasis.description: A blackfly-transmitted filarial infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus. Adult worms form firm subcutaneous nodules, while microfilariae can cause itching, dermatitis, and eye disease.

Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richards.description: A progressive tau-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early backward falls, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and bulbar dysfunction. This is the strongest fit; the supplied MRI appears to show disproportionate midbrain atrophy with relative pontine preservation.

Multiple system atrophy.description: A progressive synuclein-related disorder causing parkinsonism, cerebellar dysfunction, autonomic failure, and sometimes severe swallowing impairment.

Corticobasal degeneration presenting wit.normalized_text: Corticobasal degeneration presenting with a progressive supranuclear palsy syndrome
Corticobasal degeneration presenting wit.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually causes asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, and cortical dysfunction, but occasionally presents with a PSP-like pattern of falls and gaze palsy.

Adult-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C.description: An inherited intracellular lipid-trafficking disorder that can produce slowly progressive neurologic disease, including vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, movement abnormalities, and dysphagia.

Central nervous system Whipple disease.description: A rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can mimic neurodegenerative disease, including supranuclear gaze palsy, gait dysfunction, and progressive neurologic impairment.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: An opportunistic fungal infection of the meninges, usually caused by Cryptococcus neoformans in advanced HIV. This is strongly favored by the elevated CSF pressure and microscopy showing yeast-like organisms with prominent capsular halos.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute infection of the meninges caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with increased susceptibility in advanced HIV.

Cytomegalovirus meningoencephalitis.description: An opportunistic viral infection of the meninges and brain that occurs particularly in patients with HIV and CD4 counts below 50 cells/µL.

Neurosyphilis presenting as syphilitic m.description: Treponema pallidum infection involving the nervous system can produce meningitis and should be considered in sexually active patients with HIV.

Herpes simplex virus meningoencephalitis.description: HSV infection can cause meningitis or encephalitis with fever, meningeal irritation, and altered mental status; early CT imaging may be normal.

Acute left dorsal pontine ischemic infar.normalized_text: Acute left dorsal pontine ischemic infarction causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute left dorsal pontine ischemic infar.description: A small infarction affecting the left medial longitudinal fasciculus can impair left-eye adduction and cause right-eye abducting nystagmus. The focal dorsal pontine signal abnormality on the supplied diffusion-weighted image supports this diagnosis, although confirmation of restricted diffusion requires the ADC map.

Posterior circulation transient ischemic.description: Transient ischemia affecting brainstem ocular motor pathways can cause isolated diplopia and internuclear ophthalmoplegia. This diagnosis is less likely if the imaging abnormality represents an acute infarction.

Demyelinating brainstem disease causing.normalized_text: Demyelinating brainstem disease causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Demyelinating brainstem disease causing.description: Demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, as can occur in multiple sclerosis, produces impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus.

Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-int.normalized_text: Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-int.description: Autoimmune impairment of neuromuscular transmission can cause variable extraocular muscle weakness and occasionally mimic internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Partial left oculomotor nerve palsy.description: Selective dysfunction of the third cranial nerve can weaken the left medial rectus muscle and cause impaired adduction and diplopia, sometimes from microvascular ischemia in older adults.

Neonatal babesiosis, likely congenital B.normalized_text: Neonatal babesiosis, likely congenital Babesia microti infection
Neonatal babesiosis, likely congenital B.description: An infection of red blood cells that causes fever and hemolysis. Maternal exposure in coastal Massachusetts and the blood smear showing intraerythrocytic organisms, including a tetrad resembling a Maltese cross, strongly favor this diagnosis. Transmission before birth is possible.

Congenital malaria.description: A maternally acquired Plasmodium infection transmitted to an infant, producing fever, anemia, and splenomegaly. It can resemble babesiosis on a blood smear, but the apparent tetrad and reported exposure location favor Babesia.

Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis.description: A serious systemic bacterial infection in a young infant that can cause shock, respiratory distress, and kidney injury. This presentation warrants consideration of sepsis even though the smear strongly suggests a parasitic cause.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.normalized_text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute hemolysis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.description: An inherited red-cell enzyme deficiency that can cause abrupt hemolysis during infection or oxidative stress, particularly in male infants. It could explain anemia and dark urine but not the parasitic smear findings.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It is uncommon at this age, and confirmation would require laboratory evidence of this triad; the supplied smear instead favors an intraerythrocytic infection.

Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal invasion
Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarci.description: Recurrence of the previously treated high-grade prostate cancer, potentially involving the prostatectomy bed and invading the rectum. The apparent pelvic mass, pulmonary nodules, and liver lesion raise concern for metastatic disease; biopsy is needed to establish the origin.

Metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A primary rectal malignancy that can cause pain and tenesmus and spread to the liver and lungs. The apparent pelvic mass and distant lesions are compatible with this possibility, but imaging alone cannot distinguish it from recurrent prostate cancer.

High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.normalized_text: High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the prostate
High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.description: An aggressive prostate malignancy that may arise de novo or in association with prior prostate adenocarcinoma. It can produce bulky pelvic disease and visceral metastases, sometimes with relatively little PSA elevation; tissue examination is required.

Metastatic anal squamous cell carcinoma.description: A malignancy of the anal canal that can cause persistent anorectal pain and tenesmus. Advanced disease can spread to the liver and lungs, although the provided images do not establish an anal primary.

Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma with pel.normalized_text: Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma with pelvic and extranodal involvement
Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma with pel.description: A lymphoid malignancy, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, that can involve pelvic tissues, the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs. This is a less likely alternative to metastatic carcinoma and requires biopsy for confirmation.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.description: Hyperthyroidism-associated intracellular potassium shifts cause acute hypokalemic weakness. The thyroid ultrasound appears diffusely enlarged and hypervascular, supporting Graves disease; thyroid-function tests and TSH-receptor antibodies are needed for confirmation.

Autoimmune thyroiditis with hashitoxicos.normalized_text: Autoimmune thyroiditis with hashitoxicosis and hypokalemic paralysis
Autoimmune thyroiditis with hashitoxicos.description: Autoimmune thyroid inflammation can transiently release excess thyroid hormone and occasionally precipitate hypokalemic paralysis. The supplied histology shows prominent lymphocytic infiltrates and lymphoid follicles, supporting autoimmune thyroid disease, although histology alone cannot establish the cause of thyrotoxicosis.

Herbal supplement–associated hypokalemic.description: Some herbal products cause potassium depletion through laxative or diuretic effects, or through licorice-induced mineralocorticoid activity. The supplement could have precipitated the acute episode, although its ingredients and renal potassium handling must be assessed.

Hypokalemic paralysis due to renal tubul.normalized_text: Hypokalemic paralysis due to renal tubular acidosis
Hypokalemic paralysis due to renal tubul.description: Renal tubular acidification defects can produce metabolic acidosis, renal potassium wasting, and severe weakness. Venous acidemia makes this a consideration, but bicarbonate, anion gap, urine pH, and urine potassium are required to establish it.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder causes episodic weakness associated with intracellular potassium shifts, often beginning in adolescence or young adulthood. It is an alternative explanation for the acute paralysis but does not account for the thyroid findings.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign bony outgrowth along the midline of the hard palate that can become large and lobulated. This is the most likely diagnosis based on the photograph and longstanding, minimally symptomatic history; palpation would help confirm its bony consistency.

Palatal osteoma.description: A benign, slow-growing tumor composed of mature bone that can occasionally arise from the palate.

Non-torus palatal exostosis.description: A benign localized overgrowth of normal palatal bone outside the classic midline torus pattern.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A benign salivary gland tumor that may present as a painless, slowly enlarging palatal mass, typically away from the midline.

Oral irritation fibroma.description: A benign reactive overgrowth of fibrous tissue caused by chronic irritation, generally presenting as a smooth, mucosa-colored oral nodule.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation with nerve-root c.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation with nerve-root compression, likely at L4–L5
Lumbar disc herniation with nerve-root c.description: Displaced intervertebral disc material can compress lumbar nerve roots, causing sciatica and weakness. The supplied sagittal MRI appears to show a prominent posterior disc extrusion at approximately L4–L5, making this the leading possibility; full MRI review is needed to confirm its location and extent.

Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Degenerative changes, sometimes compounded by a herniated disc, narrow the spinal canal or nerve-root passages. The apparent lower-lumbar canal narrowing on the image could contribute to nerve compression.

Lumbar facet synovial cyst with nerve-ro.normalized_text: Lumbar facet synovial cyst with nerve-root compression
Lumbar facet synovial cyst with nerve-ro.description: A fluid-containing cyst arising from a degenerative facet joint can occupy the spinal canal and compress a nerve root. It is an alternative explanation for a focal compressive lesion, although the supplied image appears more suggestive of disc material.

Lumbar spinal epidural hematoma.description: Bleeding into the spinal epidural space can rapidly compress nerve roots, producing acute pain and neurological deficits. The visible lesion appears disc-related rather than clearly hemorrhagic, so this is a lower-probability alternative. New weakness of 3/5 warrants urgent in-person spinal assessment regardless of the cause.

Lumbar nerve-root schwannoma.description: A usually benign nerve-sheath tumor can cause back pain, radicular pain, and weakness through nerve-root compression. It is a less likely structural alternative because the supplied image appears to show a disc-associated lesion; additional MRI sequences would be needed to characterize a suspected tumor.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome wi.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with cerebral and cardiac involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome wi.description: A disorder characterized by marked unexplained eosinophilia and eosinophil-mediated organ injury. This is the leading consideration, although exclusion of secondary and clonal causes is required. Cerebral injury may result from thrombosis, endothelial damage, or cardiac emboli.

Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocardi.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocardial disease with cardioembolic cerebral infarctions
Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocardi.description: Eosinophilic inflammation can injure the myocardium and endocardium, sometimes producing intracardiac thrombi that embolize to multiple cerebral territories. This may be a cardiac manifestation of hypereosinophilic syndrome.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic eosinophilic small- to medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly involves the respiratory tract, peripheral nerves, and heart; cerebral ischemia can occur but is uncommon.

Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloi.normalized_text: Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloid neoplasm
Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloi.description: A hematologic neoplasm, such as chronic eosinophilic leukemia or a tyrosine kinase fusion-associated myeloid disorder, can cause pronounced eosinophilia with cardiac injury and thrombotic neurologic complications. Molecular and bone marrow testing are needed to distinguish it from idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.

Helminth-associated secondary hypereosin.normalized_text: Helminth-associated secondary hypereosinophilia with neurologic and cardiac involvement
Helminth-associated secondary hypereosin.description: Tissue-invasive helminth infections can cause marked eosinophilia and pulmonary lesions; selected infections can also affect the brain or heart. This is less likely given the reported negative parasitic evaluation.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease, commonly involving the lungs and thoracic lymph nodes. This is the leading possibility given the imaging, elevated ACE level, and apparent non-necrotizing granulomas.

Malignancy-associated sarcoid-like react.description: Non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation associated with cancer or its treatment that can resemble systemic sarcoidosis and mimic metastases on PET imaging.

Recurrent breast cancer with thoracic me.normalized_text: Recurrent breast cancer with thoracic metastases
Recurrent breast cancer with thoracic me.description: Breast cancer recurrence involving thoracic lymph nodes or lungs; FDG uptake alone cannot distinguish metastatic cancer from granulomatous inflammation.

Lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can cause intensely FDG-avid lymphadenopathy and cytopenias; granulomatous reactions occasionally accompany lymphoma.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis with pulmonary.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce granulomatous thoracic lymphadenopathy and FDG-avid pulmonary lesions. Negative immune-based tests reduce suspicion but do not completely exclude active infection.

Multiple myeloma with osteosclerotic bon.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with osteosclerotic bone involvement
Multiple myeloma with osteosclerotic bon.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing monoclonal immunoglobulin and causing organ damage. This is the leading diagnosis; the apparent diffuse skeletal sclerosis suggests an uncommon osteosclerotic presentation rather than typical lytic myeloma.

POEMS syndrome.description: A plasma-cell-associated syndrome characterized by polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein, and skin changes, often with osteosclerotic bone lesions. The available findings do not establish its required diagnostic criteria.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgG p.normalized_text: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgG paraprotein
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgG p.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation that usually produces IgM but can rarely produce IgG. Bone marrow examination and immunophenotyping distinguish it from myeloma.

Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with.normalized_text: Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell clone
Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with.description: A disorder in which monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains form amyloid deposits in organs, commonly affecting the kidneys, heart, and peripheral nerves. Tissue staining is required for confirmation.

Osteoblastic skeletal metastases from an.normalized_text: Osteoblastic skeletal metastases from an occult carcinoma
Osteoblastic skeletal metastases from an.description: Metastatic solid tumors, including breast carcinoma, can cause diffuse skeletal sclerosis and marrow infiltration. This is a less likely alternative because it does not adequately explain the pronounced monoclonal plasma-cell laboratory findings.

Intracranial germinoma with suprasellar.normalized_text: Intracranial germinoma with suprasellar and pineal involvement
Intracranial germinoma with suprasellar.description: A germ-cell tumor occurring predominantly in adolescents and young adults. Suprasellar involvement can cause diabetes insipidus and pituitary hormone deficiencies. The apparent enhancing suprasellar and pineal-region lesions make this a leading possibility, but imaging alone is not diagnostic.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.description: A disorder of abnormal inflammatory myeloid cells that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, producing central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Neurosarcoidosis with hypothalamic-pitui.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can affect the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, meninges, and other brain structures, causing endocrine and neurological dysfunction.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A generally nonmalignant epithelial tumor near the pituitary and hypothalamus that can compress the optic pathways and impair pituitary hormone production.

Pituitary macroprolactinoma.description: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma that can suppress gonadal function and, when large, compress the optic chiasm. Prolactin testing and dedicated pituitary assessment would be needed to evaluate this possibility.

MRSA aortic valve infective endocarditis.description: Infection of the aortic valve by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, causing vegetations, valve damage, and systemic septic emboli. The echocardiographic images appear to show an aortic valve vegetation, making this the leading diagnosis.

Aortic perivalvular abscess complicating.normalized_text: Aortic perivalvular abscess complicating infective endocarditis
Aortic perivalvular abscess complicating.description: Extension of valve infection into the surrounding aortic root tissue. This can damage the cardiac conduction system. The ECG strips appear to show prolonged atrioventricular conduction, and the echocardiographic abnormality adjacent to the valve raises concern for an abscess.

Acute ischemic stroke from cerebral sept.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke from cerebral septic embolism
Acute ischemic stroke from cerebral sept.description: Occlusion of a cerebral artery by infected material shed from a cardiac vegetation. This is a likely neurological complication of the suspected left-sided endocarditis, although brain imaging is needed for confirmation.

Hematogenous brain abscess.description: A localized intracerebral infection that can develop through bloodstream spread of MRSA or septic embolization from endocarditis. It can cause headache, altered consciousness, and focal neurological deficits.

Persistent or recurrent MRSA discitis wi.normalized_text: Persistent or recurrent MRSA discitis with psoas abscess
Persistent or recurrent MRSA discitis wi.description: Ongoing spinal and adjacent psoas infection could sustain MRSA bacteremia and seed the heart or other organs. It is an important potential infectious source given the recent admission, but does not adequately explain the whole presentation alone.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: Autosomal recessive acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. The markedly deficient GAA activity and two GAA variants in trans strongly establish this diagnosis. CRIM status requires protein testing and cannot be inferred solely from absence of p.D645E.

Glycogen storage disease type IIIa.description: An autosomal recessive glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency that can affect liver, skeletal muscle, and heart. It is a differential for metabolic cardiomyopathy but does not explain the confirmed GAA deficiency.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked LAMP2-related lysosomal disorder associated with cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy. Neonatal presentation in a female is very unusual, and the biochemical and genetic findings favor Pompe disease instead.

Primary mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.description: A mitochondrial energy-production disorder can cause neonatal cardiomyopathy with skeletal muscle and liver abnormalities. This is a broad alternative for the cardiac and enzyme findings, but it does not account for the specific GAA results.

Transient neonatal hypertrophic cardiomy.normalized_text: Transient neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with maternal diabetes
Transient neonatal hypertrophic cardiomy.description: Fetal hyperinsulinemia associated with maternal diabetes can produce macrosomia and transient neonatal myocardial hypertrophy. Maternal diabetes is not documented here, and this alternative cannot explain the confirmed metabolic findings.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with.normalized_text: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with extramedullary involvement
B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with.description: A malignancy of immature B lymphocytes that can infiltrate bone marrow, bone, lymph nodes, and other tissues. The blast-like cells and CD19/CD10-positive population shown favor this diagnosis; CD33 can be aberrantly expressed.

Metastatic neuroblastoma.description: A childhood tumor of sympathetic nervous tissue, commonly arising in the adrenal gland or abdominal sympathetic chain. Bone and orbital metastases can cause pain, limping, and periorbital bruising, although the displayed B-cell immunophenotype argues against it.

B-lymphoblastic lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B cells presenting predominantly as tissue masses rather than extensive marrow disease. It shares the CD19/CD10-positive phenotype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; marrow assessment is needed to distinguish them.

Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarcoma
Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.description: A malignancy of myeloid precursor cells that may produce extramedullary masses, including orbital lesions. CD33 expression raises consideration, but the strong B-cell marker pattern shown favors a B-lineage malignancy unless additional testing establishes myeloid differentiation.

Ewing sarcoma with metastatic disease.description: An aggressive bone or soft-tissue sarcoma that can cause pain, fever, and distant skeletal lesions. It is less common at age six, and the displayed lymphoid immunophenotype argues strongly against it.

Gluteal cellulitis.description: Bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The erythema and apparent subcutaneous edema on ultrasound support this possibility, although the images alone are not diagnostic.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive infection involving subcutaneous tissue and fascia that requires emergency surgical assessment when suspected. Possible gas-related ultrasound artifacts raise concern but cannot establish the diagnosis.

Gluteal abscess with surrounding celluli.description: A localized collection of pus in the gluteal soft tissues, often accompanied by surrounding skin inflammation. A definite fluid collection is not clearly demonstrated in the supplied ultrasound images.

Erysipelas.description: A bacterial infection of the superficial dermis and lymphatics that typically produces a tender, bright-red plaque with a raised, sharply defined border.

Gluteal pyomyositis.description: Bacterial infection of the gluteal muscle, sometimes progressing to an intramuscular abscess. Deeper imaging would be needed because the supplied images do not establish muscle involvement.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease with c.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with cutaneous and musculoskeletal involvement
Chronic graft-versus-host disease with c.description: A delayed immune complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation that can cause inflammatory or sclerotic skin changes, fascial restriction, myositis, and liver abnormalities. This is a leading consideration given the transplant history and positive prayer sign.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory muscle disease associated with characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions. The facial and upper-chest erythema and reddish-purple dorsal hand lesions in the photographs raise this possibility.

Systemic lupus erythematosus.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive skin eruptions, fever, and musculoskeletal inflammation. A positive ANA supports consideration but does not establish the diagnosis.

Systemic sclerosis.description: An autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by skin fibrosis and possible internal-organ involvement. Skin tightening can limit hand and wrist movement.

Eosinophilic fasciitis.description: An inflammatory fibrosing disorder of the fascia that can cause limb pain, skin induration, and joint contractures. A similar fascial process can occur in chronic graft-versus-host disease.

Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas.description: An eruption of crateriform, keratin-producing squamous tumors that can resemble squamous cell carcinoma. This is the leading diagnosis because the image timeline reports 15 histologically diagnosed keratoacanthomas.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: A malignant keratinocyte tumor that may have a crateriform appearance closely resembling keratoacanthoma. Adequate histologic assessment is needed to distinguish these overlapping lesions.

Acquired perforating dermatosis.description: A pruritic skin disorder associated with advanced kidney disease and dialysis, characterized by elimination of dermal material through the epidermis, producing centrally plugged papules.

Prurigo nodularis.description: A chronic itch-scratch disorder producing firm, excoriated papules and nodules, sometimes associated with chronic kidney disease.

Verruca vulgaris.description: A benign human papillomavirus-associated epidermal proliferation producing keratotic papules. Warts may coexist with other lesions; the image timeline reports three histologically confirmed common warts.

Zika virus-associated acute transverse m.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord associated with direct viral infection or an infection-triggered immune response. This is the leading possibility given Zika PCR positivity in serum, urine, and CSF, together with a spinal cord syndrome and apparent intramedullary T2 signal abnormalities on MRI.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can cause severe and longitudinally extensive spinal cord inflammation. Antibody testing and further imaging would be needed to evaluate this possibility.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disorder that can cause acute myelitis in children and adolescents, sometimes following infection. Serum MOG-IgG testing is needed to support the diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis presenting with acute.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis presenting with acute partial myelitis
Multiple sclerosis presenting with acute.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can initially present with an asymmetric spinal cord syndrome. Diagnosis requires additional evidence, including dissemination in space and time or qualifying supportive findings.

Zika virus-associated Guillain-Barre syn.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy associated with Zika infection that causes progressive weakness, sensory symptoms, and sometimes autonomic dysfunction. It is substantially less likely here because the findings primarily localize to the spinal cord.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-A.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), with an atypical TdT-negative phenotype
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-A.description: An aggressive malignancy of immature T cells involving blood and bone marrow. This is the leading consideration given the blast burden and T-lineage markers. The supplied cytogenetic images indicate TCRA/D-associated rearrangements, including an Xq22.3 region near IRS4, supporting a T-cell neoplasm but not independently establishing its subtype.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia usually occurring in older adults, often with marked lymphocytosis and organ enlargement. Mature T-cell marker expression and absence of TdT make it a differential consideration; confirmation requires characteristic morphology and supporting genetic findings.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, acute su.description: An aggressive mature T-cell malignancy associated with HTLV-1 infection. It can produce leukocytosis, marrow involvement, and very high LDH; HTLV-1 testing is necessary to support this diagnosis.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, with leukemic involvement
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: A heterogeneous mature T-cell lymphoma that can rarely involve blood extensively. Tissue evaluation and exclusion of other defined T-cell neoplasms are required.

Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma with leuke.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement
Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma with leuke.description: A rare aggressive mature T-cell lymphoma affecting predominantly young men, usually involving the spleen, liver, and bone marrow with little lymphadenopathy. Extensive circulating disease is uncommon.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infection or malignancy. This is the leading syndromic diagnosis, although formal diagnostic criteria and the underlying trigger require confirmation.

Disseminated tuberculosis with secondary.description: Tuberculosis involving multiple organs can trigger HLH and cause severe pulmonary disease. The apparent granulomatous tissue changes support consideration of tuberculosis, but microbiologic or molecular confirmation is necessary.

Disseminated fungal infection with secon.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection with secondary HLH
Disseminated fungal infection with secon.description: Systemic fungal infections, particularly histoplasmosis or talaromycosis, can involve the lungs and bone marrow and provoke HLH. Organism identification and exposure assessment are needed to distinguish these infections.

Lymphoma-associated HLH.description: An occult lymphoma, particularly a T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma, can trigger severe HLH before the malignancy is recognized. Tissue examination and hematologic testing are required for confirmation.

Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis,.normalized_text: Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome
Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis,.description: Severe pulmonary bacterial infection can cause shock, diffuse lung injury, and consumptive coagulopathy. It could coexist with HLH but is less satisfactory as the sole explanation for this presentation.

Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.description: Varicella-zoster virus can cause brain inflammation and infection of cerebral arteries, producing arterial narrowing and multifocal ischemic strokes, sometimes without a characteristic shingles rash.

Dengue-associated encephalitis with cere.description: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that can rarely cause encephalitis, vascular injury, and ischemic neurological complications.

Chikungunya-associated encephalitis.description: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne infection that occasionally causes severe encephalitis, particularly in older adults; cerebral vascular complications are rare.

Herpes simplex virus encephalitis.description: Herpes simplex virus causes acute, potentially devastating brain inflammation, usually involving the temporal and inferior frontal lobes.

Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with.normalized_text: Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with secondary cerebral vasculopathy
Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with.description: Bacterial infection of the meninges and brain can cause coma and inflammation or thrombosis of cerebral vessels, resulting in ischemic strokes.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura.description: An IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis, often following a respiratory infection, that causes purpura, arthritis, and sometimes gastrointestinal or renal involvement. This is the leading diagnosis given the apparent vascular IgA deposition in the supplied biopsy images.

Adalimumab-associated cutaneous small-ve.description: A potential anti-TNF treatment complication causing immune-mediated inflammation of dermal small vessels; it can sometimes have an IgA-mediated pattern. Medication causation cannot be established from this case alone.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, and kidneys and may produce skin purpura and arthritis.

Postinfectious cutaneous leukocytoclasti.description: Small-vessel skin inflammation triggered by an infection, usually causing dependent purpura and sometimes arthralgia or localized edema. IgA-dominant staining would favor the more specific diagnosis of IgA vasculitis.

Left lower-extremity deep vein thrombosi.description: A clot in a deep leg vein causing unilateral pain and swelling. Crohn’s disease increases venous thromboembolism risk; this remains an important possible concurrent diagnosis requiring prompt exclusion despite the vasculitic skin findings.

Left tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma w.normalized_text: Left tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma with cervical lymph node metastasis, potentially HPV-associated
Left tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma w.description: An oropharyngeal malignancy arising in the palatine tonsil that commonly spreads to upper cervical lymph nodes. This is the leading consideration; HPV-associated disease can occur in nonsmokers, but HPV status requires tissue testing.

Base-of-tongue squamous cell carcinoma w.normalized_text: Base-of-tongue squamous cell carcinoma with cervical lymph node metastasis
Base-of-tongue squamous cell carcinoma w.description: A malignancy of the lingual tonsil or tongue base that can cause referred ear pain and present with metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy.

Tonsillar lymphoma with cervical lymphad.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the tonsil and regional lymph nodes, potentially producing unilateral tonsillar enlargement and marked PET uptake.

Minor salivary gland carcinoma of the or.normalized_text: Minor salivary gland carcinoma of the oropharynx
Minor salivary gland carcinoma of the or.description: A rare malignancy arising from small salivary glands in the oropharynx, such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma, which may cause a local mass and cervical metastases.

Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervic.normalized_text: Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervical lymphadenopathy
Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervic.description: Persistent tonsillar inflammation can cause throat pain, referred ear pain, regional lymph node enlargement, and increased PET uptake, although the findings here are more concerning for malignancy.

Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.normalized_text: Primary urinary bladder extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma that can develop in the bladder in association with chronic inflammation. The apparent lymphoid infiltrate and lymphoepithelial involvement favor this diagnosis, but confirmation requires immunophenotyping and interpretation of the molecular testing.

Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the bla.normalized_text: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the bladder (follicular cystitis)
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the bla.description: A benign lymphoid response to chronic bladder irritation or infection that can resemble lymphoma. Organized reactive follicles and a polyclonal lymphoid population would support this diagnosis.

Primary urinary bladder diffuse large B-.normalized_text: Primary urinary bladder diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary urinary bladder diffuse large B-.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that rarely arises primarily in the bladder and may cause symptoms resembling cystitis. Diagnosis requires demonstration of a predominantly large, atypical B-cell population.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.description: A malignant tumor of the bladder lining that can produce persistent urinary irritation and cystoscopic abnormalities. Confirmation requires malignant urothelial cells on biopsy.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the.normalized_text: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the urinary bladder
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma with lymphoplasmacytic differentiation, usually involving bone marrow and often associated with a monoclonal IgM protein. Isolated bladder involvement would be unusual.

Emphysematous cystitis.description: A gas-forming infection of the bladder wall and lumen, commonly associated with diabetes and organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae. This is the leading consideration given the apparent curvilinear gas outlining the bladder on the radiograph; CT can confirm the location of the gas.

Complicated bacterial cystitis.description: A bacterial bladder infection occurring in a patient with risk factors for complications, such as diabetes and advanced age. Ordinary cystitis does not produce gas within the bladder wall.

Colovesical fistula.description: An abnormal connection between the colon and bladder, often caused by diverticular disease or malignancy, allowing bowel gas and bacteria to enter the urinary tract.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis.description: A potentially life-threatening gas-forming infection of the kidney and surrounding tissues, particularly in patients with diabetes. Renal imaging would be needed to assess this possibility.

Right femoral neck fracture.description: A fracture near the hip joint, commonly caused by a low-energy fall in an older adult. The right femoral neck appears abnormal on this image, warranting dedicated hip views or CT for confirmation; this could coexist with the urinary infection.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with an unstable or detached fragment
Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.description: A focal disorder of subchondral bone that can cause overlying cartilage and bone to separate, producing an intra-articular loose body. The apparent femoral condylar defect and displaced osteochondral fragment on these radiographs make this the leading possibility.

Chronic post-traumatic osteochondral fra.normalized_text: Chronic post-traumatic osteochondral fracture with an intra-articular loose body
Chronic post-traumatic osteochondral fra.description: An old injury involving articular cartilage and underlying bone can leave a detached fragment that later causes swelling and mechanical obstruction. This could also account for the apparent osteochondral defect and fragment.

Displaced meniscal tear.description: A torn meniscal fragment, particularly a bucket-handle tear, can become displaced and block knee motion. It explains the mechanical symptoms but would not itself explain the apparent bony defect or osteochondral fragment on the radiographs.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A benign synovial disorder that produces cartilaginous nodules, which may detach and become calcified or ossified loose bodies. It can cause atraumatic swelling and locking, although multiple bodies are more characteristic than the apparent focal osteochondral abnormality here.

Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the kne.normalized_text: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the knee
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the kne.description: A benign proliferative synovial lesion, including the diffuse form formerly called pigmented villonodular synovitis, that can cause recurrent pain, effusion, and occasionally catching or locking. The apparent osteochondral fragment is not a characteristic imaging feature.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoid malignancy involving the pancreas that can cause a pancreatic mass and biliary obstruction. The lymphoid-appearing biopsy raises this possibility, but classification requires identification of the immunohistochemical stains and assessment for disease elsewhere.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of pancreatic ductal cells, commonly causing obstructive jaundice when located in the pancreatic head.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the distal extrahepatic bile duct that can obstruct bile flow near the pancreatic head and resemble a pancreatic tumor.

Autoimmune pancreatitis.description: An inflammatory pancreatic disorder, often associated with IgG4-related disease, that can produce focal pancreatic enlargement and obstructive jaundice resembling cancer.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A pancreatic neoplasm arising from neuroendocrine cells. A nonfunctioning tumor in the pancreatic head can cause biliary obstruction; confirmation requires neuroendocrine immunohistochemical markers.

Secondary uremic tumoral calcinosis.description: Mass-like calcium phosphate deposition in soft tissues associated with advanced kidney disease and disturbed phosphate metabolism. This is the most likely diagnosis given the lobulated calcified mass and marked hyperphosphatemia.

Dystrophic calcinosis cutis.description: Calcium deposition in previously damaged or inflamed skin and subcutaneous tissue, generally occurring independently of systemic calcium and phosphate abnormalities.

Calciphylaxis.description: Calcification and thrombosis of small cutaneous vessels, usually in patients with advanced kidney disease, causing ischemic skin injury. The painless mass without skin breakdown makes this substantially less likely.

Myositis ossificans.description: Benign formation of mature bone in soft tissue, commonly following trauma and usually involving muscle. Imaging typically shows organized peripheral ossification rather than amorphous calcium deposits.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue tumor that produces osteoid or bone without originating in the skeleton. It can present as an enlarging mineralized mass in older adults.

Comminuted tibial plateau fracture.description: An intra-articular fracture of the upper tibia, often caused by high-energy trauma. The radiographs appear to show a complex proximal tibial fracture involving the plateau and extending into the metaphysis; CT would clarify the fracture pattern.

Tibial eminence avulsion fracture.description: A fracture of the tibial spine at the anterior cruciate ligament attachment, potentially producing knee instability. It may occur with other proximal tibial fractures.

Anterior cruciate ligament rupture.description: A tear of the ligament that limits forward movement of the tibia, commonly associated with skiing injuries and rapid traumatic joint swelling. It could accompany the visible fracture but cannot be confirmed on these radiographs.

Posterior cruciate ligament injury.description: An injury to the ligament that limits backward movement of the tibia, typically resulting from force applied to the upper tibia or severe knee hyperflexion. It is a possible associated injury after high-energy trauma.

Acute traumatic meniscal tear.description: A tear of a knee meniscus caused by compression or twisting. Meniscal injuries can accompany tibial plateau fractures, although radiographs do not directly demonstrate them.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall, often associated with KIT or PDGFRA mutations. The submucosal mass and spindle-cell histology make this a leading possibility; the immunostains and sequencing images require marker and gene labels for definitive interpretation.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise within the rectal wall and produce a bulky spindle-cell mass. Diagnosis requires assessment of atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and smooth-muscle immunostains.

Rectal schwannoma.description: A usually benign nerve-sheath tumor that can present as a well-circumscribed gastrointestinal submucosal mass composed of spindle cells.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that can cause a smooth submucosal rectal bulge and obstructive symptoms when sufficiently large.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant gland-forming tumor of the rectal mucosa that commonly causes altered bowel habits and tenesmus. It is less favored here because the lesion is submucosal and the supplied histology appears spindle-cell rather than gland-forming.

PIK3R1-related SHORT syndrome.description: An autosomal dominant disorder characterized by growth restriction, characteristic facial features, partial lipodystrophy, delayed dentition, and possible insulin resistance. The reported de novo PIK3R1 variant strongly supports this as the leading diagnosis.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: An imprinting-related growth disorder causing prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, low body weight, a prominent forehead, and triangular facial appearance. It is a phenotypic alternative but does not explain the PIK3R1 finding.

Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome.description: A rare neonatal progeroid disorder, usually associated with biallelic POLR3A variants, featuring prenatal growth restriction, reduced subcutaneous fat, thin skin, and characteristic craniofacial abnormalities.

Mandibular hypoplasia, deafness, progero.normalized_text: Mandibular hypoplasia, deafness, progeroid features, and lipodystrophy syndrome
Mandibular hypoplasia, deafness, progero.description: A POLD1-related disorder combining mandibular hypoplasia, sensorineural deafness, lipodystrophy, growth abnormalities, and a prematurely aged appearance. It overlaps clinically but is not explained by the reported PIK3R1 variant.

Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.description: An LMNA-related premature-aging disorder characterized by early-childhood growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, skin changes, mandibular hypoplasia, and progressive cardiovascular disease.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: An adult-onset combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, markedly reduced or absent B cells, and variable T-cell dysfunction. It can persist or become apparent after thymoma resection and is the strongest unifying diagnosis here.

Common variable immunodeficiency.description: A primary antibody deficiency causing impaired vaccine responses, recurrent respiratory infections, and sometimes chronic gastrointestinal disease. Serum immunoglobulin measurements are needed to assess this possibility; the thymoma history and profound B-cell depletion favor Good syndrome instead.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: An opportunistic pulmonary infection associated with impaired cellular immunity. Positive induced sputum together with fever, cough, and dyspnea supports this diagnosis, although organism detection alone does not always distinguish infection from colonization.

Moraxella catarrhalis pneumonia.description: A bacterial respiratory infection that can cause pneumonia in patients with impaired host defenses. Detection in sputum and focal pulmonary consolidation support possible infection, although sputum positivity can also reflect airway colonization.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A mycobacterial infection that can cause chronic constitutional symptoms and cavitary lung disease. Ethiopian origin and immunodeficiency increase its relevance, but the reported negative infectious evaluation and nonspecific biopsy reduce support without necessarily excluding it.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A lymphoma common in young adults that often involves cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes. Fibrous bands and large lacunar-type cells in the supplied biopsy favor this diagnosis, although the unlabeled immunostains require confirmation.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A T-cell lymphoma characterized by large atypical cells, usually with strong CD30 expression; ALK-positive disease frequently affects young adults.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma arising in the mediastinum, usually in young adults, that can show large pale cells and compartmentalizing fibrosis.

Rosai-Dorfman disease.description: A histiocytic disorder that often causes painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis requires characteristic histiocytes with emperipolesis and an appropriate immunophenotype.

Reactive lymphadenitis.description: Benign lymph-node enlargement caused by immune stimulation, sometimes with enlarged activated lymphoid cells. Preserved architecture and a nonmalignant immunophenotype would be needed to support this diagnosis.

Acute fulminant myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle that can rapidly cause heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and ventricular arrhythmias. The preceding infectious illness raises concern for viral myocarditis, although the cause cannot be established from these images alone.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy.description: Pregnancy-associated heart failure caused by left ventricular systolic dysfunction without another identifiable cause. Twin gestation increases risk; presentation at 32 weeks is earlier than the classic final-month presentation.

Acute pulmonary embolism arising from de.normalized_text: Acute pulmonary embolism arising from deep vein thrombosis
Acute pulmonary embolism arising from de.description: A thrombus, usually originating in a leg vein, obstructs pulmonary arteries and may cause acute right ventricular failure and cardiovascular collapse. Pregnancy and obesity increase thromboembolic risk.

Pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronar.description: Separation within a coronary artery wall can compromise coronary blood flow and cause myocardial infarction during pregnancy or postpartum. The provided angiographic still does not establish a dissection.

Takotsubo syndrome.description: An acute, usually reversible form of ventricular dysfunction associated with physical or emotional stress that can mimic myocardial infarction and occasionally cause shock or ventricular arrhythmias. Confirmation requires characteristic ventricular imaging and exclusion of competing causes.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia wi.normalized_text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with hepatic vascular malformations
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia wi.description: An autosomal dominant vascular disorder causing recurrent bleeding, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and visceral vascular malformations. The hepatic imaging appears to show enlarged vascular channels and abnormal flow, supporting hepatic vascular shunting, although definitive characterization requires further evaluation.

Portosystemic encephalopathy due to intr.normalized_text: Portosystemic encephalopathy due to intrahepatic vascular shunting
Portosystemic encephalopathy due to intr.description: Brain dysfunction caused by portal blood bypassing hepatic detoxification through abnormal vascular connections. This can occur without cirrhosis, including in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and may be precipitated by dehydration or acute illness.

Cirrhosis with portal hypertension and h.normalized_text: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension and hepatic encephalopathy
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension and h.description: Chronic hepatic scarring can cause portal hypertension, collateral vascular formation, cytopenias from hypersplenism, and encephalopathy. It is an alternative explanation, but cirrhosis is not established by the supplied findings.

Dehydration-associated metabolic encepha.description: Acute delirium caused by volume depletion and associated electrolyte disturbances or renal dysfunction. Diarrhea and poor intake support this possibility, but laboratory testing is needed to establish the metabolic abnormality.

Infection-associated delirium, including.normalized_text: Infection-associated delirium, including possible sepsis from a gastrointestinal source
Infection-associated delirium, including.description: An acute infection can produce delirium and profound lethargy in older adults, sometimes without prominent fever. Chills and diarrhea suggest an infectious trigger, but sepsis requires additional clinical and laboratory evidence.

Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (ur.description: Accumulation of mast cells in the skin causes brown or orange-brown lesions, often beginning in infancy. Rubbing may produce localized swelling and redness (Darier sign). This is the leading consideration, but examination and possibly biopsy are needed for confirmation.

Idiopathic eruptive macular pigmentation.description: A rare, benign pigmentary disorder characterized by spontaneously appearing brown macules without preceding inflammation or medication exposure. Infantile onset is unusual.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 presenting with.normalized_text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 presenting with café-au-lait macules
Neurofibromatosis type 1 presenting with.description: A genetic disorder that can initially present with multiple café-au-lait macules in infancy. Six or more lesions larger than 5 mm in a prepubertal child constitute one diagnostic criterion, but additional criteria are necessary to establish the diagnosis.

Multiple lentigines (lentigo simplex).description: Benign, localized increases in epidermal pigmentation producing discrete brown macules that can occur independently of sun exposure.

Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.description: Residual pigmentation following skin inflammation or injury, sometimes after an inflammatory episode that was subtle or unnoticed.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wil.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery, often after substantial weight loss. This is the leading possibility: the provided CT images show marked gastroduodenal dilation with an aortomesenteric distance of approximately 3.3 mm and angle of approximately 13.6 degrees.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying without a mechanical obstruction, potentially associated with malnutrition. It can cause postprandial vomiting and weight loss, but does not explain the apparent vascular compression of the duodenum.

Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.description: Impaired intestinal nerve or muscle function producing obstruction-like symptoms without a fixed mechanical blockage. Less likely here because the imaging suggests a focal duodenal compression rather than generalized dysmotility.

Crohn disease with gastroduodenal involv.normalized_text: Crohn disease with gastroduodenal involvement or stricture
Crohn disease with gastroduodenal involv.description: Inflammatory bowel disease that can rarely narrow the upper small intestine and cause obstructive vomiting. It could explain weight loss and elevated ESR, but the supplied images favor extrinsic vascular compression.

Celiac disease.description: An immune-mediated reaction to gluten that damages the small intestinal lining and can cause malnutrition, weight loss, and menstrual disturbances. It is a possible contributor to chronic weight loss but does not adequately explain the apparent focal duodenal obstruction.

Gastrocolic fistula after Roux-en-Y gast.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Gastrocolic fistula after Roux-en-Y gast.description: An abnormal connection between the gastric pouch and colon that allows food to bypass the small intestine and colonic contents to reflux into the stomach. The supplied contrast images show a fistula between the gastric pouch and transverse colon, making this the leading diagnosis.

Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anas.normalized_text: Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with fistulization
Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anas.description: Ulceration near the gastric pouch–jejunal junction after gastric bypass can penetrate adjacent structures and produce a gastrocolic fistula. The endoscopic image suggests an ulcerated area, although its cause cannot be established from the image alone.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.description: Excessive bacteria in the small intestine, sometimes promoted by altered anatomy after gastric bypass, can cause fermentation, fat malabsorption, and nutritional deficiencies. It could coexist with a fistula but does not explain the demonstrated gastric-to-colonic connection.

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.description: Insufficient pancreatic digestive enzyme activity causes maldigestion, especially of fat, resulting in steatorrhea and weight loss. Altered digestive anatomy after gastric bypass may contribute to impaired enzyme–food mixing.

Fistulizing Crohn disease.description: Transmural inflammatory bowel disease can cause diarrhea, malnutrition, and abnormal connections between gastrointestinal organs, rarely including a gastrocolic fistula. The images establish a fistula but do not establish Crohn disease as its cause.
