Spontaneous pneumomediastinum associated.description: Air leaks from ruptured alveoli into the mediastinum, often following coughing or increased airway pressure during an asthma exacerbation. The radiograph appears to show lucency outlining mediastinal structures, making this the leading possibility.

Acute asthma exacerbation.description: An episode of increased airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction causing wheezing, cough, and breathlessness, potentially triggered by inconsistent inhaler use. It may coexist with pneumomediastinum.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air accumulates in the pleural space, causing partial lung collapse and potentially sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness. Asthma can predispose to air-leak complications, although a definite pneumothorax is not evident on the supplied image.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by a blood clot can produce acute breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude it, but the case provides no clear thromboembolic risk factors.

Acute bronchitis triggering an asthma ex.normalized_text: Acute bronchitis triggering an asthma exacerbation
Acute bronchitis triggering an asthma ex.description: Inflammation of the larger airways, usually caused by a viral infection, can produce cough and sputum and trigger bronchospasm in someone with asthma.

Pellagra (niacin deficiency).description: A nutritional disorder caused by deficiency of niacin or its precursor tryptophan. It produces photosensitive dermatitis and may cause gastrointestinal and neurologic abnormalities. The photographed neck rash resembles a Casal necklace, making this a leading consideration.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis associated with hepatitis C that can cause painful peripheral neuropathy, purpura, joint symptoms, and kidney disease.

Thiamine deficiency neuropathy (dry beri.description: A nutritional deficiency causing a predominantly distal, usually symmetric peripheral neuropathy. Limited access to adequate nutrition may increase risk, although dietary deficiency is not established in this case.

Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy.description: A deficiency that can damage peripheral nerves and spinal cord pathways, causing distal paresthesias, sensory impairment, and gait instability.

Porphyria cutanea tarda.description: A disorder of hepatic heme synthesis that causes sun-exposed skin fragility, blistering, and erosions. Hepatitis C is a recognized association, but this diagnosis would not usually explain the neuropathy.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton dise.description: A BTK-related defect in B-cell maturation causing profound antibody deficiency and recurrent infections in male infants. This is overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis given the BTK p.C165Y variant and reduced BTK expression shown in the supplied figures; low-level maternal mosaicism explains the negative family history.

Autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia.description: Defects in genes involved in early B-cell development, such as IGHM or CD79A, can produce an antibody-deficiency phenotype similar to Bruton disease. This is a substantially less likely alternative because the molecular findings implicate BTK.

Severe combined immunodeficiency.description: A group of disorders causing severe T-cell dysfunction, sometimes with B-cell deficiency, leading to serious infections during infancy. The clinical presentation overlaps, but the BTK findings strongly favor isolated B-cell immunodeficiency.

X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand.description: An X-linked disorder of antibody class switching that causes low IgG and IgA, generally with normal or elevated IgM, recurrent infections, and sometimes neutropenia.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infan.description: Delayed maturation of immunoglobulin production, predominantly IgG, which may cause recurrent respiratory infections and resolves with age. It is confirmed retrospectively after immunoglobulin levels normalize and is unlikely in this case.

Proximal penile fracture of the right co.normalized_text: Proximal penile fracture of the right corpus cavernosum
Proximal penile fracture of the right co.description: Traumatic rupture of the tunica albuginea near the penile base during intercourse. This is strongly supported by the annotated MRI showing a right cavernosal tunical defect and hematoma extending into the scrotum, and requires urgent urological assessment.

Penile dorsal vein rupture (false penile.normalized_text: Penile dorsal vein rupture (false penile fracture)
Penile dorsal vein rupture (false penile.description: Injury to a penile vein during intercourse can cause bruising and hematoma without a tunica albuginea tear. It is less likely here because the annotated MRI indicates a tunical defect.

Traumatic scrotal and perineal soft-tiss.normalized_text: Traumatic scrotal and perineal soft-tissue hematoma
Traumatic scrotal and perineal soft-tiss.description: Bleeding into scrotal and perineal tissues causes painful swelling and ecchymosis. Imaging supports a hematoma, but in this case it is more likely a consequence of the proximal penile fracture than an isolated injury.

Traumatic urethral injury.description: A urethral tear can accompany intercourse-related penile trauma and produce perineal or scrotal bleeding. It is not established by the supplied images; urinary symptoms and dedicated assessment would help evaluate this possibility.

Testicular torsion.description: Twisting of the spermatic cord causes sudden scrotal pain and swelling and is a surgical emergency. It is substantially less likely than penile fracture here and would not explain the annotated cavernosal tunical defect.

Muscle-eye-brain disease, commonly assoc.normalized_text: Muscle-eye-brain disease, commonly associated with POMGNT1-related dystroglycanopathy
Muscle-eye-brain disease, commonly assoc.description: An inherited congenital muscular dystrophy combining muscle weakness, structural brain abnormalities, and ocular disease. This is a strong consideration given the combined muscular, neurologic, and ocular findings.

Walker-Warburg syndrome.description: A severe congenital dystroglycanopathy characterized by muscular dystrophy, major brain malformations, and ocular abnormalities. Classic cases frequently have limited survival, although related phenotypes vary in severity.

Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy,.normalized_text: Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy, associated with FKTN
Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy,.description: An autosomal recessive dystroglycanopathy causing early muscular dystrophy, intellectual disability, and abnormal brain development, often including cortical and cerebellar abnormalities.

LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.description: A laminin-alpha-2 deficiency causing severe early muscle weakness, contractures, elevated CK, and characteristic cerebral white-matter abnormalities. Cognition is often relatively preserved unless additional brain abnormalities occur.

LARGE1-related congenital muscular dystr.normalized_text: LARGE1-related congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye abnormalities
LARGE1-related congenital muscular dystr.description: A rare dystroglycanopathy caused by defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation, producing congenital muscular dystrophy with variable intellectual disability, brain malformations, and ocular involvement.

Urachal adenocarcinoma.description: A rare gland-forming cancer arising from the urachal remnant near the bladder dome. The apparent bladder-dome mass with calcification and gland-forming histology makes this a leading possibility, although confirmation requires full pathology and anatomical assessment.

Primary adenocarcinoma of the urinary bl.normalized_text: Primary adenocarcinoma of the urinary bladder
Primary adenocarcinoma of the urinary bl.description: An uncommon bladder cancer composed of malignant glandular cells. Distinguishing it from urachal cancer or colorectal cancer involving the bladder requires assessment of the tumor location, surrounding bladder tissue, and immunohistochemistry.

Sigmoid colorectal adenocarcinoma with b.normalized_text: Sigmoid colorectal adenocarcinoma with bladder invasion
Sigmoid colorectal adenocarcinoma with b.description: A malignant gland-forming tumor of the sigmoid colon that can extend into the bladder and produce a palpable pelvic mass. Colonoscopy and imaging review are needed to establish or exclude a colorectal primary.

Urothelial carcinoma with glandular diff.description: A bladder lining cancer containing areas of glandular differentiation that can resemble adenocarcinoma. Confirmation requires identifying a urothelial component and interpreting appropriately labeled immunostains.

Infected urachal cyst.description: Infection of a persistent urachal remnant can create a tender mass above the bladder and mimic a tumor. This is less favored if the illustrated glands are confirmed to be malignant.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing early central nervous system depression and subsequent high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Its metabolites can falsely elevate lactate on some analyzers, producing a lactate gap.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion whose metabolite, formic acid, causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and can injure the retina and central nervous system.

Propylene glycol toxicity.description: Toxic accumulation of a solvent used in some pharmaceutical formulations, particularly certain intravenous medications, causing hyperosmolality, central nervous system depression, and lactic acidosis. A relevant exposure would need confirmation.

Isopropanol poisoning with secondary lac.normalized_text: Isopropanol poisoning with secondary lactic acidosis
Isopropanol poisoning with secondary lac.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing central nervous system depression and an elevated osmolal gap. Isopropanol is metabolized to acetone and typically produces ketosis without metabolic acidosis; this presentation would require an additional cause of acidosis.

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis.description: Metformin toxicity, including intentional overdose, can impair mitochondrial metabolism and cause profound lactic acidosis. Metformin exposure would need confirmation, and the marked osmolal gap suggests another or additional ingested substance.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.normalized_text: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.description: An ovarian sex cord–stromal tumor occurring mainly in children and adolescents, often producing estrogen. The large hemorrhagic mass and follicle-like spaces with eosinophilic material on the supplied histology favor this diagnosis; confirmation requires formal pathology review.

Ovarian dysgerminoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ cell tumor affecting adolescents and young adults, usually forming a large solid mass. Its characteristic histology consists of large germ cells separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes.

Ovarian yolk sac tumor.description: An aggressive malignant germ cell tumor that can grow rapidly in adolescents, producing a heterogeneous mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and characteristic pathology help establish the diagnosis.

Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion associated with an ovarian mass
Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.description: Twisting of the ovarian vascular pedicle can cause intermittent pain, congestion, hemorrhage, and infarction. It may complicate an underlying ovarian tumor and requires urgent clinical assessment when suspected.

Immature ovarian teratoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ cell tumor seen predominantly in adolescents and young adults. It may present as a rapidly enlarging heterogeneous mass, with diagnosis requiring identification of immature tissues, particularly neuroepithelium.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

GM1 gangliosidosis, infantile or late-in.normalized_text: GM1 gangliosidosis, infantile or late-infantile form
GM1 gangliosidosis, infantile or late-in.description: An inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency, resulting in accumulation of GM1 ganglioside and progressive neurologic and skeletal disease. The clinical findings suggest this possibility, but enzyme and genetic testing are required for confirmation.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An inherited deficiency of lysosomal alpha-mannosidase causing oligosaccharide accumulation, developmental impairment, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and susceptibility to infections.

Mucolipidosis II alpha/beta (I-cell dise.description: A lysosomal enzyme-targeting disorder caused by deficient N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase activity. It produces early skeletal abnormalities, joint contractures, coarse facial features, feeding difficulties, and severe developmental impairment.

Fucosidosis.description: An inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency, producing progressive neurologic impairment, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and sometimes recurrent infections.

Sialidosis type II.description: An inherited lysosomal neuraminidase deficiency causing a syndromic storage disease with coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, developmental impairment, and neurologic manifestations.

Pyogenic iliopsoas abscess.description: A bacterial infection forming a collection within the iliopsoas muscle. The CT image appears to show left iliopsoas enlargement with possible low-attenuation collections, making this a leading possibility; confirmation requires review of the complete imaging study.

Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with se.normalized_text: Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with secondary iliopsoas abscess
Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with se.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies, potentially extending into the iliopsoas muscles. The lower lumbar disc region and adjacent soft tissues on this image warrant dedicated assessment, preferably with MRI.

Septic iliocaval thrombophlebitis.description: Infected thrombosis of the iliac veins or inferior vena cava, sometimes arising next to a retroperitoneal infection. This could account for fever and bilateral leg swelling, but venous thrombosis cannot be established from the supplied image alone.

Infective endocarditis with metastatic s.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with metastatic spinal or iliopsoas infection
Infective endocarditis with metastatic s.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually a heart valve, that can cause persistent bacteremia and seed the spine or iliopsoas muscles. Blood cultures and echocardiography would be needed to evaluate this possibility.

Tuberculous spondylitis with iliopsoas a.description: Tuberculosis involving the vertebral column can extend into the iliopsoas muscle and produce a paraspinal abscess. It is an alternative explanation for back pain and constitutional symptoms, although the acute, highly inflammatory presentation favors pyogenic infection.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema.description: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema following rapid re-expansion of a collapsed lung, commonly after drainage of a large pleural effusion. This is the most likely explanation for the post-thoracentesis deterioration and right-sided airspace opacities.

Hepatic hydrothorax.description: A pleural effusion caused by movement of ascitic fluid into the chest in patients with cirrhosis, usually on the right. It likely explains the initial effusion but does not adequately explain the acute deterioration after drainage.

Aspiration pneumonitis.description: Acute chemical lung injury caused by aspiration of gastric contents, producing hypoxemia and airspace opacities that may predominantly involve the right lung.

Right-sided pneumonia.description: Infection of the right lung causing inflammatory alveolar consolidation, potentially accompanied by a parapneumonic effusion.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Pulmonary fluid accumulation caused by elevated cardiac filling pressures. It usually produces bilateral opacities, although unilateral edema can occasionally occur.

Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia invo.normalized_text: Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia involving the right renal and iliac arteries
Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia invo.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder causing stenoses alternating with dilatations. The renal angiogram shows a beaded appearance strongly suggestive of fibromuscular dysplasia; iliac involvement could explain the claudication.

Atherosclerotic aortoiliac peripheral ar.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the aorta or iliac arteries reduces blood flow during exertion, causing buttock or thigh claudication.

External iliac artery endofibrosis.description: Exercise-associated fibrous thickening of the iliac arterial lining, usually in endurance athletes, producing flow limitation that may be apparent only during exertion.

Takayasu arteritis.description: An inflammatory disease of the aorta and its major branches that can cause arterial stenoses, limb claudication, abdominal bruits, and renovascular hypertension.

Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic c.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic c.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal compresses nerve roots, causing buttock and leg discomfort during standing or walking, usually relieved by sitting or bending forward.

Sotalol-induced torsades de pointes.description: A potentially life-threatening polymorphic ventricular tachycardia caused by prolonged cardiac repolarization. The ECG appears to show a brief polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia following prolonged repolarization, making this the leading concern.

Drug-induced acquired long QT syndrome.description: Prolongation of ventricular repolarization due to medication, particularly sotalol, which can predispose to torsades de pointes. QT prolongation is suggested by the ECG but requires formal measurement.

Medication-induced sinus node dysfunctio.normalized_text: Medication-induced sinus node dysfunction or atrioventricular block
Medication-induced sinus node dysfunctio.description: Excessive slowing of sinus or atrioventricular conduction from the combined effects of sotalol and verapamil. Bradycardia or pauses can cause presyncope and facilitate torsades.

Recurrent atrial tachycardia with aberra.normalized_text: Recurrent atrial tachycardia with aberrant ventricular conduction
Recurrent atrial tachycardia with aberra.description: A recurrent rapid atrial rhythm that produces wide QRS complexes when ventricular conduction is abnormal. It is a differential diagnosis for wide-complex tachycardia but appears less consistent with this tracing.

Acute myocardial ischemia-associated pol.normalized_text: Acute myocardial ischemia-associated polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Acute myocardial ischemia-associated pol.description: A dangerous ventricular arrhythmia triggered by acute myocardial ischemia, often occurring without preceding QT prolongation. It is an alternative cause of polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia.

Tuberculosis-associated reactive arthrit.normalized_text: Tuberculosis-associated reactive arthritis (Poncet disease) with cutaneous involvement
Tuberculosis-associated reactive arthrit.description: A sterile inflammatory polyarthritis associated with active tuberculosis elsewhere in the body. Tuberculosis may also produce skin nodules, lymphadenopathy, and hepatic involvement. The apparent upper-lung opacities and granulomatous inflammation with possible necrosis in the supplied images favor this possibility, but microbiologic confirmation is necessary.

Systemic sarcoidosis with sarcoid arthro.description: A multisystem granulomatous disorder that can affect the lungs, skin, lymph nodes, liver, and joints. Normal ACE and calcium levels do not exclude it. Substantial tissue necrosis, if confirmed in the biopsy, would favor an infectious granulomatous disorder instead.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection that can involve the lungs, lymph nodes, liver, and skin. Pulmonary histoplasmosis can also provoke reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum. Tissue fungal stains, culture, or antigen testing would be needed to support this diagnosis.

Coccidioidomycosis with reactive arthrit.normalized_text: Coccidioidomycosis with reactive arthritis or dissemination
Coccidioidomycosis with reactive arthrit.description: A fungal infection acquired in endemic regions that may cause pulmonary disease, fever, erythema nodosum, and inflammatory joint symptoms. Dissemination can produce skin lesions and osteoarticular disease; geographic exposure and fungal testing are important for assessment.

Multibacillary leprosy with erythema nod.normalized_text: Multibacillary leprosy with erythema nodosum leprosum
Multibacillary leprosy with erythema nod.description: A mycobacterial infection in which an inflammatory reaction can cause crops of tender red nodules, fever, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, and systemic organ involvement. Confirmation requires examination for sensory loss or nerve enlargement and appropriate tissue staining.

Kienböck disease (osteonecrosis of the l.description: Loss of blood supply to the lunate causes bone injury and potentially collapse. The indicated lunate appears to have abnormal marrow signal, making this a leading consideration. A treatment-associated cause is possible, but the treatment regimen is unspecified.

Lunate stress fracture or occult fractur.normalized_text: Lunate stress fracture or occult fracture
Lunate stress fracture or occult fractur.description: A subtle fracture of the lunate can cause localized pain and marrow abnormalities on MRI, sometimes without an obvious abnormality on radiographs. A fracture line is not clearly established by this single image.

Ulnocarpal impaction syndrome.description: Excessive loading between the distal ulna and the ulnar carpus can produce lunate marrow changes and wrist pain. Diagnosis requires assessment of ulnar variance and associated cartilage or triangular fibrocartilage abnormalities.

Osteomyelitis of the lunate.description: Infection of the lunate is uncommon but can produce focal pain, tenderness, restricted movement, and abnormal marrow signal. Laboratory testing and additional imaging would be needed to evaluate this possibility.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.normalized_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the wrist
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.description: An inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 can involve the wrist and cause pain, restricted motion, synovitis, and secondary marrow changes. Persistent arthritis and exclusion of other causes are required for diagnosis.

Classic Menkes disease.description: An X-linked ATP7A-related copper transport disorder causing systemic copper deficiency, progressive neurologic impairment, abnormal hair and connective-tissue weakness. This is the strongest diagnostic fit.

Occipital horn syndrome.description: A milder ATP7A-related copper transport disorder dominated by connective-tissue abnormalities, hernias and vascular tortuosity; neurologic impairment is usually substantially less severe than in classic Menkes disease.

Acquired copper deficiency.description: Copper depletion from inadequate intake, malabsorption or excess zinc exposure can cause impaired growth, hypopigmentation, hematologic abnormalities and neurologic dysfunction.

Biotinidase deficiency.description: An inherited defect in biotin recycling that can cause infantile neurologic dysfunction, visual impairment, hair loss and metabolic decompensation; it is treatable with biotin.

Trichothiodystrophy.description: A group of inherited disorders characterized by sulfur-deficient brittle hair, often accompanied by growth impairment, developmental disability and recurrent infections.

Adrenocortical oncocytoma.description: A rare adrenal cortical tumor composed of mitochondria-rich cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, resembling the supplied histology. Most are nonfunctioning; malignant potential requires formal pathological assessment.

Nonfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma.description: A benign adrenal cortical tumor frequently found incidentally. An eosinophilic or oncocytic variant can resemble the supplied histology, although substantial growth warrants exclusion of malignancy.

Adrenocortical carcinoma, including an o.normalized_text: Adrenocortical carcinoma, including an oncocytic variant
Adrenocortical carcinoma, including an o.description: A malignant adrenal cortical tumor that may be hormonally active or nonfunctioning. Size and interval growth raise concern, but diagnosis requires assessment of invasion, mitoses, necrosis, and other pathological criteria.

Pheochromocytoma.description: An adrenal medullary tumor that often secretes catecholamines. Some are discovered incidentally in normotensive patients; biochemical testing and immunohistochemistry help distinguish them from cortical tumors.

Adrenal schwannoma.description: A rare, usually benign nerve-sheath tumor in the adrenal region that commonly presents as an asymptomatic, nonfunctioning mass. Its usual spindle-cell histology is less consistent with the supplied tissue image.

Linear morphea (en coup de sabre).description: Localized scleroderma causing a firm, linear plaque on the forehead and scalp, sometimes with scarring hair loss. This is a leading clinical possibility, although biopsy interpretation is needed to distinguish it from lupus-related disease.

Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.normalized_text: Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus profundus), linear variant
Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.description: A form of cutaneous lupus involving inflammation of deep skin and subcutaneous fat, producing firm plaques that may heal with atrophy. Rare linear lesions can resemble en coup de sabre.

Discoid lupus erythematosus.description: Chronic cutaneous lupus that causes inflammatory plaques, typically with scale, follicular plugging, pigment changes, and eventual scarring; scalp involvement can cause permanent hair loss.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory disorder targeting scalp hair follicles, causing perifollicular inflammation and progressive scarring alopecia.

Plaque-type cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can produce persistent, firm facial or scalp plaques and occasionally scarring alopecia.

ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.normalized_text: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis
ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.description: The leading diagnosis is systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory or vasculitic bowel involvement. CT appears to show bowel-wall thickening with layered enhancement, compatible with lupus enteritis. Negative ANA testing is unusual but does not entirely exclude lupus when other findings are strongly supportive.

Lupus-associated intestinal pseudo-obstr.description: An uncommon lupus complication causing impaired intestinal motility without a mechanical blockage. It can accompany urinary tract smooth-muscle dysfunction and bilateral collecting-system dilation, which appears present on the CT; confirmation requires excluding mechanical obstruction.

Intestinal Behçet disease.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent oral ulcers and sometimes intestinal ulceration, which can cause severe abdominal pain and acute abdominal complications.

IgA vasculitis with gastrointestinal inv.description: A small-vessel vasculitis occurring predominantly in children that can cause acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and bowel-wall edema. Gastrointestinal symptoms occasionally precede the characteristic purpuric rash.

Crohn disease.description: An inflammatory bowel disease that may present in adolescence with abdominal pain, oral aphthous ulcers, anemia, and bowel-wall thickening. Vomiting can occur with severe inflammation or intestinal obstruction.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection.description: A nontraumatic separation of the coronary arterial wall or intramural hematoma that restricts blood flow and causes acute coronary ischemia. This is the leading consideration given the clinical presentation and apparent long-segment coronary narrowing.

Fibromuscular dysplasia with associated.normalized_text: Fibromuscular dysplasia with associated coronary artery dissection
Fibromuscular dysplasia with associated.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder that causes stenoses, aneurysms, and dissections, especially in renal and cervical arteries. It is frequently associated with spontaneous coronary artery dissection.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.description: An inherited connective-tissue disorder, usually related to COL3A1 variants, that predisposes to arterial fragility, dissection, and rupture. The reported family history of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome does not establish the vascular subtype.

Vasospastic angina.description: Transient coronary arterial spasm causing reversible myocardial ischemia, sometimes with myocardial infarction. Demonstrating resolution of narrowing after intracoronary vasodilators would help distinguish spasm from structural arterial disease.

Atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome.description: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption and thrombosis, presenting as unstable angina or myocardial infarction. ECG evolution and cardiac troponin measurements are needed to establish myocardial injury.

Congenital duodenal web with partial obs.normalized_text: Congenital duodenal web with partial obstruction
Congenital duodenal web with partial obs.description: A congenital membrane narrows the duodenal lumen, sometimes allowing enough passage for symptoms to emerge gradually. The apparent proximal duodenal distention and limited downstream contrast passage raise this possibility, although the supplied images are not definitive.

Congenital duodenal stenosis.description: An intrinsic narrowing of the duodenum causes partial intestinal obstruction, impaired feeding tolerance, and poor growth.

Annular pancreas.description: Pancreatic tissue encircles the duodenum and can produce partial or complete obstruction. Additional imaging may be needed to distinguish it from intrinsic duodenal narrowing.

Intestinal malrotation with obstructing.normalized_text: Intestinal malrotation with obstructing Ladd bands
Intestinal malrotation with obstructing.description: Abnormal intestinal rotation can produce bands that compress the duodenum and can predispose to midgut volvulus. Assessment requires clear localization of the duodenojejunal junction, which cannot be confidently established from these selected images alone.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: Thickening of the pyloric muscle obstructs gastric emptying, typically in infants several weeks old. Ultrasound is the usual diagnostic test; the apparent duodenal abnormality makes this less favored.

Dermatomyositis with prominent subcutane.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy affecting muscle and skin. An edematous presentation can cause marked facial and limb swelling and involve swallowing muscles. This is the strongest overall possibility.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and sometimes swallowing dysfunction without characteristic dermatomyositis skin findings. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other inflammatory myopathy subtypes.

Overlap connective tissue disease-associ.description: Autoimmune muscle inflammation occurring with another connective tissue disease, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or mixed connective tissue disease. Positive ANA supports consideration but does not establish an overlap syndrome.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: An autoimmune myopathy characterized by substantial muscle injury, markedly elevated CK, and proximal weakness. Myositis-specific antibodies can be negative, although biopsy typically demonstrates prominent muscle-fiber necrosis.

Bradykinin-mediated angioedema.description: Nonallergic swelling caused by excess bradykinin, potentially associated with ACE inhibitors or C1-inhibitor abnormalities. It fits the initial painless facial and upper-airway swelling but does not explain the subsequent inflammatory myopathy.

Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phen.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine in black henna
Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phen.description: A delayed hypersensitivity reaction to para-phenylenediamine, an additive commonly used in black henna. This is the most likely diagnosis given the timing and tattoo-shaped eruption.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial infection, usually caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, that produces fragile blisters and crusted erosions. It could complicate tattoo-associated dermatitis.

Irritant contact dermatitis.description: Direct inflammatory injury from chemicals in the tattoo mixture, without requiring an allergic immune response.

Phototoxic contact dermatitis.description: An inflammatory skin reaction caused by a photosensitizing substance combined with ultraviolet exposure, sometimes producing patterned redness and blisters.

Cellulitis complicating tattoo-associate.description: A bacterial infection of deeper skin tissue that can develop through disrupted skin. It is a less likely primary explanation but a possible complication.

Severe chronic tophaceous gout.description: Long-standing monosodium urate deposition causes bulky tophi, joint destruction, and restricted movement. This is overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis given the crystal-confirmed gout, marked hyperuricemia, and extensive nodules visible in the photographs.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: An autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that can cause symmetric hand deformities and subcutaneous nodules. It is a much less likely explanation than gout here, although coexistence is possible.

Chronic calcium pyrophosphate deposition.description: Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals can produce chronic inflammatory arthritis and occasionally mass-like deposits. It is unlikely to account for this presentation compared with established gout.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare histiocytic disorder causing papulonodular skin lesions and potentially severe destructive polyarthritis. Tissue biopsy would be needed to establish this alternative.

Tumoral calcinosis.description: A disorder of bulky periarticular calcium-phosphate deposits that can impair joint movement. It is a low-probability mimic; radiographs and mineral metabolism testing would help distinguish it from tophi.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, most likely.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, most likely nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, most likely.description: A lymphoma characterized by Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background. The nodular sclerosis subtype commonly affects young adults and involves mediastinal and cervical lymph nodes. This is the strongest fit, although definitive subtyping may require additional tissue.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma arising in the anterior mediastinum, usually in young adults, that can cause compressive respiratory symptoms and spread to nearby lymph nodes.

Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.description: A rare mediastinal B-cell lymphoma with overlapping pathological features of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive T-cell lymphoma composed of large atypical cells with strong CD30 expression. ALK-positive disease often occurs in young people.

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma of immature T cells that commonly affects adolescent and young adult men and frequently presents with an anterior mediastinal mass.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia associated with advanced HIV infection. This is the leading consideration, although imaging alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A mycobacterial lung infection that can produce atypical or diffuse radiographic findings in patients with HIV.

Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.description: An opportunistic viral lung infection generally occurring with profound immunosuppression; confirmation requires additional testing.

Atypical community-acquired pneumonia.description: Pneumonia caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae or respiratory viruses, sometimes producing diffuse rather than focal pulmonary opacities.

Pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma.description: An HIV-associated vascular malignancy that can involve the lungs and produce perihilar or peribronchovascular opacities.

Lung carcinoma with pulmonary lymphangit.normalized_text: Lung carcinoma with pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis
Lung carcinoma with pulmonary lymphangit.description: Lung cancer spreading through pulmonary lymphatic vessels can cause progressive breathlessness and interlobular septal thickening. The apparent right hilar soft-tissue abnormality and predominantly right-sided septal thickening make this a leading consideration, although tissue sampling is needed for confirmation.

Thoracic lymphoma with pulmonary lymphat.normalized_text: Thoracic lymphoma with pulmonary lymphatic involvement
Thoracic lymphoma with pulmonary lymphat.description: Lymphoma involving hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes can infiltrate or obstruct pulmonary lymphatics, producing interstitial thickening and breathlessness.

Asymmetric pulmonary edema.description: Fluid accumulation in the pulmonary interstitium can produce septal thickening and breathlessness. Although usually bilateral, edema can be asymmetric because of regional vascular or lymphatic obstruction.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Thromboembolic obstruction of pulmonary arteries can cause breathlessness, chest pain and syncope. The supplied lung-window CT image cannot establish or exclude embolism; pulmonary arterial imaging is required.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disorder that can cause hilar lymphadenopathy and pulmonary abnormalities along lymphatic pathways, including peribronchovascular and septal thickening.

Large pericardial cyst with compressive.normalized_text: Large pericardial cyst with compressive atelectasis
Large pericardial cyst with compressive.description: A usually benign, fluid-filled sac adjacent to the pericardium. The apparent large, well-defined fluid-density lesion at the right cardiophrenic region favors this diagnosis; compression of adjacent lung can cause respiratory symptoms. The profound hypoxemia requires urgent evaluation and may have additional causes.

Bronchogenic cyst with airway or lung co.normalized_text: Bronchogenic cyst with airway or lung compression
Bronchogenic cyst with airway or lung co.description: A congenital fluid-filled lesion arising from abnormal development of the airways. Large mediastinal bronchogenic cysts can compress bronchi and adjacent lung, although the apparent cardiophrenic location is less typical.

Morgagni diaphragmatic hernia.description: Herniation of abdominal contents through an anterior diaphragmatic defect, often producing a right cardiophrenic opacity and sometimes lung compression. The apparently homogeneous fluid-density lesion is less supportive than visible herniated fat or bowel would be.

Loculated pleural effusion with compress.normalized_text: Loculated pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis
Loculated pleural effusion with compress.description: A localized collection of pleural fluid that can resemble a mass and compress adjacent lung. The smooth cardiophrenic lesion could represent a localized fluid collection, although its appearance favors a discrete cyst.

Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructiv.normalized_text: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructiv.description: Acute worsening of airflow obstruction, potentially triggered by a respiratory infection. Smoking, wheeze, and severe hypoxemia support this possibility, but it would not explain the large cardiophrenic lesion and could coexist with it.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the right maxilla
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.description: An aggressive lymphoma that can involve maxillary bone and oral soft tissues. The large atypical lymphoid cells and apparent CD10-negative, BCL6-positive, MUM1-positive staining pattern favor this diagnosis, potentially a non-germinal-center phenotype; confirmation requires a complete immunohistochemical panel.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: A rare metastasis of colorectal cancer to jawbone or gingival tissue that can cause swelling, bone destruction, and failure of extraction sockets to heal.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary gingiva or maxillary sinus
Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary.description: An epithelial malignancy that can invade the maxilla and present as cheek swelling, an oral mass, or a nonhealing extraction site.

Plasmablastic lymphoma of the oral cavit.normalized_text: Plasmablastic lymphoma of the oral cavity
Plasmablastic lymphoma of the oral cavit.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasma-cell differentiation that often affects the oral cavity. It may resemble other large-cell lymphomas and requires additional lineage markers and Epstein–Barr virus testing for distinction.

Post-extraction osteomyelitis of the rig.normalized_text: Post-extraction osteomyelitis of the right maxilla
Post-extraction osteomyelitis of the rig.description: Infection and inflammation of maxillary bone following dental infection or extraction, potentially causing persistent socket defects, swelling, and bone destruction.

Steroid-modified dermatophytosis (tinea.normalized_text: Steroid-modified dermatophytosis (tinea incognito involving the groin and body)
Steroid-modified dermatophytosis (tinea.description: A superficial fungal infection whose appearance and spread are altered by potent topical corticosteroids. This is the leading possibility; skin scrapings for fungal microscopy and culture can confirm it.

Nummular eczema.description: An inflammatory dermatitis producing intensely itchy, coin-shaped, scaly plaques that can resemble fungal infection.

Annular psoriasis.description: An uncommon pattern of psoriasis characterized by ring-shaped inflammatory plaques, sometimes with central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption producing slowly expanding annular plaques, often with fine scale just inside the advancing edge.

Allergic contact dermatitis to a topical.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis to a topical medication
Allergic contact dermatitis to a topical.description: A delayed hypersensitivity reaction to an ingredient in a topical preparation, causing itchy inflammation where the product is applied and sometimes beyond.

Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma caus.normalized_text: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma causing gastric outlet obstruction
Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma caus.description: An infiltrative stomach cancer that can thicken and narrow the gastric wall without forming a discrete intraluminal mass. This is the leading possibility; the supplied histology appears concerning for malignant epithelial infiltration, requiring formal pathology confirmation.

Primary gastric lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the stomach that can cause thickened folds, nodular mucosa, and occasionally obstruction.

Peptic ulcer-related pyloric stenosis.description: Chronic ulcer-associated inflammation and scarring can narrow the pylorus, producing benign gastric outlet obstruction.

Adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: A rare thickening of the pyloric muscle in adults that narrows the gastric outlet and impairs gastric emptying.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying caused by impaired gastric motility rather than a mechanical blockage; it can be idiopathic or associated with systemic disease or medications.

Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency).description: An X-linked bleeding disorder caused by deficient factor IX. The sequencing image appears to show a nucleotide substitution in the infant with a mixed peak in the mother, compatible with an inherited X-linked variant, but the gene and variant are not labeled, so hemophilia B cannot be established from this image alone.

Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency).description: An X-linked coagulation disorder caused by deficient factor VIII, which can present in newborn boys with bruising or bleeding after procedures. Factor assays and gene-specific testing are needed to distinguish it from hemophilia B.

Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocyt.description: Maternal antibodies against fetal platelet antigens cause severe thrombocytopenia, often producing petechiae and bruising at birth in an otherwise healthy term infant.

Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytope.description: A rare inherited disorder of platelet production, commonly associated with MPL variants, that can cause severe thrombocytopenia from birth without obvious congenital anomalies.

Early vitamin K deficiency bleeding.description: Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors can cause bleeding within the first 24 hours, particularly after maternal exposure to medications that interfere with vitamin K. Such exposure is not reported here.

Subacute or chronic right-sided subdural.normalized_text: Subacute or chronic right-sided subdural hematoma
Subacute or chronic right-sided subdural.description: The leading diagnosis: blood collecting between the dura and arachnoid, potentially caused by bridging-vein injury during forceful headbanging. The CT appears to show a crescent-shaped right-sided extra-axial collection with mass effect.

Subdural hygroma.description: A collection of cerebrospinal fluid in the subdural space, sometimes following an arachnoid tear from minor mechanical injury. It can resemble a low-density chronic subdural hematoma.

Right middle cranial fossa arachnoid cys.normalized_text: Right middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst complicated by subdural hemorrhage
Right middle cranial fossa arachnoid cys.description: An arachnoid cyst is a usually congenital cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sac. A middle cranial fossa cyst may predispose adjacent vessels to bleeding after minor mechanical stress; the marked right temporal finding could represent such a cyst, but requires imaging confirmation.

Epidural hematoma.description: Bleeding between the skull and dura, usually following trauma. This is a substantially less likely alternative because epidural hematomas generally have a lens-shaped appearance rather than a crescent-shaped collection.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.description: Thrombosis of intracranial venous drainage pathways can cause progressive headache, sometimes without early neurological deficits. It is less consistent with the supplied CT than a subdural collection and would require venous imaging for assessment.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor.description: An aggressive sarcoma that commonly involves abdominal and peritoneal tissues. It usually carries an EWSR1::WT1 fusion and can express neuroendocrine markers. This is a leading consideration, but EWSR1 rearrangement alone does not confirm it.

Extraosseous Ewing sarcoma.description: A malignant round-cell sarcoma arising outside bone, usually associated with an EWSR1::FLI1 or related fusion. Tumors with neural differentiation may express neuroendocrine markers; fusion identification and additional immunostains are needed.

Malignant gastrointestinal neuroectoderm.description: A rare gastrointestinal sarcoma with neural differentiation, often carrying EWSR1::CREB1 or EWSR1::ATF1 fusions. It may spread to abdominal tissues, although a bowel-wall primary and supporting S100/SOX10 staining would strengthen this diagnosis.

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.description: An aggressive epithelial malignancy with neuroendocrine differentiation that can arise in gastrointestinal organs and metastasize to the peritoneum or omentum. The reported EWSR1 rearrangement favors an alternative sarcoma diagnosis.

Postoperative abdominal wall abscess.description: A localized infection after hernia repair that can cause pain, wound drainage, and a complex mass. It could coexist with the malignancy but cannot explain the malignant histology or EWSR1 rearrangement.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), potentially triggered by dabrafenib/trametinib
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by excessive immune activation. The timing suggests a treatment-related trigger, although malignancy or infection could contribute. The marrow image appears compatible with hemophagocytosis, which supports but does not independently establish HLH.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: A severe drug hypersensitivity reaction involving fever, widespread rash, blood abnormalities, and internal-organ injury. Prior immune checkpoint treatment may complicate subsequent drug reactions.

Sepsis with disseminated intravascular c.description: A severe infection causing systemic inflammation, organ dysfunction, and potentially widespread activation of coagulation. Infection can also trigger secondary HLH.

Dabrafenib/trametinib-associated pyrexia.normalized_text: Dabrafenib/trametinib-associated pyrexia syndrome with systemic toxicity
Dabrafenib/trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A recognized adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition that can cause fever and systemic illness, sometimes with organ dysfunction. Severe cytopenias and hyperinflammation warrant evaluation for HLH rather than attribution to uncomplicated pyrexia.

Progressive metastatic melanoma with bon.normalized_text: Progressive metastatic melanoma with bone marrow involvement
Progressive metastatic melanoma with bon.description: Disseminated melanoma can infiltrate the bone marrow, causing cytopenias, and involve the liver, causing biochemical abnormalities. Advanced malignancy can also provoke systemic inflammation or secondary HLH.

Traumatic anterior panhypopituitarism.description: Deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones caused by penetrating injury. The images show a retained metallic projectile projected over the sellar region, strongly suggesting pituitary injury, although CT metal artifact limits precise localization.

Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to t.normalized_text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to traumatic ACTH deficiency
Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to t.description: Inadequate pituitary ACTH secretion causes insufficient adrenal cortisol production. The profoundly low morning cortisol is particularly concerning during acute trauma; ACTH measurement would help establish the mechanism.

Central hypothyroidism.description: Insufficient hypothalamic or pituitary stimulation of the thyroid produces low free thyroxine without an appropriately elevated TSH. The borderline thyroid results require confirmation because acute illness can also alter thyroid tests.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to tra.normalized_text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to traumatic pituitary injury
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to tra.description: Inadequate pituitary gonadotropin secretion leads to insufficient testicular testosterone production and may interrupt pubertal progression. Pubertal-stage-specific reference ranges and follow-up testing are important.

Acquired growth hormone deficiency due t.normalized_text: Acquired growth hormone deficiency due to traumatic pituitary injury
Acquired growth hormone deficiency due t.description: Damage to pituitary growth hormone secretion can reduce IGF-1 and impair subsequent growth. Low IGF-1 supports suspicion but is not diagnostic alone, especially during acute illness or concurrent endocrine deficiencies.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to cerebra.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to cerebral aqueduct stenosis or an aqueductal web
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to cerebra.description: Narrowing or a membrane within the cerebral aqueduct blocks cerebrospinal fluid flow. This is the leading possibility: the supplied MRI appears to show marked lateral and third ventricular enlargement with a relatively small fourth ventricle and possible aqueductal obstruction. Symptomatic hydrocephalus warrants urgent pediatric neurosurgical assessment.

Tectal plate glioma causing obstructive.normalized_text: Tectal plate glioma causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Tectal plate glioma causing obstructive.description: A typically slow-growing midbrain tumor can compress the cerebral aqueduct and cause hydrocephalus. The ventricular enlargement is compatible, but a definite tectal mass is not established by the supplied images.

Intracranial arachnoid cyst causing obst.normalized_text: Intracranial arachnoid cyst causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Intracranial arachnoid cyst causing obst.description: A cerebrospinal fluid-filled cyst, particularly near the third ventricle or quadrigeminal cistern, can compress ventricular outflow pathways. This is an alternative structural cause, although no definite separate cyst is identifiable in the supplied images.

Postinfectious hydrocephalus.description: Prior meningitis or ventriculitis can impair cerebrospinal fluid absorption or produce scarring that obstructs ventricular flow. Hydrocephalus fits the presentation, but no preceding infection is reported, and the apparent aqueduct-level obstruction favors a focal structural cause.

Dandy-Walker malformation with hydroceph.description: A congenital posterior fossa malformation involving the cerebellar vermis and cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle can cause hydrocephalus. It is substantially less likely here because the supplied MRI does not appear to show the characteristic enlarged fourth ventricle or posterior fossa cyst.

Obstructive sleep apnea–associated hyper.description: Sleep-disordered breathing can cause sustained hypertension through intermittent oxygen deprivation and increased sympathetic activity, particularly in people with obesity.

Primary hypertension.description: Hypertension without a single identifiable secondary cause; obesity and sleep apnea increase its likelihood. These severe readings warrant prompt clinical assessment.

Primary aldosteronism.description: Excess aldosterone production causes sodium retention and hypertension. Potassium can remain normal, so normal electrolytes do not exclude it.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor that can cause sustained or episodic hypertension, headaches, and tachycardia.

Cushing syndrome.description: Chronic cortisol excess can cause secondary hypertension, weight gain, and fatigue. The absence of characteristic physical findings makes this possibility less strongly supported.

Vasospastic angina with spasm-induced my.normalized_text: Vasospastic angina with spasm-induced myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest
Vasospastic angina with spasm-induced my.description: Transient coronary artery constriction can cause severe myocardial ischemia, infarction, and fatal arrhythmias despite otherwise normal coronary arteries. Sumatriptan can provoke coronary spasm. This is a leading possibility given the previous documented spasm.

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction from coronary thrombosis
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute coronary obstruction, usually involving the left anterior descending artery in an anterior infarction, causes myocardial necrosis and can trigger cardiac arrest. The supplied ECG and troponin require urgent evaluation for acute coronary occlusion.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection.description: A spontaneous tear or intramural hematoma in a coronary artery can obstruct blood flow and produce acute myocardial infarction, particularly in middle-aged women without substantial atherosclerosis.

Takotsubo syndrome.description: Transient ventricular dysfunction that can mimic acute myocardial infarction with chest pain, ST elevation, and elevated troponin despite no obstructive coronary disease. Severe cases may cause shock or cardiac arrest.

Acute myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium can cause chest pain, myocardial injury, ST elevation, and life-threatening arrhythmias, mimicking an acute coronary syndrome.

Fecal impaction with stercoral colitis a.normalized_text: Fecal impaction with stercoral colitis and obstructive megacolon
Fecal impaction with stercoral colitis a.description: Impacted stool can obstruct the colon and cause extreme dilation, pressure-related inflammation, and bowel ischemia. The substantial pelvic stool burden and massive colonic dilation on the supplied images favor this possibility; suspected bowel-wall gas raises concern for complications.

Sigmoid volvulus.description: Twisting of a redundant sigmoid colon causes a closed-loop large-bowel obstruction and can compromise its blood supply. Severe chronic constipation and neurologic disease are predisposing factors, although a definite twist cannot be established from the supplied images alone.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction.description: Also called Ogilvie syndrome, this is acute colonic dilation without a mechanical blockage, usually associated with illness, neurologic dysfunction, or medications. Severe dilation can progress to ischemia or perforation.

Paralytic ileus.description: Failure of intestinal propulsion produces functional obstruction without a physical blockage. Neurologic dysfunction, medications, metabolic disturbances, and inflammation can contribute.

Acute colonic ischemia secondary to seve.normalized_text: Acute colonic ischemia secondary to severe distension or obstruction
Acute colonic ischemia secondary to seve.description: Reduced blood supply to the colon can result from excessive intraluminal pressure or strangulating obstruction. Suspected pneumatosis on the supplied CT images warrants urgent assessment, although it does not by itself prove bowel necrosis.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia, usually associated with impaired cellular immunity. The fluorescent image appears compatible with clustered Pneumocystis cyst forms, although the stain and specimen must be confirmed. This diagnosis alone would not explain the meningitic symptoms.

Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmona.normalized_text: Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmonary infection and meningitis
Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmona.description: Cryptococcus infection can involve the lungs and spread to the central nervous system, causing subacute meningitis. It provides a potential unifying explanation for the respiratory and neurological illness, but requires cryptococcal antigen testing and microbiological confirmation.

Tuberculosis with pulmonary involvement.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with pulmonary involvement and tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculosis with pulmonary involvement.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause chronic pulmonary disease and disseminate to the meninges. Healthcare employment may increase exposure risk, depending on the work setting.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with central nervous system involvement
Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.description: Histoplasma capsulatum is an inhaled fungus that can cause pulmonary infection and, less commonly, disseminated disease with meningitis. Travel to endemic regions makes exposure possible, but does not establish the diagnosis.

Legionella pneumonia.description: Legionella bacteria cause pneumonia with prominent systemic symptoms, sometimes after travel-associated exposure to contaminated water aerosols. Neurological symptoms can occur, but true meningitis is unusual.

C3 glomerulopathy, dense deposit disease.description: A complement-mediated glomerular disease characterized by dominant C3 deposition and highly electron-dense deposits within glomerular basement membranes. The apparent basement-membrane deposits in the electron micrographs make this a leading consideration, although stain identities and a formal pathology interpretation are needed.

C3 glomerulopathy, C3 glomerulonephritis.description: An alternative-complement-pathway disorder producing predominantly C3-containing glomerular deposits. Unlike dense deposit disease, deposits are generally distributed in mesangial and capillary-wall locations without the characteristic continuous, highly dense intramembranous ribbons.

IgA nephropathy.description: An immune-complex glomerular disease defined by predominant mesangial IgA deposition, often causing visible hematuria. Confirmation requires identification of the immunofluorescence stains.

Immune-complex-mediated membranoprolifer.description: A glomerular injury pattern caused by immune-complex deposition, with mesangial proliferation and capillary-wall remodeling. It may be associated with infection, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal proteins, but can remain idiopathic.

Fibrillary glomerulonephritis.description: A rare glomerular disease caused by deposition of randomly arranged fibrils, usually associated with IgG staining and DNAJB9 positivity. Electron microscopy and specific immunostaining are necessary for confirmation.

Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformat.description: Abnormal connections between uterine arteries and veins can develop after pregnancy loss and cause recurrent, severe bleeding. This is an important possibility, but the supplied images appear black and cannot support diagnostic interpretation. Active bleeding with this degree of anaemia requires urgent assessment.

Retained products of conception.description: Placental or other pregnancy tissue remaining in the uterus after miscarriage can cause persistent or recurrent bleeding, sometimes with increased uterine vascularity.

Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.description: A contained injury to a uterine artery can cause intermittent or sudden major uterine haemorrhage. It is usually associated with pregnancy-related vascular injury or uterine instrumentation, which is not documented here.

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.description: Persistent or malignant pregnancy-related trophoblastic tissue, including choriocarcinoma, can develop after miscarriage and cause uterine bleeding. Assessment requires serum beta-hCG testing and appropriate imaging.

Submucosal uterine leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumour protruding into the uterine cavity can cause heavy menstrual bleeding, anaemia, and occasionally pregnancy loss.

Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.description: Post-infectious bowel dysfunction can cause abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits after an acute diarrheal illness. This best fits the second presentation, although three weeks of symptoms is insufficient to meet formal IBS duration criteria. Positive C. difficile PCR may reflect colonization rather than active infection.

Clostridioides difficile infection, with.normalized_text: Clostridioides difficile infection, with possible recurrence
Clostridioides difficile infection, with.description: An antibiotic-associated intestinal infection that typically causes frequent unformed stools and abdominal pain. The initial illness is compatible with this diagnosis, but recurrent active infection is less convincing because the current stools are formed. PCR detects toxigenic organisms but does not establish active toxin-mediated disease.

Non–C. difficile antibiotic-associated d.description: Antibiotics can disrupt intestinal microbiota and cause diarrhea without active C. difficile infection. This could explain the initial episode; residual microbiome disruption could contribute to later bowel changes.

Giardiasis.description: A protozoal intestinal infection that can cause prolonged or fluctuating diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. It is a less likely alternative because no exposure history is provided and the current stools are formed.

Inflammatory bowel disease.description: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis cause chronic or relapsing intestinal inflammation with abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. They are less likely here because the current presentation lacks clear inflammatory features, although normal laboratory studies do not exclude mild disease.

Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis.normalized_text: Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis with gastrointestinal involvement
Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic fungal infection that can disseminate to the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, lymph nodes, and bone marrow in advanced HIV. Residence in Central America and agricultural exposure increase its plausibility; tissue examination and fungal antigen testing are needed for confirmation.

Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary pulmonary and abdominal involvement
Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.description: Disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce innumerable small pulmonary nodules and abdominal lymph node or intestinal disease, especially in advanced HIV.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: A disseminated opportunistic mycobacterial infection seen predominantly when CD4 counts fall below 50/mm³. It can involve abdominal lymph nodes, intestinal tissue, liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

Cytomegalovirus esophagitis or gastritis.description: CMV can cause ulcerative gastrointestinal disease in advanced HIV, producing painful swallowing or upper abdominal pain and sometimes bleeding. Endoscopy with biopsy is needed to establish the diagnosis.

HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with.normalized_text: HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with gastrointestinal involvement
HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with.description: An aggressive lymphoid malignancy associated with HIV that may involve abdominal lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract, causing systemic symptoms, pain, obstruction, or bleeding.

HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/.description: A mature T-cell malignancy associated with HTLV-1 that can involve skin, lymph nodes, and blood. This is a leading consideration, but confirmation requires immunophenotyping and additional hematologic and molecular testing.

Mycosis fungoides.description: A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma typically presenting with chronic, pruritic patches and plaques. Epidermotropism and intraepidermal lymphocyte collections, called Pautrier microabscesses, support this possibility.

Sézary syndrome.description: A leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by widespread erythroderma, marked pruritus, lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells.

Secondary syphilis due to reinfection or.normalized_text: Secondary syphilis due to reinfection or treatment failure
Secondary syphilis due to reinfection or.description: Disseminated Treponema pallidum infection that can produce a generalized rash, palmoplantar lesions, and lymphadenopathy. Prior treatment does not exclude reinfection.

Chronic eczematous dermatitis.description: An inflammatory skin disorder causing itching, scaling, and chronic thickened or hyperpigmented plaques. Renal-associated pruritus may aggravate scratching and eczematous changes.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A potentially rapidly progressive inflammatory heart disease causing myocardial injury, conduction block, and ventricular arrhythmias. The biopsy image appears to show multinucleated giant cells within inflamed myocardium, making this a leading possibility; urgent specialist evaluation is warranted.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation involving the heart that can produce atrioventricular block, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular dysfunction. Histologic distinction from giant cell myocarditis requires assessment for well-formed noncaseating granulomas and the pattern of myocardial injury.

Acute lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium, often viral or immune-mediated, that may cause chest discomfort, dyspnea, conduction abnormalities, and ventricular arrhythmias.

Coronary artery disease with myocardial.normalized_text: Coronary artery disease with myocardial ischemia
Coronary artery disease with myocardial.description: Reduced coronary blood flow can cause exertional angina and dyspnea and may provoke ventricular arrhythmias. Normal troponin does not exclude ischemia without infarction.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: An often inherited disorder of myocardial thickening that can cause exertional chest discomfort, dyspnea, and ventricular arrhythmias, with or without outflow obstruction.

Postoperative pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A sterile neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder that can be triggered by surgery and cause progressive ulceration. The photographed wound's broad ulceration and violaceous borders are suggestive, but infection must be excluded.

Cesarean surgical-site infection.description: A bacterial infection involving the cesarean incision or deeper tissues, potentially causing wound breakdown, abscess formation, and systemic inflammation.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive infection of subcutaneous tissue and fascia that can follow surgery. It is an urgent diagnosis to exclude when wound destruction accompanies persistent systemic inflammation.

Pregnancy-associated Sweet syndrome.description: An acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis associated with pregnancy or preceding infection. Trauma can provoke lesions, although extensive postoperative ulceration is less typical than in pyoderma gangrenosum.

Pregnancy-associated listeriosis with in.description: Listeria monocytogenes infection during pregnancy can produce a maternal flu-like illness and infect the placenta or fetus, causing preterm labor and fetal compromise. It would not usually explain the photographed wound by itself.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) with anterior cervical osteophytes
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.description: A disorder causing ossification along spinal ligaments and prominent anterior bony growths. The image appears to show bulky anterior cervical ossification, which can compress the pharynx and impair swallowing; additional imaging is needed to confirm DISH.

Degenerative cervical spondylosis with l.normalized_text: Degenerative cervical spondylosis with large anterior osteophytes
Degenerative cervical spondylosis with l.description: Age-related cervical degeneration can produce anterior bone spurs that mechanically obstruct swallowing and interfere with airway protection.

Zenker diverticulum.description: An outpouching of the posterior hypopharynx that retains food and can cause dysphagia, choking, regurgitation, and aspiration in older adults.

Cricopharyngeal dysfunction.description: Impaired relaxation or thickening of the upper esophageal sphincter can restrict passage of swallowed material and cause aspiration; a cricopharyngeal bar may produce a posterior indentation on swallow imaging.

Retropharyngeal or prevertebral mass.description: A tumor or other space-occupying lesion behind the pharynx can externally compress the swallowing passage. Cross-sectional imaging would distinguish a soft-tissue mass from osteophyte-related compression.

NUT carcinoma of the mediastinum.description: An aggressive, poorly differentiated carcinoma defined by a NUTM1 gene rearrangement, often arising in thoracic midline structures in young people. It can resemble thymic carcinoma; confirmation requires NUT immunohistochemistry or molecular testing.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the thymus that can invade adjacent thoracic structures and cause respiratory symptoms. The initial biopsy interpretation supports consideration, although the patient's age is unusually young.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that commonly affects young women and produces a bulky anterior mediastinal mass. Tissue morphology and immunohistochemistry are needed because flow cytometry alone may not reliably exclude it.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A lymphoma frequently affecting young adults, often with bulky mediastinal involvement. Routine flow cytometry may be negative because the malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells are sparse.

Primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ.normalized_text: Primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumor
Primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ.description: A malignant extragonadal germ cell tumor that can present as a large mediastinal mass in young adults. Some components can resemble poorly differentiated carcinoma; serum AFP, beta-hCG, and tissue immunohistochemistry help distinguish it.

Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical.description: A rare cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome involving small cortisol-producing nodules in both adrenal glands. The apparent small bilateral adrenal abnormalities could fit, but imaging alone cannot establish this diagnosis.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: Bilateral adrenal nodular enlargement that can produce ACTH-independent cortisol excess, often with a mild or slowly progressive presentation in older adults.

Cortisol-producing adrenal adenoma.description: A benign adrenal tumor that secretes cortisol independently of ACTH, causing mild autonomous cortisol secretion or overt adrenal Cushing syndrome.

Cushing disease.description: Pituitary ACTH secretion, usually from an adenoma, causing excess adrenal cortisol production. ACTH measurement and further endocrine testing are needed to distinguish it from adrenal causes.

Non-neoplastic hypercortisolism.description: Also called pseudo-Cushing syndrome, this is cortisol elevation associated with conditions such as depression, alcohol use disorder, or severe physiological stress. Borderline endocrine results can overlap with mild Cushing syndrome.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Membranous nephropathy with nephrotic sy.description: An immune-mediated glomerular disease causing substantial urinary protein loss, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. Associated hypercoagulability can cause renal vein or inferior vena cava thrombosis.

Renal vein thrombosis with inferior vena.normalized_text: Renal vein thrombosis with inferior vena cava involvement
Renal vein thrombosis with inferior vena.description: Venous thrombosis can cause flank pain, hematuria, and impaired lower-body venous drainage. The CT images raise concern for central venous thrombosis with associated soft-tissue edema and pelvic fluid; nephrotic syndrome is a possible underlying trigger.

Minimal change disease.description: A podocyte disorder that causes nephrotic syndrome, often with profound protein loss and edema despite preserved kidney function. Diagnosis generally requires kidney biopsy in adults.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.description: Scarring affecting portions of some glomeruli, which can cause nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and progressive kidney dysfunction. Kidney function may remain normal early in the disease.

Lupus nephritis, particularly class V me.normalized_text: Lupus nephritis, particularly class V membranous lupus nephritis
Lupus nephritis, particularly class V me.description: Immune-complex kidney disease associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. Class V disease can present predominantly with nephrotic syndrome and preserved kidney function.

Epstein–Barr virus-associated acute acal.description: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, occurring as a rare complication of acute Epstein–Barr virus infection. The supplied images appear to show gallbladder wall thickening and edema without an obvious stone, supporting this possibility, although hepatitis can also cause reactive wall thickening.

Epstein–Barr virus infectious mononucleo.normalized_text: Epstein–Barr virus infectious mononucleosis with cholestatic hepatitis
Epstein–Barr virus infectious mononucleo.description: Acute Epstein–Barr virus infection causing liver inflammation and impaired bile flow. This strongly fits the confirmed infection, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and cholestatic jaundice; reactive gallbladder edema may accompany hepatitis.

Acute ascending cholangitis due to bilia.normalized_text: Acute ascending cholangitis due to biliary obstruction
Acute ascending cholangitis due to bilia.description: Infection of the bile ducts, usually caused by obstruction such as a common bile duct stone. Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain warrant consideration of this potentially urgent diagnosis, although the confirmed Epstein–Barr virus infection offers a stronger unifying explanation.

Acute calculous cholecystitis with possi.normalized_text: Acute calculous cholecystitis with possible choledocholithiasis
Acute calculous cholecystitis with possi.description: Gallstone-related gallbladder inflammation, with a possible common bile duct stone accounting for jaundice and cholestasis. Gallbladder wall thickening is compatible, but the supplied images do not establish a gallstone or ductal obstruction.

Cytomegalovirus-associated mononucleosis.description: A viral mononucleosis-like illness that can produce fever and liver inflammation, occasionally with cholestasis. It is substantially less likely here because the Monospot and Epstein–Barr virus serology support Epstein–Barr virus infection.
