Polyarteritis nodosa with bilateral rena.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa with bilateral renal infarction
Polyarteritis nodosa with bilateral rena.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause renal arterial narrowing, microaneurysms, and infarction. The apparent bilateral renal perfusion defects on CT and multiple renal arterial aneurysmal abnormalities on angiography strongly favor this diagnosis.

Segmental arterial mediolysis.description: A noninflammatory disorder involving degeneration of medium-sized arterial walls, producing aneurysms, dissections, stenoses, and abdominal organ ischemia.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.normalized_text: Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia with renal ischemia
Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease causing stenoses and sometimes aneurysms or dissections. Renal involvement commonly causes hypertension and can occasionally cause infarction.

Bilateral renal infarction from arterial.normalized_text: Bilateral renal infarction from arterial thromboembolism
Bilateral renal infarction from arterial.description: Occlusion of renal arterial branches by emboli or thrombi causes acute renal ischemia. A cardiac embolic source or hypercoagulable disorder can produce infarcts in both kidneys.

Acute pyelonephritis.description: An infection of the renal parenchyma that can cause flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea, leukocytosis, and focal reduced enhancement on CT.

Mass-forming ischemic colitis.description: Reduced blood flow to the colon can cause ulceration, inflammation, and occasionally a mass-like lesion that mimics cancer. The patient's extensive vascular disease and apparent right-colonic abnormality make this an important possibility, but confirmation requires clinical correlation and biopsy.

Cecal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the proximal colon that can cause weight loss, altered bowel habits, and an ulcerated mass. The apparent cecal lesion warrants exclusion of cancer by biopsy.

Primary colorectal lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphoid tissue that can involve the cecum and produce substantial bowel-wall thickening, ulceration, and systemic weight loss.

Ileocecal tuberculosis.description: Intestinal infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis commonly affecting the ileocecal region, where it can produce ulceration and inflammatory thickening resembling malignancy. Microbiologic and histologic evidence would be needed.

Crohn disease involving the ileocecal re.normalized_text: Crohn disease involving the ileocecal region
Crohn disease involving the ileocecal re.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause deep ulcers and mass-like thickening in the terminal ileum and adjacent colon. New presentation at age 80 is possible but less typical.

Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.normalized_text: Pancreatic panniculitis associated with acute pancreatitis
Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.description: Pancreatic enzymes released into the circulation cause inflammation and necrosis of subcutaneous fat. This is the leading explanation for the tender nodules; the biopsy appears to show lobular fat necrosis compatible with pancreatic panniculitis.

Acute pancreatitis, possibly necrotizing.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation causes abdominal pain and substantial pancreatic enzyme elevation. The CT suggests significant peripancreatic inflammation or fluid, although pancreatic necrosis cannot be confirmed from this image alone.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with li.normalized_text: Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with lipase hypersecretion syndrome
Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with li.description: A rare pancreatic malignancy that can release large amounts of lipase, producing subcutaneous fat necrosis and pancreatic panniculitis. It is an alternative underlying cause if enzyme elevation and nodules persist or a pancreatic mass is identified.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat that causes tender red nodules, usually on the lower legs. It is a clinical mimic of pancreatic panniculitis but generally shows septal rather than enzymatic lobular inflammation.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis associated with chronic hepatitis C, typically causing palpable purpura and sometimes neuropathy, joint pain, or kidney disease.

Lambda light-chain multiple myeloma.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing monoclonal lambda light chains and causing bone lesions and organ damage. This is the leading diagnosis; low plasma-cell infiltration on an aspirate does not exclude patchy marrow involvement.

Solitary bone plasmacytoma with minimal.normalized_text: Solitary bone plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement
Solitary bone plasmacytoma with minimal.description: A localized clonal plasma-cell tumor in bone with absent or minimal marrow involvement, without systemic myeloma-defining organ damage attributable to the tumor.

Multiple solitary plasmacytomas.description: An uncommon presentation with multiple localized clonal plasma-cell tumors and little marrow involvement, generally without systemic organ damage attributable to myeloma.

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasma-cell differentiation that can express CD138 and restricted light chains. Additional morphology, immunophenotyping, and viral studies are needed to distinguish it from plasma-cell neoplasms.

Metastatic renal cell carcinoma with ske.normalized_text: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma with skeletal metastases
Metastatic renal cell carcinoma with ske.description: A kidney malignancy that can produce expansile, vascular bone metastases involving the skull and spine. It is an imaging differential but is strongly disfavored by the plasma-cell biopsy.

Chronic extrahepatic portal vein thrombo.normalized_text: Chronic extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis with cavernous transformation
Chronic extrahepatic portal vein thrombo.description: Chronic portal vein obstruction produces collateral veins around the porta hepatis and may cause compensatory caudate-lobe enlargement resembling a liver mass. The apparent vascular collaterals and prominent caudate region make this a leading possibility; Doppler imaging is needed for confirmation.

Budd-Chiari syndrome.description: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow can cause abdominal pain, liver congestion, and disproportionate caudate-lobe enlargement. Confirmation requires assessment of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava.

Focal nodular hyperplasia.description: A benign hepatic lesion composed of hyperplastic liver tissue that can appear as a well-defined, relatively homogeneous mass. Multiphase contrast imaging is necessary to distinguish it from enlarged normal liver tissue.

Mass-forming hepatic tuberculosis.description: Localized hepatic tuberculosis can form a granulomatous mass that mimics a tumor. Previous tuberculosis makes it relevant, but prior successful treatment does not establish active disease.

Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A rare malignant liver tumor affecting adolescents and young adults, often without underlying cirrhosis. It may present as a large hepatic mass, but the supplied images do not establish a discrete tumor.

Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrom.description: The most likely diagnosis. Cholesterol crystals released from atherosclerotic plaques after vascular procedures obstruct small arteries, causing renal injury, distal skin ischemia, and systemic inflammation.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: Necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized arteries that can cause skin ischemia, renal vascular injury, hypertension, and neurologic abnormalities.

Infective endocarditis with systemic emb.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually a heart valve, can produce peripheral emboli, cerebral complications, and immune-mediated kidney injury.

Thrombotic microangiopathy.description: Small-vessel platelet-rich thrombosis, including thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndromes, can cause severe renal and neurologic injury.

Drug-induced acute interstitial nephriti.description: An inflammatory kidney injury, often caused by recently introduced medications, that may produce eosinophilia, hematuria, proteinuria, and severe renal dysfunction.

Severe hypothermia.description: Profound reduction in core body temperature causing impaired consciousness and cardiovascular depression. The ECG shows marked bradycardia and apparent Osborn (J) waves, strongly supporting this diagnosis.

Myxedema coma.description: Life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism that can cause profound hypothermia, altered consciousness, bradycardia, and hypotension.

Beta-blocker toxicity.description: Excessive beta-adrenergic blockade can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, and impaired consciousness. Ophthalmic beta-blockers used for glaucoma can also produce systemic toxicity, although exposure is not documented here.

Sepsis with hypothermic shock.description: Severe infection can cause circulatory failure and altered consciousness; older adults may present with hypothermia rather than fever.

Severe hypoglycemia.description: Critically low blood glucose can cause coma and impaired temperature regulation, potentially producing secondary hypothermia.

Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.normalized_text: Seronegative anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture disease)
Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.description: An autoimmune disease targeting pulmonary and renal basement membranes, causing alveolar hemorrhage and often glomerulonephritis. Circulating anti-GBM antibodies can occasionally be undetectable; linear tissue IgG deposition makes this a leading consideration.

Systemic immune-complex small-vessel vas.description: Inflammation of small blood vessels associated with immune-complex deposition. Pulmonary, renal, and cerebral involvement could provide a unifying explanation, although the specific cause requires further pathological and clinical characterization.

ANCA-negative microscopic polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes pulmonary capillaritis and glomerulonephritis. Some cases lack detectable ANCA, and central nervous system involvement is possible but uncommon.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmon.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmonary hemorrhage and neuropsychiatric involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmon.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause immune-complex renal disease, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, seizures, and cerebrovascular complications.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis.description: A diagnosis of exclusion characterized by recurrent alveolar bleeding, pulmonary hemosiderin accumulation, anemia, and lung opacities, generally without systemic vasculitis or renal disease.

Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicu.normalized_text: Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor with gastrointestinal involvement
Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicu.description: The leading possibility is a testicular cancer containing multiple germ cell components, potentially including teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac tumor. Gastrointestinal invasion or metastasis can cause ulceration and bleeding. Histologic confirmation and staging are required.

Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastroint.normalized_text: Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastrointestinal metastasis
Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastroint.description: A malignant nonseminomatous germ cell tumor that characteristically produces alpha-fetoprotein. In adults, it more commonly occurs as part of a mixed germ cell tumor than as a pure tumor.

Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gast.normalized_text: Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gastrointestinal metastasis
Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gast.description: An aggressive nonseminomatous germ cell malignancy that can spread to retroperitoneal nodes and distant organs. It may produce alpha-fetoprotein or human chorionic gonadotropin, particularly when present within a mixed tumor.

NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease.description: NSAIDs can damage gastric and duodenal mucosa, causing ulcers, abdominal pain, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. This could coexist with a separate testicular malignancy but does not explain the entire presentation.

Lymphoma involving the testicle and gast.normalized_text: Lymphoma involving the testicle and gastrointestinal tract
Lymphoma involving the testicle and gast.description: Lymphoma can involve both the testicle and gastrointestinal tract, producing painless testicular swelling, abdominal lesions, and gastrointestinal bleeding. It is less likely here because the age and tumor marker pattern favor a germ cell malignancy.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens due to extensi.normalized_text: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens due to extensive iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens due to extensi.description: A limb-threatening form of massive venous thrombosis that obstructs venous drainage, producing severe edema, cyanosis, and secondary compromise of arterial inflow. This is the strongest clinical fit and requires emergency vascular evaluation.

Acute limb ischemia from arterial thromb.normalized_text: Acute limb ischemia from arterial thromboembolism
Acute limb ischemia from arterial thromb.description: An abrupt reduction in arterial blood supply, potentially caused by an embolus associated with atrial fibrillation. This is a vascular emergency; arterial imaging is needed to establish the obstruction.

Gastric adenocarcinoma with cancer-assoc.description: A malignant gastric glandular tumor that can cause a hypercoagulable state and extensive venous thrombosis. The supplied gastric endoscopic and histologic images raise concern for adenocarcinoma, but definitive interpretation requires the formal pathology report.

Acute compartment syndrome secondary to.normalized_text: Acute compartment syndrome secondary to severe limb swelling
Acute compartment syndrome secondary to.description: Elevated pressure within a muscle compartment compromises tissue perfusion. Severe venous obstruction can precipitate this limb-threatening complication even without trauma.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive infection of fascia and adjacent tissues that can cause severe pain, swelling, skin necrosis, and shock. It is an emergency alternative diagnosis, although the vascular findings favor thrombosis.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma invo.normalized_text: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma involving the penis
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma invo.description: A rare aggressive lymphoma in which malignant B cells accumulate within small blood vessels, potentially obstructing penile circulation and causing priapism. The apparent intravascular atypical cells in the biopsy strongly suggest this possibility, although the immunostains require identification and formal interpretation.

Primary penile diffuse large B-cell lymp.normalized_text: Primary penile diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary penile diffuse large B-cell lymp.description: An aggressive lymphoma arising in penile tissue that can infiltrate the erectile bodies and impair venous drainage. Tissue immunophenotyping is needed to distinguish it from an intravascular lymphoma.

Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma invol.normalized_text: Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma involving the penis
Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma invol.description: Prostate cancer can rarely spread to the penile erectile tissues and obstruct venous drainage, producing malignant priapism.

Metastatic urothelial carcinoma involvin.normalized_text: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma involving the penis
Metastatic urothelial carcinoma involvin.description: Urothelial cancer of the bladder or urinary tract can rarely metastasize to the penis, causing pain, swelling, and priapism through infiltration or vascular obstruction.

Chronic myeloid leukemia with hyperleuko.normalized_text: Chronic myeloid leukemia with hyperleukocytosis-related priapism
Chronic myeloid leukemia with hyperleuko.description: A myeloproliferative malignancy that can cause priapism through leukostasis and impaired penile venous outflow when the white blood cell count is extremely elevated. A blood count and BCR::ABL1 testing would be necessary to assess this possibility.

Struma ovarii with pseudo-Meigs syndrome.description: An ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue. It can cause benign ascites, pleural effusion, and markedly elevated CA 125 despite normal thyroid function. This is a leading consideration, but histopathology is needed for confirmation.

Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Mei.normalized_text: Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Meigs syndrome
Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Mei.description: A usually benign ovarian stromal tumor that can produce the triad of an ovarian mass, ascites, and pleural effusion. CA 125 may rise substantially because of irritation of the serosal surfaces.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the ovarian epithelium that commonly presents after menopause with a complex adnexal mass, ascites, and elevated CA 125. Negative ascitic cytology does not exclude it.

Ovarian cystadenofibroma with pseudo-Mei.description: A usually benign epithelial ovarian tumor containing abundant fibrous tissue. Its complex solid-cystic appearance can mimic malignancy, and rarely it accompanies ascites and pleural effusion.

Adult-type granulosa cell tumor.description: An ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor that often produces estrogen and may present in peri- or postmenopausal women as an enhancing solid-cystic mass. Ascites can occur, but tissue examination and markers such as inhibin are needed for diagnosis.

Medullary astrocytoma (brainstem glioma).description: A glial tumor arising within the medulla that can expand the brainstem and enhance variably on MRI. This is a leading consideration for the apparent expansile medullary lesion, although the provided images are not diagnostic.

Ependymoma of the lower fourth ventricle.normalized_text: Ependymoma of the lower fourth ventricle or medulla
Ependymoma of the lower fourth ventricle.description: A tumor of ependymal cells that may arise near the fourth ventricle and extend toward the medulla or upper cervical canal. MRI commonly shows heterogeneous enhancement.

Medullary hemangioblastoma.description: A highly vascular, usually benign tumor that can occur in the posterior fossa or spinal cord. It typically appears as an intensely enhancing nodule, sometimes with an associated cyst or prominent vessels.

Subependymoma of the lower fourth ventri.normalized_text: Subependymoma of the lower fourth ventricle
Subependymoma of the lower fourth ventri.description: A slow-growing, usually benign tumor typically arising along the ventricular lining. A lesion near the fourth ventricular outlet can produce symptoms through compression of the medulla.

Medullary cavernous malformation.description: A cluster of abnormal, low-flow blood vessels within the brainstem that may cause symptoms through small hemorrhages. Dedicated susceptibility-sensitive MRI is important for identifying characteristic blood products.

Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma.description: A rare benign skin malformation containing increased eccrine sweat glands and vascular channels, usually appearing in childhood. This is a leading possibility given the localized sweating; confirmation requires histopathologic assessment.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of smooth muscle in the skin, often presenting in infancy as a firm, hairy plaque on the trunk or lower back.

Eccrine nevus.description: A benign localized increase in the number or size of eccrine sweat glands, which may cause focal excessive sweating with little visible skin change or an associated plaque.

Connective tissue nevus (collagenoma).description: A benign hamartoma composed predominantly of excess dermal collagen, producing a firm, skin-colored plaque that may occur on the lower back.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A benign soft-tissue lesion arising predominantly in the first two years of life, composed of fibrous tissue, fat, and immature mesenchymal tissue. It usually presents as a painless enlarging subcutaneous mass.

Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.description: A clonal disorder of dendritic cells that can involve skin, lungs, bones, and liver. This is the strongest unifying possibility, although tissue biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and can cause cavitating lung nodules and skin lesions.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the lungs and potentially additional sites such as bone, skin, or liver.

Disseminated blastomycosis.description: A fungal infection that can spread from the lungs to the skin and bones. Its likelihood depends strongly on geographic exposure and microbiological or tissue confirmation.

Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and extrapulm.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and extrapulmonary involvement
Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and extrapulm.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease that can affect the lungs, skin, liver, and occasionally bones; it is less consistent with the supplied cystic lung pattern.

Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.normalized_text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type, grade 2
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.description: An invasive epithelial breast cancer, also called invasive ductal carcinoma NST. This is the biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of the original left breast lesion.

Postoperative breast fat necrosis.description: Benign inflammation and breakdown of fatty tissue following surgery or trauma. It can produce an enhancing mass that mimics cancer; the postoperative right breast lesion appears compatible with this possibility.

Invasive lobular carcinoma.description: An invasive breast cancer arising from lobular cells that may be difficult to detect on mammography. It is an imaging differential, not the reported histologic diagnosis.

Contralateral primary breast carcinoma.description: A separate malignancy arising in the right breast is a consideration for an enhancing contralateral lesion, although the apparent internal fat and surgical history favor a benign postoperative explanation.

Fibroadenoma.description: A benign fibroepithelial breast tumor that commonly presents as a palpable mass. It is a much less likely explanation for the original lesion given its suspicious imaging and confirmed malignant histology.

Hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy.description: Toxic damage to the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium from hydroxychloroquine, causing bilateral parafoveal degeneration and potentially irreversible visual loss. This is the leading diagnosis given the prolonged exposure and imaging findings.

Cone or cone-rod dystrophy.description: A retinal degeneration affecting cone photoreceptors, sometimes followed by rod involvement, that can cause reduced central vision, impaired color discrimination, and bull's-eye maculopathy.

Autoimmune retinopathy.description: An uncommon immune-mediated photoreceptor disorder that can produce photopsias, bilateral visual decline, color vision abnormalities, and visual field defects despite initially subtle fundus findings.

Age-related macular degeneration.description: Age-associated degeneration of the macula that can impair central vision through drusen, retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, or abnormal blood vessel growth.

Age-related cataract.description: Clouding of the lens that can cause blurred vision, reduced visual acuity, and diminished color perception. It may contribute to this patient's symptoms but does not explain the retinal findings.

Primary nasopharyngeal classical Hodgkin.normalized_text: Primary nasopharyngeal classical Hodgkin lymphoma, possibly lymphocyte-rich subtype
Primary nasopharyngeal classical Hodgkin.description: A lymphoma characterized by scattered Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells in a reactive inflammatory background. The large atypical cells and illustrated CD30 and CD15 staining favor classical Hodgkin lymphoma, although additional immunophenotyping is needed for confirmation and subtyping.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell ly.description: An indolent lymphoma, formerly called nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, featuring scattered large lymphocyte-predominant cells within nodules of small lymphocytes. Its large cells usually express B-cell markers rather than CD15 or CD30.

EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lympho.description: An Epstein–Barr virus-associated aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can involve extranodal sites and contain Hodgkin-like, sometimes CD30-positive large cells. Confirmation requires B-cell immunophenotyping and EBV testing.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A T-cell lymphoma typically containing numerous large atypical cells with strong CD30 expression. ALK staining and a broader T-cell and cytotoxic-marker panel help distinguish it from other CD30-positive lymphomas.

Reactive adenoidal lymphoid hyperplasia.normalized_text: Reactive adenoidal lymphoid hyperplasia with activated immunoblasts
Reactive adenoidal lymphoid hyperplasia.description: A benign enlargement of nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue caused by immune stimulation. Reactive immunoblasts can be large and CD30-positive, potentially mimicking lymphoma.

Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopath.normalized_text: Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopathy) with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopath.description: Transient ventricular dysfunction that mimics myocardial infarction despite nonobstructive coronary arteries. The ventriculographic appearance suggests apical ballooning, and basal hypercontractility can cause severe outflow obstruction.

Ipilimumab-associated immune checkpoint.description: Immune-mediated myocardial inflammation caused by checkpoint inhibitor therapy. It can produce chest pain, troponin elevation, ECG abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiac dysfunction even with relatively preserved ejection fraction.

Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A myocardial disorder characterized by ventricular hypertrophy that can cause dynamic outflow obstruction, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and myocardial ischemia despite unobstructed coronary arteries. Confirming this diagnosis requires evidence of otherwise unexplained hypertrophy.

Acute myocardial infarction with nonobst.normalized_text: Acute myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Acute myocardial infarction with nonobst.description: An ischemic myocardial infarction occurring without major coronary stenosis, potentially from coronary spasm, microvascular dysfunction, or a transient thrombotic event. This remains a provisional diagnosis until myocarditis and Takotsubo syndrome are excluded.

Cardiac metastasis from vaginal melanoma.description: Melanoma can spread to the myocardium or pericardium, potentially causing chest pain, dyspnea, myocardial injury, arrhythmias, or obstructive physiology. Dedicated cardiac imaging would be needed to establish cardiac involvement.

Syphilitic proctitis.description: Rectal infection caused by Treponema pallidum that can produce bleeding, pain, and ulceration. The biopsy appears to show prominent chronic inflammation and numerous immunostained organisms, strongly suggesting syphilis if panel D is a T. pallidum stain; confirmation requires the stain report and syphilis testing.

Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis.description: An invasive rectal infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3, which can cause painful, bleeding proctitis and mimic inflammatory bowel disease.

Crohn disease with perianal involvement.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause rectal inflammation, anal fissures, skin tags, fistulas, and abscesses; perianal disease may precede other intestinal symptoms.

Ulcerative proctitis.description: Ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum, causing chronic mucosal inflammation and rectal bleeding, sometimes without systemic symptoms.

Chronic anal fissures with coexisting he.normalized_text: Chronic anal fissures with coexisting hemorrhoidal disease
Chronic anal fissures with coexisting he.description: Persistent tears in the anal lining cause pain during defecation and small-volume bright red bleeding; sentinel tags indicate chronicity. Coexisting hemorrhoids can contribute additional bleeding.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.description: Noncancerous prostate enlargement that can cause urinary bleeding. It is common in older men, although trace dipstick blood alone does not establish this diagnosis.

Nephrolithiasis.description: Kidney or urinary tract stones can cause microscopic urinary bleeding, sometimes without pain. Dipstick blood should be confirmed by urine microscopy.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.description: A malignancy of the bladder lining that can present with painless microscopic or visible hematuria. Persistent, microscopy-confirmed hematuria in an older man warrants risk-based evaluation.

Renal cell carcinoma.description: A malignancy of kidney tissue that may be asymptomatic or cause urinary bleeding. An isolated trace-positive dipstick is nonspecific and is insufficient to diagnose it.

Prostate cancer.description: A malignancy of the prostate that is often asymptomatic early. Age and a first-degree family history increase risk, but normal PSA and digital rectal examination reduce suspicion; isolated trace dipstick blood is not a typical early presentation.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia, likely ass.normalized_text: Congenital dysfibrinogenemia, likely associated with a de novo FGG variant
Congenital dysfibrinogenemia, likely ass.description: An inherited qualitative fibrinogen disorder in which fibrinogen is present but functions abnormally. The sequencing image appears to show a heterozygous nucleotide change in the patient's FGG sequence that is absent from the parental sequences, supporting a possible de novo variant; its pathogenicity requires confirmation.

Acquired dysfibrinogenemia.description: A qualitative fibrinogen abnormality arising from conditions such as liver disease, paraproteinemia, or antibodies affecting fibrinogen function.

Congenital hypodysfibrinogenemia.description: A congenital fibrinogen disorder combining reduced fibrinogen quantity with impaired function, potentially causing bleeding or thrombosis.

Congenital hypofibrinogenemia.description: A quantitative fibrinogen deficiency that can cause early-life bleeding and prolonged coagulation times when fibrinogen levels are sufficiently low.

Congenital factor II deficiency.description: A rare deficiency or functional abnormality of prothrombin that impairs the common coagulation pathway and can cause bleeding from infancy.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with superior vena cava syndrome
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with.description: A smoking-associated lung cancer that often arises centrally and obstructs major airways. The right hilar-mediastinal mass and apparent venous obstruction strongly support a lung malignancy causing superior vena cava syndrome; tissue testing is needed to confirm the subtype.

Small cell lung carcinoma with superior.normalized_text: Small cell lung carcinoma with superior vena cava syndrome
Small cell lung carcinoma with superior.description: An aggressive, strongly smoking-associated neuroendocrine lung cancer that frequently forms a central mass with bulky mediastinal disease and can obstruct the superior vena cava.

Lung adenocarcinoma with mediastinal ext.normalized_text: Lung adenocarcinoma with mediastinal extension and superior vena cava syndrome
Lung adenocarcinoma with mediastinal ext.description: A non-small cell lung cancer that usually originates peripherally but can involve mediastinal lymph nodes, cause pleural disease, and obstruct central veins. Histologic and immunohistochemical testing distinguishes it from other lung cancers.

Large cell carcinoma of the lung with su.normalized_text: Large cell carcinoma of the lung with superior vena cava syndrome
Large cell carcinoma of the lung with su.description: A poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma lacking definitive glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation. It can present as a bulky invasive mass; diagnosis requires adequate tissue and exclusion of other subtypes.

Mediastinal lymphoma causing superior ve.normalized_text: Mediastinal lymphoma causing superior vena cava syndrome
Mediastinal lymphoma causing superior ve.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can produce bulky mediastinal tissue, compress central veins and airways, and cause upper-body swelling. It is an alternative to primary lung cancer, although the smoking history and apparent bronchial involvement favor lung carcinoma.

BCL11B-related immunodeficiency with neu.normalized_text: BCL11B-related immunodeficiency with neurodevelopmental and craniofacial abnormalities
BCL11B-related immunodeficiency with neu.description: A rare genetic disorder affecting T-cell development and development of the brain, skeleton, teeth, and craniofacial structures. It is the strongest unifying possibility for this combination of findings; a de novo variant can occur without a family history.

Complete DiGeorge syndrome with congenit.normalized_text: Complete DiGeorge syndrome with congenital athymia
Complete DiGeorge syndrome with congenit.description: Failure of thymic development causing profound T-cell deficiency, often associated with 22q11.2 deletion or another developmental genetic disorder and congenital cardiac abnormalities.

CHD7-related CHARGE syndrome with thymic.normalized_text: CHD7-related CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia or aplasia
CHD7-related CHARGE syndrome with thymic.description: A developmental disorder that can involve congenital heart defects, brain abnormalities, and impaired thymic development, occasionally producing severe T-cell deficiency.

Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic severe.normalized_text: Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic severe combined immunodeficiency
Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic severe.description: A form of severe combined immunodeficiency in which a small population of abnormal, activated T cells causes inflammatory dermatitis. Absence of maternal engraftment does not exclude this diagnosis.

FOXN1-related congenital athymia.description: A genetic disorder of thymic epithelial development that causes severe T-cell deficiency. Classic biallelic FOXN1 deficiency also causes congenital alopecia and nail dystrophy.

Rectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma.normalized_text: Rectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Rectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma that can rarely involve the rectum. The apparent dense lymphoid infiltrate and possible lymphoepithelial lesions in the supplied biopsy images favor this possibility, but confirmation requires pathology review and immunophenotyping.

Rectal follicular lymphoma.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma that occasionally involves gastrointestinal mucosa and produces nodular lesions. Distinguishing it from MALT lymphoma requires assessment of follicular architecture and immunohistochemical markers.

Mantle cell lymphoma involving the rectu.normalized_text: Mantle cell lymphoma involving the rectum
Mantle cell lymphoma involving the rectu.description: A B-cell lymphoma that can involve the gastrointestinal tract, sometimes producing multiple lymphomatous polyps. Diagnosis requires characteristic immunophenotyping, including cyclin D1 or associated genetic testing.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of rectal glandular epithelium that can cause tenesmus and mucus discharge. It is an important clinical differential, although the supplied biopsy images appear more lymphoid than glandular.

Ulcerative proctitis.description: Inflammatory bowel disease limited to the rectum, commonly causing urgency, tenesmus, mucus passage, and rectal bleeding. Endoscopic and histologic confirmation is needed.

May-Thurner syndrome with left iliofemor.normalized_text: May-Thurner syndrome with left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
May-Thurner syndrome with left iliofemor.description: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery predisposes to extensive left-sided venous thrombosis. The patient's presentation and pelvic CT raise concern for this condition.

Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombo.normalized_text: Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombo.description: A blood clot in the deep veins of the left thigh and pelvis causes impaired venous drainage. Oral contraceptive use increases risk, and proximal thrombosis can embolize to the lungs.

Acute bilateral pulmonary embolism.description: Clots, usually originating in deep leg or pelvic veins, obstruct pulmonary arteries. The chest CT appears to show bilateral pulmonary arterial filling defects, strongly supporting this potentially life-threatening diagnosis.

Left leg cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues can cause a painful, warm, red, swollen limb. It is less likely than venous thrombosis here and does not explain the apparent pulmonary arterial filling defects.

Inherited thrombophilia-associated venou.description: Inherited clotting predispositions, such as factor V Leiden or the prothrombin gene mutation, can increase the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, particularly with estrogen-containing contraceptives. Young age and family history make this a possible contributor, but neither establishes the diagnosis.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease.description: An inherited defect in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase system, usually caused by a CYBB variant, that impairs microbial killing. This is the leading possibility: the rhodamine plots appear to show absent oxidative burst in the patient, a mosaic pattern in a carrier, and a normal control, with sequencing supporting an inherited variant.

Myeloperoxidase deficiency.description: A neutrophil enzyme deficiency that can produce an abnormal dihydrorhodamine oxidative-burst assay despite preserved NADPH oxidase activity. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic, although some develop fungal infections.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia.description: A BTK-associated disorder of B-cell development causing markedly reduced antibody production and recurrent infections, particularly after maternal antibodies decline during infancy.

X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.description: A CD40 ligand deficiency that disrupts antibody class switching and immune-cell cooperation, causing recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections; associated neutropenia can cause oral ulcers.

Cyclic neutropenia.description: A disorder, often associated with ELANE variants, in which neutrophil counts periodically fall, leading to recurrent fever, mouth ulcers, and bacterial infections.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising from bile ducts within the liver. This is the leading possibility given the hepatic mass, elevated CA 19-9, and apparent irregular malignant glands within fibrous stroma on the histology images.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma.description: Colorectal cancer can spread to the liver and produce gland-forming tumors. Establishing this diagnosis requires investigation for a colorectal primary and appropriate pathology testing.

Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcin.description: An adenocarcinoma arising in the pancreatic ducts that frequently spreads to the liver and exhibits malignant glands in desmoplastic stroma. No pancreatic primary is established by the supplied images.

Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcino.description: A primary liver malignancy containing both hepatocellular and bile-duct carcinoma components. The supplied histology appears more supportive of a glandular component, but additional sampling would be needed to establish a mixed tumor.

Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver wi.normalized_text: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver with associated invasive carcinoma
Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver wi.description: A rare cyst-forming biliary neoplasm occurring predominantly in women that can develop invasive adenocarcinoma. This is less favored because the depicted lesion appears predominantly solid rather than clearly multiloculated and cystic.

Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.normalized_text: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the parotid region
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.description: A malignant spindle-cell tumor arising from a peripheral nerve or its sheath. The painful, progressively enlarging mass and spindle-cell histology make this a consideration, but confirmation requires labeled immunohistochemical results and assessment of atypia, mitoses and necrosis.

Intraparotid schwannoma.description: A benign, usually encapsulated tumor of Schwann cells that can arise from the facial nerve or another nerve within the parotid region. It may produce a mobile mass while preserving facial nerve function.

Localized neurofibroma of the parotid re.normalized_text: Localized neurofibroma of the parotid region
Localized neurofibroma of the parotid re.description: A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells and other supporting cells. A localized lesion can present as a soft mass associated with a nerve.

Spindle-cell myoepithelial carcinoma of.normalized_text: Spindle-cell myoepithelial carcinoma of the parotid gland
Spindle-cell myoepithelial carcinoma of.description: A rare malignant salivary gland tumor composed predominantly of myoepithelial cells, sometimes with spindle-cell morphology. Diagnosis requires evidence of invasion and an appropriate epithelial and myoepithelial immunohistochemical profile.

Nodular fasciitis of the parotid region.normalized_text: Nodular fasciitis of the parotid region
Nodular fasciitis of the parotid region.description: A benign, self-limited myofibroblastic proliferation that can mimic a sarcoma because of relatively rapid growth and cellular spindle-cell histology.

Fucosidosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency, producing progressive neurological deterioration and coarse facial features. The apparent low T2 signal in the globus pallidus and periventricular white-matter abnormalities on the supplied images support consideration of this diagnosis, but are not diagnostic.

GM1 gangliosidosis, late-infantile form.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency, leading to lysosomal accumulation of GM1 ganglioside and progressive neurodegeneration. Late-infantile disease can present with developmental decline, spasticity, and dystonia.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency, characterized by intellectual disability, hearing impairment, coarse facial features, and variable progressive neurological involvement.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type I, severe for.normalized_text: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I, severe form (Hurler syndrome)
Mucopolysaccharidosis type I, severe for.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, resulting in glycosaminoglycan accumulation, coarse facial features, macroglossia, hearing loss, and progressive developmental impairment.

Sialidosis type II.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by neuraminidase deficiency. Childhood forms can cause coarse facial features, developmental impairment, and progressive neurological disease.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Impaired movement of both vocal folds can leave them near the midline, severely narrowing the airway. The apparent narrow glottic opening is compatible with this diagnosis, but confirmation requires assessment of vocal fold movement during breathing.

Congenital anterior glottic web.description: A congenital membrane connecting the anterior vocal folds can restrict the glottic airway and cause neonatal stridor. The apparent tissue spanning part of the glottis raises this possibility, although the provided images are not definitive.

Post-intubation laryngeal edema.description: Inflammatory swelling following endotracheal intubation can narrow the neonatal larynx and produce post-extubation airway obstruction.

Post-intubation posterior glottic stenos.description: Intubation-related injury to the posterior larynx can cause adhesions or scarring that restrict vocal fold movement and mimic bilateral vocal fold paralysis.

Laryngomalacia.description: Dynamic inward collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration is a common cause of infant stridor. Diagnosis requires observing supraglottic collapse during spontaneous breathing.

Infected pyriform sinus fistula, likely.normalized_text: Infected pyriform sinus fistula, likely a fourth branchial pouch anomaly
Infected pyriform sinus fistula, likely.description: A congenital tract arising from the pyriform sinus that can cause recurrent left-sided neck abscesses or thyroid infection. The apparent tract near the left hypopharynx on the supplied image supports this possibility, although confirmation is needed.

Infected third branchial pouch sinus.description: A congenital sinus communicating with the pyriform sinus that can become infected and produce recurrent lateral neck abscesses. Distinguishing it from a fourth pouch anomaly requires defining the tract's anatomical course.

Infected second branchial cleft cyst.description: A congenital lateral neck cyst that may first become apparent in young adulthood when infection causes enlargement or abscess formation.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyro.normalized_text: Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyroid abscess
Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyro.description: A bacterial infection of the thyroid that can produce fever and an anterior neck abscess. Recurrent left-sided episodes in a young person can be associated with a congenital pyriform sinus fistula.

Infected thyroglossal duct cyst.description: A congenital remnant along the thyroid's developmental descent that can become infected, causing recurrent neck swelling or abscess formation.

Normocomplementemic urticarial vasculiti.description: Inflammation of small skin vessels producing persistent urticaria-like lesions, often with burning, pain, and residual pigmentation. Normal complement supports the normocomplementemic subtype; the biopsy is suggestive but not definitively diagnostic.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A systemic hypersensitivity reaction, often triggered by a medication, causing fever, urticarial rash, joint symptoms, and extremity swelling, usually without complement consumption or renal injury.

Acute drug-induced urticaria with angioe.description: A medication-associated hypersensitivity reaction producing itchy wheals and deeper tissue swelling. The diet pills are a possible trigger, although ordinary urticaria does not explain all findings.

Viral infection-associated urticarial er.description: An acute viral illness can trigger urticaria or an urticaria-like exanthem alongside systemic inflammatory symptoms.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: A systemic autoinflammatory disease causing high fevers, joint symptoms, and an inflammatory rash. Persistent pruritic or urticarial eruptions can occur, but this presentation lacks several usual supporting findings.

Gastric trichobezoar with possible dista.normalized_text: Gastric trichobezoar with possible distal small-bowel involvement
Gastric trichobezoar with possible dista.description: A mass of swallowed hair accumulates in the stomach and can cause obstruction, ulceration, or passage of obstructing fragments into the intestine. The visible hair-containing mass strongly favors this diagnosis; Rapunzel syndrome requires confirmation of a continuous tail extending into the small bowel.

Gastric phytobezoar.description: An accumulation of indigestible plant fibers in the stomach can produce abdominal pain, impaired gastric emptying, and intestinal obstruction. This is an alternative bezoar diagnosis, but the visible hair strongly favors a trichobezoar.

Peptic ulcer disease with possible gastr.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease with possible gastric outlet obstruction
Peptic ulcer disease with possible gastr.description: An ulcer in the stomach or duodenum can cause epigastric pain and bleeding; associated inflammation or scarring can impair gastric emptying. Ibuprofen can worsen mucosal injury.

Intermittent small-bowel intussusception.description: A segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing intermittent obstruction. In adolescents, an intraluminal lesion or foreign-body mass may serve as a lead point.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction causes nausea, vomiting, upper abdominal discomfort, and reduced intake. It can predispose to bezoar formation but would not independently explain the demonstrated hair mass.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: The most likely diagnosis: disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the lungs, ileum, and possibly kidney. The images show granulomatous inflammation, necrosis, and numerous acid-fast bacilli. Ileal perforation with purulent peritonitis provides a plausible cause of death.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: An opportunistic nontuberculous mycobacterial infection that can involve the lungs and gastrointestinal tract, particularly in patients with significant immune suppression. Species identification is necessary to distinguish it from tuberculosis.

Disseminated Mycobacterium bovis infecti.description: A member of the tuberculosis complex that can cause intestinal tuberculosis and systemic dissemination, classically after exposure to infected animals or unpasteurized dairy products. Histology cannot reliably distinguish it from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection that can produce pulmonary nodules, granulomatous inflammation, and gastrointestinal ulcers, sometimes with perforation. It is substantially less likely given the apparent acid-fast bacilli.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural inflammation, ileal ulceration, and sometimes granulomas or perforation. It does not adequately explain the acid-fast organisms and disseminated necrotizing lesions.

Cardioinhibitory vasovagal presyncope.description: A reflex autonomic response causing hypotension and slowing or transient arrest of the sinus node. This is the leading explanation for the observed episode.

Sinus node dysfunction with intermittent.normalized_text: Sinus node dysfunction with intermittent sinus arrest
Sinus node dysfunction with intermittent.description: Failure of the sinus node to generate or transmit impulses, producing pauses and symptoms of reduced cerebral perfusion. A vagally mediated pause must be distinguished from intrinsic sinus node disease.

Acute viral myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the heart muscle, sometimes following a viral illness, that can cause chest pain, arrhythmias, or conduction disturbances. The supplied ECGs alone cannot establish this diagnosis.

Vasospastic angina.description: Transient coronary artery spasm causing myocardial ischemia and episodic chest pain, occasionally accompanied by bradyarrhythmias. Confirmation requires evidence of ischemia during symptoms or specialized testing.

Acute hyperventilation syndrome.description: Excessive ventilation can lower carbon dioxide levels and cause chest discomfort, breathlessness, dizziness, and distal tingling. It could explain some symptoms but does not adequately explain the documented pause by itself.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Air leaks from ruptured alveoli into the mediastinum without trauma. This is the leading diagnosis: the CT shows mediastinal air around the trachea and great vessels, and precordial crepitus is consistent with Hamman's sign.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air enters the pleural space spontaneously, often in young adults. It may coexist with pneumomediastinum, although no definite pneumothorax is evident in the supplied images.

Esophageal perforation.description: A tear in the esophagus can release air and digestive contents into the mediastinum. This is an important dangerous alternative, although the history and lack of inflammatory abnormalities make it less likely.

Tracheobronchial rupture.description: An airway tear can allow air to escape into the mediastinum and cervical tissues. It usually follows trauma or airway instrumentation; spontaneous rupture is rare.

Pneumopericardium.description: Air accumulates within the pericardial sac, sometimes accompanying other thoracic air leaks. The supplied CT favors pneumomediastinum rather than demonstrating pericardial air.

Lyme disease presenting as erythema migr.normalized_text: Lyme disease presenting as erythema migrans
Lyme disease presenting as erythema migr.description: A tick-transmitted Borrelia infection that can cause an expanding erythematous patch with central clearing. This is a leading consideration given the appearance and Highland exposure; a negative early serology and lack of a recalled tick bite do not exclude it.

Tinea corporis.description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection producing an itchy, expanding ring-shaped rash, usually with a raised, scaly border.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly expanding annular or arcuate lesions, sometimes with a fine trailing scale inside the advancing border.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory skin condition causing persistent rings of smooth dermal papules, usually without surface scale.

Allergic contact dermatitis.description: An inflammatory skin reaction to an external allergen that can produce persistent itchy erythema when exposure continues.

Vasospastic angina (coronary artery spas.description: Transient constriction of an epicardial coronary artery causes myocardial ischemia, typically at rest overnight or in the early morning. This is the leading possibility given the timing, smoking, alcohol association, and apparent variation in coronary narrowing between angiographic panels, although the imaging sequence and medication response are not provided.

Atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome,.normalized_text: Atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome, potentially non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome,.description: Acute coronary plaque disruption or erosion can reduce coronary blood flow and cause myocardial injury. Chest pain, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated troponin warrant consideration, but myocardial infarction requires a troponin rise or fall and supporting evidence of ischemia.

Coronary microvascular dysfunction with.normalized_text: Coronary microvascular dysfunction with microvascular angina
Coronary microvascular dysfunction with.description: Abnormal dilation or spasm of small coronary vessels causes ischemia despite the absence of major epicardial coronary obstruction. Angiography alone cannot establish this diagnosis.

Myocardial bridging with myocardial isch.description: A coronary artery segment, usually in the left anterior descending artery, travels beneath heart muscle and may undergo dynamic compression. Confirmation requires demonstration of systolic compression or characteristic intravascular imaging findings, which cannot be established from these still images alone.

Anemia-associated myocardial oxygen supp.description: Reduced oxygen delivery from anemia can provoke myocardial ischemia or injury, particularly when another coronary abnormality is present. Type 2 myocardial infarction would require a dynamic troponin change and evidence of ischemia rather than a single elevated measurement.

Suspected acetazolamide-associated embry.description: A possible prenatal drug-related developmental disorder involving limb and dental abnormalities. Acetazolamide exposure has been reported with these findings, but a causal relationship in humans is not established.

Ectrodactyly–ectodermal dysplasia–clefti.description: A usually TP63-related genetic disorder characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformations, ectodermal abnormalities, missing teeth, and variably present cleft lip or palate.

Isolated split-hand/split-foot malformat.description: A genetically heterogeneous congenital limb disorder involving absent or underdeveloped central digits, sometimes with syndactyly, without a broader syndromic phenotype.

Acro-dermato-ungual-lacrimal-tooth syndr.description: A TP63-related disorder, also called ADULT syndrome, that can combine split-hand/split-foot malformations, syndactyly, dental agenesis, and variable skin, nail, and lacrimal abnormalities, usually without clefting.

Limb-mammary syndrome.description: A TP63-related developmental disorder characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformations and mammary or nipple hypoplasia, sometimes accompanied by dental agenesis and cleft palate.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: Intermittent episodes of disorganized atrial electrical activity causing an irregular heartbeat. This diagnosis is documented by the Holter report and is the strongest explanation for the patient's symptoms.

Alcohol-triggered atrial fibrillation (h.description: An alcohol-associated atrial arrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation. This is a possible trigger for the documented atrial fibrillation rather than a separate rhythm diagnosis; the amount and timing of alcohol consumption require clarification.

Frequent premature atrial contractions.description: Early electrical impulses arising in the atria that can cause palpitations and trigger atrial fibrillation. The Holter report documents a substantial burden of supraventricular ectopy, although rhythm-strip review is needed to characterize it precisely.

Paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.description: An episodic rapid rhythm originating from an atrial focus. It could coexist with atrial fibrillation and account for some Holter-reported supraventricular runs, but those runs require direct rhythm review before this diagnosis can be established.

Paroxysmal atrial flutter.description: An organized atrial reentrant rhythm that can cause episodic tachycardia and may coexist with atrial fibrillation. It is a less likely alternative here because the report identifies atrial fibrillation and does not document flutter.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colonic mucosa, sometimes involving the entire colon. The endoscopic findings are compatible but not diagnostic.

Crohn disease involving the colon.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can produce patchy ulceration and transmural inflammation. Disease limited to the colon can occur despite a normal ileum.

Cytomegalovirus colitis.description: A viral infection of the colon that can cause extensive inflammation and irregular ulcers, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Confirmation requires tissue evidence or appropriate viral testing.

Amebic colitis.description: An intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica that may produce chronic diarrhea and discrete, exudative colonic ulcers resembling inflammatory bowel disease.

Gastrointestinal lymphoma involving the.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the bowel that can mimic inflammatory colitis. The dense lymphoid-appearing infiltrates in the supplied biopsy images warrant consideration, but classification requires pathology review, labeled immunostains, and potentially clonality testing.

Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic.normalized_text: Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic stomach
Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic.description: A congenital defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal organs to enter the chest. This is the leading consideration because the large left-sided air-fluid level and subsequent tube configuration suggest an intrathoracic stomach.

Acute gastric volvulus associated with d.normalized_text: Acute gastric volvulus associated with diaphragmatic herniation
Acute gastric volvulus associated with d.description: Twisting of a herniated stomach can cause obstruction, rapid gastric distension, and potentially ischemia. It is an urgent possible complication, although radiographs alone do not confirm the rotation.

Left diaphragmatic eventration with gast.normalized_text: Left diaphragmatic eventration with gastric distension
Left diaphragmatic eventration with gast.description: An abnormally elevated but intact diaphragm can allow the stomach to rise high beneath it, compressing the lung. Associated gastric distension or volvulus can produce acute symptoms.

Left hydropneumothorax.description: Air and fluid in the pleural space can compress the lung and produce a horizontal air-fluid level. It is an important imaging mimic but is less supported by the subsequent tube configuration.

Infected congenital pulmonary airway mal.description: A congenital cystic lung lesion may remain undetected until childhood and can develop an air-fluid level when infected. This is a less likely alternative to an intrathoracic stomach.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.description: A localized tumor of clonal plasma cells outside bone marrow. This is the leading consideration given the plasma-cell-like biopsy appearance and absence of systemic myeloma findings; confirmation requires immunophenotyping and light-chain restriction studies.

Multiple myeloma with hepatic involvemen.description: A systemic plasma-cell malignancy that can occasionally form an extramedullary hepatic mass. The normal systemic evaluation makes this substantially less likely than a solitary plasmacytoma.

Primary hepatic marginal zone lymphoma w.normalized_text: Primary hepatic marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation
Primary hepatic marginal zone lymphoma w.description: An uncommon B-cell lymphoma arising predominantly in the liver that may contain many plasma cells and resemble a plasmacytoma. B-cell markers and clonality studies help distinguish these entities.

Hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor.description: A benign mass-forming inflammatory lesion composed of inflammatory cells, often including plasma cells, with variable fibrosis. It can mimic malignancy radiologically; tissue clonality testing is important when plasma cells predominate.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes. It is an important imaging differential for a hepatic mass, even with normal alpha-fetoprotein, but the apparent biopsy morphology argues against it.

Gonorrhea.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that can cause cervicitis and abnormal vaginal discharge. Symptoms may develop within days of exposure; laboratory testing is needed for diagnosis.

Chlamydia.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that is often asymptomatic but can cause cervicitis and vaginal discharge. Recent intercourse with a new partner makes it an important consideration.

Trichomoniasis.description: A sexually transmitted parasitic infection that can cause vaginal discharge, sometimes accompanied by odor, irritation, or painful urination.

Bacterial vaginosis.description: An imbalance of vaginal bacteria that commonly causes thin discharge and a fishy odor. It is associated with new sexual partners but is not classified as a conventional sexually transmitted infection.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis.description: An overgrowth of Candida yeast that can cause thick vaginal discharge, usually with itching or vulvar irritation. It is generally not sexually transmitted.

Giant bullous emphysema (vanishing lung.description: Extensive emphysema with giant air-filled bullae that compress functioning lung. Tobacco and cannabis exposure are risk factors. The images show very large left-sided bullae, making this the leading diagnosis.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air entering the pleural space because of underlying lung disease, often following rupture of an emphysematous bulla. This is an urgent consideration, although the supplied images predominantly demonstrate giant bullae rather than a clearly established pneumothorax.

Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.normalized_text: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema
Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.description: Chronic airflow limitation caused by smoking-related airway injury and destruction of alveolar tissue. Bullous emphysema is one manifestation.

Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A smoking-associated lung disease producing nodules and irregular cysts, usually in the upper and middle lung zones. It can cause airflow obstruction and spontaneous pneumothorax.

Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.description: An inherited FLCN-related disorder causing pulmonary cysts and recurrent pneumothorax, sometimes accompanied by characteristic skin lesions and renal tumors.

Multiple myeloma with extramedullary inv.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with extramedullary involvement and light-chain cast nephropathy
Multiple myeloma with extramedullary inv.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing monoclonal immunoglobulin. This is the leading possibility given anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure, elevated total protein, apparent marrow plasma-cell infiltration, and renal tubular casts. The abdominal mass could represent extramedullary disease; confirmation requires monoclonal protein studies and tissue immunophenotyping.

Plasma cell leukemia.description: An aggressive plasma-cell malignancy characterized by circulating malignant plasma cells, often accompanied by extensive marrow and extramedullary involvement. A peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry are necessary to establish this diagnosis.

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasma-cell differentiation that can form bulky extranodal masses and involve bone marrow. It can resemble aggressive myeloma histologically, requiring immunophenotyping, Epstein–Barr virus testing, and monoclonal protein evaluation for distinction.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that may produce bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy, marrow infiltration, elevated LDH, and spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome. Tissue immunophenotyping is needed to distinguish it from plasma-cell neoplasms.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with Waldenst.description: A lymphoplasmacytic B-cell malignancy usually producing monoclonal IgM, which can cause elevated total protein, cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. The aggressive presentation here is less typical unless transformation has occurred.

Lymphocytic thrombophilic arteritis (mac.description: A rare skin-predominant vasculopathy causing persistent macules or livedoid patches. Biopsy typically shows lymphocytes surrounding small or medium-sized arteries with a concentric fibrin ring, resembling the supplied histology. Peripheral nerve involvement has occasionally been reported.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa.description: A skin-predominant necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries that can cause livedo, painful nodules, ulcers, and occasionally peripheral neuropathy.

Systemic polyarteritis nodosa.description: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can produce livedo and mononeuritis multiplex, as well as renal, gastrointestinal, and other organ involvement.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex vasculitis associated with circulating cryoglobulins, sometimes related to hepatitis C or hematologic disease, that can cause skin lesions and peripheral neuropathy.

Microscopic polyangiitis.description: A systemic small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis that can cause purpura and mononeuritis multiplex, usually with renal involvement and sometimes pulmonary disease.

Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.normalized_text: Classical homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency
Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.description: An inherited disorder of methionine metabolism that causes elevated homocysteine and methionine, ocular abnormalities, skeletal changes, and increased thromboembolic risk. This is the strongest diagnostic match.

Marfan syndrome.description: An inherited connective tissue disorder, usually caused by FBN1 variants, affecting the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system. It resembles homocystinuria clinically but does not explain the biochemical findings.

Stickler syndrome.description: An inherited collagen disorder associated with high myopia, vitreoretinal abnormalities, craniofacial differences, and skeletal or joint disease.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome.description: An inherited connective tissue disorder involving abnormal transforming growth factor-beta signaling, with arterial aneurysms, craniofacial abnormalities, and skeletal deformities.

Weill-Marchesani syndrome.description: A rare inherited connective tissue disorder characterized by small spherical lenses, lens displacement, lenticular myopia, short stature, brachydactyly, and joint stiffness.

Brainstem cavernous malformation with re.normalized_text: Brainstem cavernous malformation with recent hemorrhage
Brainstem cavernous malformation with re.description: A low-flow vascular malformation that can bleed repeatedly. This is the leading possibility: the focal pontine hyperdensity on CT and mixed-signal lesion with a dark peripheral rim on MRI suggest a hemorrhagic cavernous malformation. Brainstem hemorrhage requires urgent specialist assessment.

Primary pontine hemorrhage.description: Bleeding into the pons can disrupt motor, sensory, eye-movement, and coordination pathways. The CT appearance supports a focal hemorrhage, although a structural vascular lesion is more plausible than hypertensive hemorrhage in this young patient.

Brainstem arteriovenous malformation wit.description: An abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins can rupture and produce a focal brainstem hemorrhage. It is a relevant alternative in a young adult, although the supplied MRI appearance favors a cavernous malformation rather than a high-flow vascular lesion.

Hemorrhagic brainstem glioma.description: A tumor arising within the brainstem can cause progressive cranial nerve, motor, sensory, and coordination deficits; intratumoral bleeding may accelerate symptoms. The focal hemorrhagic imaging appearance is less typical of an infiltrative glioma, making this a lower-probability alternative.

Chiari I malformation.description: Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum can cause neck pain, headache, and brainstem or cerebellar symptoms. The sagittal image suggests possible low-lying tonsils, but formal measurements are needed; this alone would not explain the focal hemorrhagic pontine lesion.

Iliopsoas pyomyositis with possible absc.normalized_text: Iliopsoas pyomyositis with possible abscess formation
Iliopsoas pyomyositis with possible absc.description: A bacterial infection of the iliopsoas muscles, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. The pelvic images appear to show iliopsoas enlargement and inflammation with possible fluid collections; formal radiologic interpretation is needed.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A potentially life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome, often triggered by infection. The marrow images appear to show histiocytes engulfing blood cells, suggesting hemophagocytosis, but this finding alone does not establish the diagnosis; blood counts, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, and other criteria are required.

Brucellosis with osteoarticular or genit.normalized_text: Brucellosis with osteoarticular or genitourinary involvement
Brucellosis with osteoarticular or genit.description: A zoonotic bacterial infection acquired through infected animals or unpasteurized dairy products. It can cause sacroiliitis, spinal infection, iliopsoas abscesses, epididymo-orchitis, and occasionally secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Exposure history and microbiologic testing would be needed.

Acute pyelonephritis with possible compl.normalized_text: Acute pyelonephritis with possible complicated urinary infection
Acute pyelonephritis with possible compl.description: A bacterial infection of the kidney that can cause systemic illness and, in complicated cases, renal or perinephric abscesses. Urinalysis, urine culture, and review of renal imaging would help assess this possibility.

Acute bacterial epididymo-orchitis.description: Infection and inflammation of the epididymis and sometimes the testis. Negative gonorrhea and chlamydia testing reduces the likelihood of those causes but does not exclude infection by urinary or other bacteria.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Jawbone necrosis associated with antiresorptive or certain antiangiogenic medications, potentially involving a reconstructed fibular graft. This is a leading consideration, but medication exposure and the duration of bone exposure are not provided.

Delayed ischemic osteonecrosis of the fi.normalized_text: Delayed ischemic osteonecrosis of the fibular free flap
Delayed ischemic osteonecrosis of the fi.description: Death of transplanted bone due to compromised blood supply, potentially from delayed vascular dysfunction or local tissue injury.

Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.normalized_text: Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstructed mandible
Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.description: Chronic infection and inflammation of mandibular bone that can produce necrosis, sequestration, and exposed bone, sometimes without overt acute infection.

Recurrent mandibular metastasis from cle.normalized_text: Recurrent mandibular metastasis from clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma
Recurrent mandibular metastasis from cle.description: Recurrent metastatic tumor at or near the reconstructed mandible can destroy bone and compromise the overlying oral mucosa.

Osteoradionecrosis of the reconstructed.description: Persistent devitalization and exposure of jawbone following radiation injury. This would require a history of radiation involving the jaw, which is not documented.

Fulminant giant cell myocarditis.description: A rapidly progressive inflammatory disease causing myocardial destruction, heart failure, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock. The supplied myocardial histology appears to show multinucleated giant cells amid inflammation and myocyte injury, making this the leading possibility; specialist pathology review is needed for confirmation.

Acute myocardial infarction complicated.normalized_text: Acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock
Acute myocardial infarction complicated.description: Acute coronary artery obstruction can cause myocardial necrosis, severe ventricular dysfunction, and shock; ischemic mitral regurgitation may produce an apical systolic murmur. This remains an urgent alternative, although the supplied biopsy favors an inflammatory myocardial disease.

Acute necrotizing eosinophilic myocardit.description: An aggressive eosinophil-mediated myocardial inflammation that can cause extensive myocyte necrosis and fulminant cardiogenic shock. It may be related to hypersensitivity, systemic eosinophilic disease, or occur without an identified trigger.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation of the myocardium can cause conduction abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, and heart failure. Giant cells can occur, but well-formed noncaseating granulomas favor sarcoidosis, whereas extensive myocyte destruction with diffuse giant-cell inflammation favors giant cell myocarditis.

Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Acute myocardial inflammation, often associated with a viral infection or immune response, can mimic myocardial infarction and progress rapidly to severe heart failure and cardiogenic shock. Biopsy typically shows lymphocyte-predominant inflammation with myocyte injury.

Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.normalized_text: Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome type 8)
Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.description: A multisystem calcium-channel disorder causing prolonged cardiac repolarization and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias, sometimes accompanied by syndactyly and distinctive facial features. The illustrated heterozygous p.G406R variant strongly supports this diagnosis; normal neurodevelopment does not exclude it.

Long QT syndrome type 1 (KCNQ1-related).description: An inherited potassium-channel disorder causing delayed ventricular repolarization and susceptibility to torsades de pointes, particularly during adrenergic stimulation. Resting QT intervals can be normal in affected relatives.

Long QT syndrome type 2 (KCNH2-related).description: An inherited potassium-channel disorder that prolongs the QT interval and predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias, which may be precipitated by sudden arousal or QT-prolonging medications.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related).description: An inherited ion-channel disorder characterized by ventricular arrhythmias, prominent U waves or prolonged QU intervals, periodic paralysis, and variable facial and skeletal abnormalities.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricula.description: An inherited calcium-handling disorder causing adrenergically triggered bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, usually with a normal resting ECG and structurally normal heart.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and a tyrosine kinase gene fusion
