Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A clonal blood disorder, often associated with FIP1L1::PDGFRA, that causes excessive eosinophil production and tissue injury. The marked blood and marrow eosinophilia shown is suggestive but requires molecular testing for confirmation.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A syndrome of marked eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ injury, diagnosed only after excluding parasitic, drug-related, clonal, and other secondary causes.

Strongyloidiasis.description: Intestinal infection with Strongyloides stercoralis, acquired through contaminated soil in endemic areas. Chronic infection can cause diarrhea, weight loss, skin manifestations, and eosinophilia.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis or eosinoph.description: An eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorder causing bowel dysfunction and tissue eosinophilia after secondary causes, including parasites and systemic eosinophilic disorders, are excluded.

Mesalamine-associated drug hypersensitiv.description: An uncommon medication reaction that can produce rash, eosinophilia, and systemic symptoms. A temporal relationship to medication initiation or dose changes and evidence of organ injury would help establish this diagnosis.

High-grade astrocytic glioma with intrat.normalized_text: High-grade astrocytic glioma with intratumoral hemorrhage
High-grade astrocytic glioma with intrat.description: An aggressive glial brain tumor that can bleed and provoke seizures. The ring-enhancing frontal lesion and apparent GFAP and OLIG2 positivity favor a glial neoplasm; definitive subtype and grade require formal pathology and molecular testing.

Cerebral cavernous malformation with hem.description: A low-flow vascular malformation that can cause intracerebral bleeding and seizures and may be invisible on conventional angiography.

Ruptured cerebral arteriovenous malforma.description: An abnormal connection between cerebral arteries and veins that can rupture, producing a lobar hemorrhage and seizures in a young adult.

Hemorrhagic brain metastasis.description: A secondary brain tumor, sometimes from melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, or another cancer, that can bleed and produce a ring-enhancing mass with edema.

Brain abscess.description: A localized intracerebral infection that may appear as a ring-enhancing lesion with edema and cause seizures or impaired consciousness. Diffusion-weighted imaging and microbiological evaluation help distinguish it from a tumor.

Histoplasma vertebral osteomyelitis.description: A rare fungal infection of the vertebrae caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. The destructive lumbar lesion, adjacent soft-tissue involvement, calcified thoracic lymph nodes, and apparent yeast forms in the biopsy make this an important possibility; fungal culture or molecular testing is needed for confirmation.

Cryptococcal vertebral osteomyelitis.description: An uncommon bone infection caused by Cryptococcus species that can produce destructive vertebral lesions and chronic pain. Rounded yeast-like structures in the biopsy warrant consideration, but organism size, capsule-specific staining, and culture are needed to distinguish it from other fungi.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: A chronic mycobacterial infection of the spine that can destroy adjacent vertebral endplates and produce paraspinal extension. Its indolent course can occur without fever, although apparent fungal organisms in the biopsy favor another cause.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis with di.description: A bacterial infection of the vertebral bodies and intervening disc, commonly acquired through bloodstream spread. Older adults may have chronic pain without fever or neurologic deficits.

Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the lumbar spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.description: Cancer spreading to vertebral bone can cause destructive lesions, persistent pain, and weight loss. The clinical red flags support consideration, but endplate-centered destruction and apparent fungal organisms favor infection.

Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell ly.description: A rare cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma involving subcutaneous fat, often causing fever and weight loss. The apparent lymphocytic infiltration around adipocytes in the biopsy makes this an important possibility, but confirmation requires immunophenotyping and molecular studies.

Primary cutaneous gamma-delta T-cell lym.description: An aggressive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that can infiltrate subcutaneous fat and resemble panniculitis. Distinguishing it from subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma requires specific immunohistochemical testing.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive, usually Epstein-Barr virus-associated lymphoma that commonly involves nasal structures but can affect skin, orbital tissues, and lungs. Diagnosis requires tissue examination, immunophenotyping, and Epstein-Barr virus testing.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus panniculitis
Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus.description: An autoimmune disease that can produce inflammation of subcutaneous fat, lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary inflammation. Lupus panniculitis can resemble a panniculitic lymphoma histologically, so clinical findings and laboratory testing are needed.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and can cause orbital inflammation. Pulmonary nodules and eyelid swelling make it a consideration, although the supplied biopsy appears less characteristic.

Congenital Zika virus infection.description: Prenatal Zika infection can disrupt fetal brain development and cause ventriculomegaly and cortical abnormalities, sometimes without microcephaly. This is the leading consideration given residence in an endemic area, the maternal illness, and positive maternal serum NAT results shown in the timeline. Negative amniotic-fluid NAT does not reliably exclude fetal infection.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: Congenital CMV can cause fetal ventriculomegaly, periventricular injury, calcifications, and abnormal cortical development. The negative TORCH evaluation reduces its likelihood; the strength of exclusion depends on the specific tests performed.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: Transplacental Toxoplasma gondii infection can cause fetal hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. Negative TORCH testing makes this less likely, depending on the testing method and timing.

Congenital aqueductal stenosis.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct produces enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles. It may be isolated or associated with genetic conditions not detected by chromosomal microarray.

Congenital lymphocytic choriomeningitis.description: Prenatal infection with this rodent-associated virus can cause severe hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. It is generally not included in routine TORCH panels, although no rodent exposure is documented here.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

SPG11-related hereditary spastic paraple.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG11 variants. Progressive spastic weakness, cognitive decline, and a thin corpus callosum are characteristic. The depicted SPG11 p.M245fs and p.F2343fs variants make this the strongest diagnosis.

SPG15-related hereditary spastic paraple.description: An autosomal recessive complicated spastic paraplegia caused by ZFYVE26 variants, often associated with cognitive impairment, a thin corpus callosum, and sometimes retinal degeneration or peripheral neuropathy.

SPG35-related fatty acid hydroxylase-ass.description: An autosomal recessive FA2H-related disorder that can produce complicated spastic paraplegia, cognitive deterioration, dysphagia, and white-matter changes. Brain iron accumulation, dystonia, and cerebellar involvement may occur.

Adult-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy.description: A recessively inherited disorder, usually caused by ARSA deficiency, in which sulfatide accumulation damages central and peripheral myelin. Adult presentations can include cognitive decline followed by progressive motor dysfunction.

Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.description: An autosomal recessive CYP27A1-related disorder of bile acid synthesis that causes cholestanol accumulation. Neurologic manifestations can include progressive spasticity, cognitive impairment, ataxia, and swallowing difficulties.

Functional cardiac or pericardiac paraga.description: An extra-adrenal neuroendocrine tumor arising from paraganglia near the heart that can secrete catecholamines. This is the leading diagnosis given the apparent pericardiac mass and marked norepinephrine and normetanephrine elevations.

Adrenal pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that causes spells of headache, sweating, palpitations, and hypertension. The biochemical findings fit, but the identified abdominal lesion was brown fat rather than an adrenal tumor.

Catecholamine-secreting mediastinal gang.description: A usually benign sympathetic nervous system tumor that can arise in the mediastinum and occasionally secrete catecholamines. It is a less likely alternative to paraganglioma.

Hyperthyroidism.description: Excess thyroid hormone production can cause adrenergic symptoms, including palpitations, sweating, and elevated blood pressure, but does not adequately explain the tumor imaging or biochemical pattern.

Pre-eclampsia.description: A pregnancy-related hypertensive disorder developing after 20 weeks, associated with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction. It is an important initial differential but was reportedly excluded in this case.

Cerebral nocardiosis (Nocardia brain abs.description: An opportunistic bacterial infection that can cause multiloculated brain abscesses in immunosuppressed patients. The enhancing left frontal lesion, surrounding edema, suppurative histology, and apparent filamentous organisms make this a leading possibility; microbiologic testing is needed for confirmation.

Listeria monocytogenes brain abscess.description: An uncommon central nervous system infection that can produce brain abscesses, particularly in older or immunosuppressed adults. Culture or molecular testing would be required to distinguish it from other bacterial infections.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic parasitic infection that causes necrotizing brain lesions, often with ring enhancement and edema, in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: A lymphoma confined to the central nervous system that can cause enhancing brain masses and focal neurologic deficits. Immunosuppression increases risk, and lesions in immunocompromised patients may be necrotic or ring-enhancing.

Glioblastoma.description: An aggressive primary brain tumor, most common in older adults, that frequently appears as an irregular enhancing mass with central necrosis and extensive surrounding edema.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.description: An acute bacterial lung infection, often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing airspace consolidation. This is a strong initial consideration, although imaging alone cannot identify the organism.

Pulmonary blastomycosis.description: A fungal infection acquired by inhaling Blastomyces spores from soil, particularly in wooded areas near freshwater in endemic regions. It can mimic bacterial pneumonia and cause progressive multifocal consolidation.

Legionella pneumonia.description: A bacterial pneumonia acquired through inhalation of contaminated water aerosols. Diabetes and smoking increase susceptibility, and pulmonary infiltrates may progress rapidly.

Pneumonic tularemia.description: An infection caused by Francisella tularensis that can involve the lungs after inhalation of contaminated environmental material or dissemination following an arthropod bite. Outdoor exposure and a short incubation period make it a consideration.

Active pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Diabetes increases the risk of active disease, but a positive Mantoux test indicates immune sensitization and does not establish active tuberculosis.

CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic synd.normalized_text: CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic syndrome with acetylcholine receptor deficiency
CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: An inherited postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, usually caused by recessive CHRNE variants that reduce functional acetylcholine receptors. The electron micrographs appear to show abnormal postsynaptic junctional architecture, supporting a congenital neuromuscular junction disorder but not establishing its genetic subtype.

RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: An inherited disorder of acetylcholine receptor clustering at the motor endplate. It can cause severe neonatal weakness and respiratory crises, often exacerbated by infections.

MUSK-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A rare inherited defect in muscle-specific kinase signaling that disrupts neuromuscular junction formation and maintenance. This genetic disorder is distinct from autoimmune MuSK-antibody myasthenia gravis.

DOK7-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: An inherited impairment of signaling required for motor endplate development, typically producing limb-girdle weakness and sometimes severe respiratory involvement.

CHAT-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: An inherited presynaptic defect in acetylcholine synthesis, classically causing episodic apnea and respiratory crises beginning in infancy, particularly during infections or other stress.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol poisoning in which acidic metabolites cause severe metabolic acidosis and calcium oxalate deposition causes kidney injury. This is the leading diagnosis; the urine microscopy appears to show elongated crystals compatible with calcium oxalate monohydrate.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol poisoning in which formic acid accumulation causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, neurological impairment, and characteristic retinal or optic nerve injury.

Propylene glycol toxicity.description: Accumulation of propylene glycol, often from solvent-containing medications, can cause hyperosmolality, lactic acidosis, neurological dysfunction, and kidney injury.

Salicylate poisoning.description: Salicylate toxicity causes respiratory stimulation and impaired cellular energy metabolism, typically producing respiratory alkalosis combined with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Sepsis-associated lactic acidosis.description: Severe infection can impair tissue perfusion and cellular metabolism, causing lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.description: A usually postviral inflammatory thyroid disorder that can cause prolonged fever and transient thyrotoxicosis. The apparent diffuse thyroid enlargement and low attenuation on the provided CT images support thyroid inflammation, although laboratory testing is needed.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis.description: An uncommon bacterial infection of the thyroid that can cause high fever and neck swelling, sometimes with an abscess. The supplied images suggest thyroid involvement but do not clearly demonstrate a discrete drainable collection.

Painless (silent) thyroiditis.description: A destructive inflammatory thyroid disorder that releases stored thyroid hormones, producing temporary thyrotoxicosis without thyroid pain. Thyroid function tests and, when appropriate, uptake testing help distinguish it from other causes.

Hashimoto thyroiditis with transient thy.description: Autoimmune thyroid inflammation that often produces a firm, painless goiter and occasionally a temporary hyperthyroid phase before normal or reduced thyroid function develops.

Graves disease.description: An autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism that can produce a diffuse, painless goiter and tachycardia. It is a less convincing explanation for this febrile presentation unless biochemical testing confirms significant hyperthyroidism.

Celiac disease.description: An immune-mediated response to gluten causing small-intestinal injury and malabsorption. The biopsy appears to show villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, supporting this diagnosis; confirmation requires serologic testing and clinical correlation.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation producing upper abdominal pain and elevated pancreatic enzymes. The presentation is suggestive, although enzyme values relative to the upper limit of normal and definitive pancreatic imaging findings are not provided.

Small-intestinal lymphoma.description: A malignancy of intestinal lymphoid tissue that can cause malabsorption, weight loss, abdominal pain, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. The CT findings make it a consideration, but the provided biopsy does not establish lymphoma.

Whipple disease.description: A systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can produce small-intestinal malabsorption and abdominal lymphadenopathy. Confirmation requires characteristic tissue findings and organism-specific testing.

Medication-induced enteropathy.description: Medication-related intestinal injury or intolerance can cause persistent diarrhea and weight loss; some drugs produce a sprue-like biopsy pattern. The specific cholesterol medication and other exposures would need review before attributing these findings to a drug.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.description: Dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a mucosal infection can cause migratory joint symptoms or septic arthritis. This is a leading consideration given the recent sexual exposure and acute joint inflammation. The supplied microbiology images show coccoid organisms, some paired, but species identification requires laboratory confirmation.

Nongonococcal bacterial septic arthritis.description: Direct bacterial infection of joints, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci. Multiple joints can be involved, and fever may be absent. This requires urgent exclusion through synovial fluid analysis and cultures; the microbiology images alone cannot establish the organism.

Sexually acquired reactive arthritis.description: Sterile inflammatory arthritis arising after a genitourinary infection, often Chlamydia trachomatis. It commonly affects lower-extremity joints within several weeks of infection.

Lyme arthritis.description: An inflammatory arthritis caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, usually occurring months after infection. Residence in New England increases exposure risk, but the typical presentation is intermittent swelling of one or a few large joints, especially a knee.

Acute gouty arthritis.description: Inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition. It can affect ankles and hand joints and may become oligoarticular, particularly in older adults. Confirmation requires identification of urate crystals in synovial fluid while also excluding infection.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Primary adrenal lymphoma, most commonly.normalized_text: Primary adrenal lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary adrenal lymphoma, most commonly.description: An aggressive lymphoma predominantly involving the adrenal glands, often bilaterally. The apparent bilateral adrenal masses and retroperitoneal infiltration make this a leading consideration; tissue biopsy is required for confirmation.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with.normalized_text: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with adrenal involvement
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with.description: A rare aggressive lymphoma in which malignant cells grow within small blood vessels. It can cause fever, cytopenias, high lactate dehydrogenase, and adrenal involvement without prominent lymphadenopathy.

Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral adrenal involvement
Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.description: Tuberculosis can spread to both adrenal glands, producing enlargement and sometimes adrenal failure. Disseminated infection may also affect the pleura, liver, and bone marrow.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with adrenal.description: A systemic fungal infection that may enlarge both adrenal glands and cause fever, hepatic abnormalities, and cytopenias. Confirmation requires fungal testing or tissue examination.

Bilateral pheochromocytomas.description: Tumors of adrenal chromaffin cells that may produce catecholamines. Bilateral tumors in a young adult raise the possibility of a hereditary syndrome, although the systemic laboratory findings here are less typical.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation.description: An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and vein that bypasses the capillary bed and causes a right-to-left shunt. This is the leading consideration given the apparent vascular sac and enlarged connecting vessels.

Peripheral pulmonary artery aneurysm.description: A focal dilation of a pulmonary arterial branch that can appear as an enhancing lung mass. CT angiography is needed to distinguish it from an arteriovenous malformation.

Pulmonary venous varix.description: A focal dilation of a pulmonary vein, either congenital or acquired, that can mimic a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation on imaging.

Systemic artery-to-pulmonary vessel fist.description: An abnormal communication between a systemic artery, such as a bronchial or intercostal artery, and a pulmonary artery or vein. High-flow connections may cause a chest bruit and respiratory symptoms.

Pulmonary sequestration.description: A congenital region of abnormal lung tissue supplied by a systemic artery, usually from the aorta. It can resemble a lung mass with prominent vessels but is less favored by the supplied images.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder that can form tissue around the abdominal aorta, ureters, and major veins. Venous compression can cause bilateral leg edema. The apparent periaortic soft-tissue thickening on the supplied CT and elevated IgG4 make this the leading consideration, although serum IgG4 alone is not diagnostic.

Idiopathic non-IgG4-related retroperiton.description: Fibrous inflammatory tissue develops in the retroperitoneum without an identified cause, potentially encasing the aorta, ureters, or iliocaval veins and producing obstructive complications.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes or soft tissues that can surround major vessels and obstruct venous drainage, mimicking retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Malignancy-associated retroperitoneal fi.description: A retroperitoneal fibrotic or infiltrative reaction caused by an underlying solid tumor, sometimes from metastatic carcinoma. It can resemble idiopathic fibrosis and compress central veins.

Erdheim-Chester disease.description: A rare non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder that can produce periaortic and perirenal infiltration resembling retroperitoneal fibrosis, occasionally compromising venous drainage.

Primary spontaneous left pneumothorax.description: Air enters the pleural space without trauma or known underlying lung disease, causing lung collapse. This is the leading possibility: the radiograph appears to show a large left pneumothorax. Prompt clinical assessment is necessary.

Secondary spontaneous left pneumothorax.description: Pleural air and lung collapse caused by underlying lung disease, which can occasionally be previously unrecognized.

Giant pulmonary bulla.description: A large air-filled space within the lung that compresses surrounding lung tissue and can resemble a pneumothorax on radiographs. CT may be needed if the distinction is uncertain.

Congenital lobar overinflation.description: Abnormal overexpansion of a pulmonary lobe due to impaired air outflow, potentially compressing adjacent lung. Presentation in adulthood is uncommon.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by a blood clot, which can cause sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. It is substantially less supported than pneumothorax in this case.

Acute rheumatic fever with carditis, pos.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic fever with carditis, possibly recurrent on chronic rheumatic heart disease
Acute rheumatic fever with carditis, pos.description: An immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal infection that causes migratory arthritis and cardiac inflammation. The echocardiographic images appear compatible with mitral valve disease and regurgitation; childhood dyspnea raises concern for preexisting rheumatic valve damage.

Infective endocarditis involving the mit.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis involving the mitral valve
Infective endocarditis involving the mit.description: Infection of a cardiac valve can produce fever, inflammatory joint symptoms, valve destruction, and heart failure. Underlying rheumatic valve disease would increase susceptibility, but these images alone do not establish vegetation or infection.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with cardia.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with cardiac involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with cardia.description: An autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, fever, and fatigue. Myocarditis or noninfectious valvular inflammation, including Libman-Sacks endocarditis, can occasionally cause cardiac dysfunction.

Viral myocarditis with associated viral.normalized_text: Viral myocarditis with associated viral arthritis
Viral myocarditis with associated viral.description: Viral infection can cause joint inflammation and myocardial injury, resulting in tachycardia and acute heart failure. Ventricular dysfunction can produce secondary mitral regurgitation.

Poststreptococcal reactive arthritis.description: Inflammatory arthritis following streptococcal infection that does not meet criteria for acute rheumatic fever. Arthritis is usually persistent or additive rather than migratory; significant concurrent valve disease would favor rheumatic fever or a separate cardiac disorder.

Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epi.normalized_text: Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epidural extension
Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epi.description: A benign vascular vertebral tumor that can extend into the spinal canal and compress nerve roots. The apparent coarse trabecular pattern, high T2 signal, and epidural and paravertebral extension make this a leading imaging consideration, although confirmation requires specialist review.

Vertebral metastasis with epidural exten.description: Cancer spreading to a vertebra can replace bone marrow and extend into adjacent soft tissues or the spinal canal. The vertebral signal abnormality and extraosseous tissue warrant consideration, although the apparent trabecular pattern may favor a hemangioma.

Solitary bone plasmacytoma.description: A localized tumor of plasma cells that commonly involves vertebrae and may produce an epidural or paravertebral mass. It is a possible alternative explanation for a dominant vertebral lesion, requiring laboratory evaluation and potentially biopsy.

Vertebral lymphoma with epidural involve.description: Lymphoma can infiltrate vertebral marrow and form substantial epidural or paravertebral soft tissue, sometimes with relatively preserved vertebral height. This is a less specific imaging alternative that would require tissue confirmation.

Giant cell tumor of the vertebra.normalized_text: Giant cell tumor of the vertebra
Giant cell tumor of the vertebra.description: A locally aggressive bone tumor that can involve a vertebral body and extend into the spinal canal. It is less favored because these tumors usually occur in younger adults and typically have a more expansile, lytic appearance.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.description: A malignant tumor of the lip epithelium that can resemble a persistent cold sore. A nonhealing lesion warrants prompt examination and biopsy; enlarged regional lymph nodes may indicate spread.

Chronic herpes simplex labialis.description: Herpes simplex virus infection causes lip blisters that ulcerate and crust. Persistence for months is unusual in an otherwise healthy person and may suggest underlying immunosuppression.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia.description: A blood cancer involving mature lymphocytes that can cause fatigue, lymph node enlargement, and impaired immunity with recurrent infections. Diagnosis requires blood testing, including a complete blood count and flow cytometry.

HIV infection with immunosuppression.description: HIV can impair immune function, leading to fatigue, lymphadenopathy, recurrent infections, and unusually prolonged herpes simplex ulcers. The photographs and history alone cannot establish HIV infection.

Primary oral syphilis.description: Syphilis can produce an oral or lip chancre with regional lymph node enlargement. Diagnosis requires serologic testing and, where available, direct testing of the lesion.

Chronic enteropathy associated with SLCO.description: A rare inherited disorder causing chronic small-intestinal ulceration, gastrointestinal blood and protein loss, and sometimes intestinal narrowing. Associated joint manifestations can occur. Confirmation requires exclusion of other causes and genetic testing.

Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosin.description: A rare small-intestinal disorder characterized by recurrent superficial ulcers and multiple strictures, often causing chronic blood loss and anemia without marked systemic inflammation.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any gastrointestinal segment and produce ulcers, strictures, intestinal bleeding, malnutrition, and inflammatory joint symptoms.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculous infection of the intestine, frequently involving the ileocecal region, that can cause ulceration, bowel-wall thickening, strictures, and nutritional impairment.

Whipple disease.description: A systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that commonly produces small-intestinal malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, and migratory arthralgia. Diagnosis requires tissue evaluation and organism-specific testing.

Dupuytren disease (palmar fibromatosis).description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that produces nodules and cords, progressively pulling fingers into fixed flexion. This is the most likely diagnosis.

Stenosing flexor tenosynovitis (trigger.description: Thickening of a flexor tendon or its pulley causes impaired tendon gliding, usually producing catching, locking, or pain; longstanding cases may develop flexion contractures.

Fibroma of the tendon sheath.description: A benign, slow-growing fibrous tumor attached to a tendon sheath, commonly occurring in the hand and occasionally limiting finger movement.

Localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor.description: A usually benign nodular tumor arising from tendon-associated synovial tissue, often presenting as a slowly enlarging finger mass that can restrict movement.

Camptodactyly.description: A congenital or developmental, sometimes inherited flexion deformity of the proximal interphalangeal joint, most commonly affecting the little finger.

Syphilitic lymphadenitis.description: Lymph-node inflammation caused by Treponema pallidum. The supplied histology appears to show numerous spirochete-shaped organisms, making this a leading possibility; confirmation requires identification of the stain and syphilis testing.

Lymphogranuloma venereum.description: An invasive infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3 that can cause painful inguinal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.

HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid proliferation, often an aggressive B-cell lymphoma, whose risk remains elevated in people with HIV despite effective antiretroviral therapy.

Mycobacterium avium complex lymphadeniti.description: An opportunistic mycobacterial infection that can involve lymph nodes or disseminate, particularly in patients with advanced HIV-related immunosuppression.

Bartonella henselae lymphadenitis.description: Cat-scratch disease is a bacterial infection causing regional lymphadenopathy, sometimes with suppurative inflammation and systemic symptoms; presentations may be atypical in people with HIV.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Primary osteosarcoma of the left fifth r.normalized_text: Primary osteosarcoma of the left fifth rib
Primary osteosarcoma of the left fifth r.description: A malignant bone tumor that produces osteoid. The rib-associated chest wall mass and apparent osteoid among atypical cells in the supplied histology make this a leading possibility, although specialist pathology review is necessary.

Ewing sarcoma of the rib.description: An aggressive bone or soft-tissue malignancy occurring predominantly in children and adolescents. Rib involvement can produce a chest wall mass and pleural effusion; typical histology consists of uniform small round cells rather than malignant osteoid.

Chondrosarcoma of the rib.description: A malignant cartilage-producing tumor that can arise in the chest wall and cause a painful rib mass. It is uncommon at age 16, and confirmation requires identification of malignant cartilage rather than osteoid.

Aneurysmal bone cyst of the rib.normalized_text: Aneurysmal bone cyst of the rib
Aneurysmal bone cyst of the rib.description: A benign, expansile bone lesion containing blood-filled spaces, usually occurring in younger patients. Rib lesions can cause pain or pathological fracture, but the supplied apparent cellular atypia and osteoid would favor a malignant lesion instead.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib
Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib.description: A disorder of abnormal Langerhans-cell proliferation that can produce a painful destructive rib lesion in children and adolescents. Diagnosis requires characteristic cellular morphology and immunohistochemistry; the supplied histology is not clearly typical.

Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.normalized_text: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can present as a splenic mass without peripheral lymphadenopathy. This is a leading consideration given the constitutional symptoms and apparent large atypical cells; confirmation requires tissue examination and identification of the immunohistochemical markers.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma involving the.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma involving the spleen
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma involving the.description: A lymphoid malignancy characterized by Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background. Splenic involvement can cause fever, night sweats, weight loss, and anemia, although isolated splenic disease is rare.

Splenic marginal zone lymphoma with poss.normalized_text: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma with possible large-cell transformation
Splenic marginal zone lymphoma with poss.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma predominantly affecting the spleen and bone marrow in older adults. Transformation to an aggressive large-cell lymphoma could explain severe constitutional symptoms and a focal splenic lesion.

Primary splenic histiocytic sarcoma.description: A rare aggressive malignancy of histiocytic cells that may involve the spleen and produce large atypical cells with abundant cytoplasm. Diagnosis requires a histiocytic immunophenotype and exclusion of lymphoma and other malignancies.

Splenic tuberculosis.description: An uncommon extrapulmonary tuberculosis presentation producing splenic granulomas or abscess-like lesions. Negative initial testing does not completely exclude it, but the apparent atypical-cell pathology makes malignancy more concerning.

Fabry disease with cardiac and renal inv.normalized_text: Fabry disease with cardiac and renal involvement
Fabry disease with cardiac and renal inv.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A, producing glycosphingolipid accumulation in the heart, kidneys, and other tissues. This is the leading diagnosis given the markedly reduced leukocyte enzyme activity.

Hypertensive heart disease with left ven.normalized_text: Hypertensive heart disease with left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive heart disease with left ven.description: Chronic hypertension can cause ventricular hypertrophy and impaired relaxation, predisposing to atrial fibrillation and myocardial injury during severe tachycardia.

Sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A usually inherited myocardial disorder characterized by ventricular hypertrophy not adequately explained by loading conditions, sometimes with outflow obstruction, diastolic dysfunction, and arrhythmias.

Cardiac amyloidosis.description: An infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by amyloid deposition, producing increased ventricular wall thickness, impaired filling, and arrhythmias. Some forms also cause proteinuric kidney disease.

Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.description: Acute myocardial ischemia with myocardial injury, potentially from coronary plaque disruption. Severe atrial fibrillation can alternatively cause supply-demand myocardial injury without an acute coronary blockage.

Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke, like.normalized_text: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke, likely involving the left middle cerebral artery territory
Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke, like.description: A focal interruption of cerebral arterial blood flow around birth. The supplied MRI appears to show focal left-sided diffusion restriction, making acute arterial infarction the leading possibility; definitive interpretation requires the complete imaging study.

Neonatal cerebral sinovenous thrombosis.normalized_text: Neonatal cerebral sinovenous thrombosis with venous infarction
Neonatal cerebral sinovenous thrombosis.description: Thrombosis of cerebral veins or dural sinuses can cause focal brain injury and neonatal seizures. MR venography is needed to assess this possibility; the supplied arterial angiographic images do not exclude it.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Brain injury from inadequate oxygen delivery or cerebral perfusion around delivery. Early seizures and fetal distress can fit, but the reassuring neonatal condition and apparently focal imaging abnormality make this less likely than stroke.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage.description: Bleeding within or around the brain can irritate the cortex and produce focal neonatal seizures. Susceptibility-sensitive MRI or other appropriate imaging is necessary to identify blood products.

Self-limited neonatal epilepsy.description: An early-life epilepsy syndrome, sometimes associated with KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 variants, characterized by brief recurrent seizures in otherwise well newborns. A structural cerebral lesion argues against this diagnosis.

Takayasu arteritis with aortic regurgita.normalized_text: Takayasu arteritis with aortic regurgitation and acute heart failure
Takayasu arteritis with aortic regurgita.description: Large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, most often in young women. The images suggest diffuse aortic and branch-vessel wall thickening, branch-vessel narrowing, and substantial aortic regurgitation, making this the leading possibility.

Infective endocarditis with severe aorti.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with severe aortic regurgitation
Infective endocarditis with severe aorti.description: Infection of a cardiac valve can damage its leaflets and cause acute regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and systemic emboli. Blood cultures and detailed valve imaging would be needed to establish this diagnosis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with aortit.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with aortitis and valvular involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with aortit.description: An autoimmune disease that can cause sterile valvular lesions, regurgitation, and, rarely, inflammation of the aorta. It is a less likely alternative to primary large-vessel vasculitis in this case.

IgG4-related aortitis and periaortitis.description: A fibroinflammatory disorder that can produce thickening around the aorta and other arteries. Its vascular imaging findings can resemble large-vessel vasculitis, although it is very unusual in a 19-year-old woman.

Bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic.normalized_text: Bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic regurgitation and associated aortopathy
Bicuspid aortic valve with severe aortic.description: A congenital two-leaflet aortic valve can become incompetent and may coexist with ascending-aortic disease. Severe regurgitation can cause heart failure, but this would not adequately explain diffuse inflammatory arterial changes.

Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis.description: A clot in the vein draining the small intestine, potentially causing intestinal congestion and ischemia. The arrowed mesenteric venous filling defect on the supplied CT appears most consistent with this diagnosis, although formal radiological confirmation is needed.

Portal vein thrombosis.description: Thrombosis of the portal vein, sometimes extending from the superior mesenteric vein. The second CT image appears to show a portal venous filling defect, making combined portomesenteric thrombosis a significant possibility.

Acute pancreatitis, potentially medicati.description: Inflammation of the pancreas causing upper abdominal pain and nausea. Recent orlistat exposure warrants consideration of a possible medication association, but normal pancreatic enzymes and the apparent vascular CT abnormalities make this diagnosis less likely.

Mesenteric panniculitis.description: Inflammation of mesenteric fat that can produce abdominal pain and increased inflammatory markers. It can cause mesenteric haziness on CT, but true intravascular filling defects would favor thrombosis instead.

Acute sigmoid diverticulitis.description: Inflammation of sigmoid colonic diverticula, usually producing left lower abdominal pain and inflammatory marker elevation. It could explain the left iliac fossa tenderness, but the dominant epigastric symptoms and apparent venous CT abnormalities favor another diagnosis.

Imperforate hymen with hematocolpos.description: A congenital blockage of the vaginal opening causes menstrual blood to accumulate in the vagina, sometimes extending into the uterus. The images appear to show a large pelvic fluid collection with internal echoes, favoring retained blood, although examination is needed to establish the obstruction.

Transverse vaginal septum with hematocol.description: A congenital partition across the vagina can obstruct menstrual outflow and produce a blood-filled, distended vagina. It can resemble an imperforate hymen clinically and on ultrasound.

Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.normalized_text: Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly syndrome
Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.description: A congenital reproductive tract anomaly, typically involving a duplicated uterus and obstruction of one vaginal compartment, causes retained menstrual blood and pelvic pain. Associated renal abnormalities and uterine duplication must be assessed; neither is established by these images.

Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion associated with an ovarian cyst
Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.description: Twisting of the ovarian vascular pedicle can compromise blood supply and requires urgent assessment. An ovarian cyst can predispose to torsion, but these still images do not establish ovarian origin or assess blood flow.

Acute appendicitis.description: Inflammation of the appendix causes progressive abdominal pain, sometimes localized to the hypogastrium when the appendix lies in the pelvis. The supplied images do not demonstrate an inflamed appendix.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (11p11.2 deleti.description: The strongest diagnostic fit: a contiguous-gene deletion syndrome characterized by multiple osteochondromas, enlarged parietal foramina, developmental impairment, and craniofacial abnormalities. The supplied microarray appears to show a deletion encompassing EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A, supporting this diagnosis despite a normal conventional karyotype.

Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II (.description: A contiguous-gene deletion disorder involving TRPS1 and EXT1 on chromosome 8, causing multiple osteochondromas, short stature, characteristic facial features, sparse hair, and variable intellectual disability. It is an important clinical alternative, but the supplied chromosome 11 deletion favors Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.

Hereditary multiple osteochondromas.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, producing multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the growth plates. It explains the skeletal lesions but does not ordinarily explain the neurological and cranial findings.

ALX4-related enlarged parietal foramina.description: A genetic skull-ossification disorder, usually caused by a heterozygous ALX4 pathogenic variant, characterized by paired defects in the parietal bones. Isolated ALX4-related disease explains the skull findings but not the full multisystem presentation.

PHF21A-related neurodevelopmental disord.description: A disorder caused by PHF21A haploinsufficiency, associated with developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and craniofacial abnormalities. Isolated PHF21A involvement could explain much of the neurological phenotype, but additional deletion of EXT2 and ALX4 better explains the complete case.

Atypical ulcerative scabies.description: Infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei that can present atypically in immunocompromised patients, with minimal itching and ulcerated or crusted lesions. The mite shown within the stratum corneum strongly supports this diagnosis.

Bacterial ecthyma.description: A deeper bacterial skin infection, usually caused by streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, producing crusted ulcers. It could complicate an underlying scabies infestation.

Pyoderma gangrenosum.description: An inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis causing progressive ulcers, often associated with myelodysplastic syndromes and other hematologic disorders.

Cutaneous fusariosis.description: An opportunistic Fusarium fungal infection that can produce multiple necrotic skin lesions in patients with neutropenia or hematologic malignancy.

Sweet syndrome.description: An acute neutrophilic dermatosis associated with myeloid disorders and sometimes G-CSF exposure. It usually produces tender erythematous plaques, with ulceration occurring in atypical cases.

Collapsing glomerulopathy.description: An aggressive pattern of podocyte injury characterized by collapse of glomerular capillaries and proliferation of overlying epithelial cells. The supplied biopsy image raises this possibility, although additional stains and pathology review are needed to distinguish it from crescentic glomerulonephritis.

ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic gl.description: A rapidly progressive inflammatory kidney disease with crescent formation and little or no immune deposition. It can be confined to the kidneys and occur despite negative ANCA testing.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune disease causing rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis, sometimes accompanied by pulmonary hemorrhage. Kidney-limited disease is possible; confirmation requires anti-GBM antibody testing and assessment for linear IgG staining on biopsy.

Crescentic IgA nephropathy.description: An immune-complex glomerular disease caused by predominantly mesangial IgA deposition. A severe crescentic variant can cause rapidly progressive kidney failure in adolescents and young adults.

Infection-related crescentic glomerulone.description: Immune-mediated glomerular inflammation associated with a recent or ongoing infection. Severe cases can develop crescents and rapidly progressive renal failure.

Isolated myeloid sarcoma of the bile duc.normalized_text: Isolated myeloid sarcoma of the bile duct
Isolated myeloid sarcoma of the bile duc.description: An extramedullary tumor of immature myeloid cells that can obstruct the bile duct even when blood counts and bone marrow are normal. This is a leading consideration; confirmation requires myeloid markers such as myeloperoxidase, CD33, CD117, and lysozyme.

Primary biliary diffuse large B-cell lym.normalized_text: Primary biliary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary biliary diffuse large B-cell lym.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma rarely arising in or around the bile ducts and causing obstructive jaundice. CD20, PAX5, and other B-cell markers are needed to assess this possibility.

Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the.normalized_text: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the bile duct
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the.description: An indolent mature B-cell lymphoma that can rarely involve biliary tissue and produce a localized stricture. Diagnosis requires characteristic morphology and confirmation of B-cell lineage.

Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising near the hepatic bile duct confluence, commonly producing a hilar stricture and obstructive jaundice. It is an important imaging differential but is strongly disfavored by the reported tumor immunophenotype.

Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliar.normalized_text: Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliary tract
Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliar.description: A rare malignant tumor showing mature histiocytic differentiation that can arise outside lymph nodes. Confirmation requires markers such as CD163, CD68, and lysozyme, with exclusion of myeloid and lymphoid tumors.
